exp.0:2:
This verse says that God blesses, that is, fills with happiness, the one who reads this book aloud, those who hear it, and those who obey what is written in it. "Prophecy" here means a message from God. "The time is near" means that what is announced is urgent and that it is not wise to put it off until later.

John writes to seven churches in Asia, and what he passes on is the revelation that Jesus Christ gave him. In that time, the book was read aloud at gatherings, which is why the reader and those who listen are both mentioned. Christians faced pressure and persecution and needed hope. There are different ways of understanding how these things will come to pass, but all of them agree on the call to faithfulness.

For today: do not stop at reading or listening. Choose one truth from the Word and put it into practice this week, for example by forgiving, by being faithful, or by trusting God.
exp.0:13:
This verse describes the head and hair of Jesus as bright white, like white wool and like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, meaning intense and piercing.

John is on the island of Patmos and sees Christ in his glory standing among seven lampstands, which represent the churches. White is usually understood as purity, eternity and wisdom; it recalls the image of the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9. The eyes of fire are understood as his gaze that sees everything and examines it. Some interpreters give these details different nuances, but all agree that they show his holiness and authority.

For today: Jesus sees you completely and loves you. You can come to Him with sincerity, without pretending, trusting that His gaze also purifies and heals.
exp.0:14:
John describes the risen and glorious Jesus. His feet shine like polished brass, a metal resembling bronze, and they glow as metal does when it is heated in a furnace. His voice sounds like the rushing of many waters, like a waterfall or the sea in a great storm. It is not a weak voice but a powerful one that cannot be ignored.

The one speaking is John, who writes what he saw on the island of Patmos. He tells seven churches that were going through hardships what Jesus is really like. Feet of bronze are usually understood as firmness and judgment, though some interpret them in other ways. The image is meant to show his authority.

For today: when you feel weak or confused, remember that Jesus is firm and powerful. Listen to his voice in the Bible above other voices, and trust that he sustains his Church.
exp.0:16:
It says that John, when he saw Jesus in all his glory, fell to the ground as if he were dead. Then Jesus laid his right hand upon him and told him not to be afraid. He reminded him that he is "the first and the last," meaning that he existed before all things and will remain after all things.

The one speaking here is the risen Jesus Christ. John, already an old man and exiled on Patmos, receives this vision and is overcome with fear before the holiness and power of Jesus. Many understand that "the first and the last" shows the divinity of Christ and his control over history. Jesus says this to comfort John before giving him the message for the churches.

For today: when you feel fear or feel small in the face of your problems, remember that Jesus is still the first and the last, and that his hand is upon you with tenderness. You can pray calmly, trusting that he sustains your life.
exp.1:1:
Jesus tells the church in Ephesus that he knows everything they do. He recognizes their hard work and their endurance. He also praises them because they do not put up with evil people, and because they tested those who claimed to be apostles without being apostles, and discovered that they were liars. The word "tolerate" here means to bear with or put up with.

He is the one speaking, the one who holds the seven stars and walks among the golden lampstands. He writes to a church that worked hard to hold on to the truth. First he commends them, although he will soon rebuke them for leaving their first love. Exactly who those false apostles were is not known for certain.

Today we can learn to test what is taught against the Bible, without ceasing to love God and people. Defending the truth is good, but it must come from love.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that the church in Ephesus has something good: it rejects the deeds of the Nicolaitans, and Jesus also rejects them. Little is known about the Nicolaitans; many think they were a group that tolerated immorality and idolatry, but there is no certainty.

Jesus, risen, speaks through John to a church that worked hard and defended the truth, but had lost its first love. Before correcting it, Jesus acknowledges what it does well. His rejection of evil shows that his love has clear limits.

For today: reject what God rejects, but do not let your firmness cool your heart. Make sure your defense of the truth springs from love for Christ, not merely from habit or pride.
exp.1:6:
He who has an ear should listen carefully to what the Holy Spirit says to the churches. To the one who overcomes, God will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.

The one speaking is Jesus, who addresses this message to the church in Ephesus. He had praised them for rejecting what was evil, but he asked them to return to their first love and their first works. The promise recalls the tree of life in Eden (Genesis 2), and suggests that God offers a full and lasting life with him. Scholars understand in various ways who the Nicolaitans were, since the text gives few details.

Today we can examine whether we still love Christ with the same simplicity we had at the beginning. A sincere prayer and an act of service this week can be a good first step toward returning.
exp.1:9:
Jesus tells the church in Smyrna not to be afraid of what is coming. The devil will cause some of them to be thrown into prison, so that they will be tested, and they will suffer tribulation for ten days. Those who are faithful even to death will receive from Jesus the crown of life.

Christ speaks here, the one who died and came back to life. Smyrna was a poor church, persecuted and slandered by those who claimed to be Jews. The ten days may refer to a short and limited period of time, though some understand it in a different way. Jesus knows their suffering and does not promise to prevent it, but he does promise a certain end.

For today: when your faith costs you something, remember that Jesus already knows your situation. Today, for example, you can choose to be honest even when it hurts you, trusting that he sustains you and will reward you.
exp.1:10:
He who has ears ready should listen carefully to what the Holy Spirit teaches the churches. He promises that the one who overcomes, that is, the one who remains faithful despite trials, will not be harmed by the second death.

Jesus is speaking to the Christians of Smyrna, who suffered poverty, slander, and persecution. He asked them to be faithful even to death. The second death appears later in Revelation as the final separation from God (20:14). Even if a believer dies physically, that final death will not be able to touch him.

For today: when faith costs you something, remember that Christ sees your effort and sustains you. Ask him today for strength to remain faithful in one specific thing.
exp.1:11:
Jesus tells John to write a letter to the church in Pergamos, a city in Asia Minor. The word "angel" can refer to a messenger or to the one who led the church; it is understood in several ways. Jesus presents himself as the one who has the sharp sword with two edges, an image of his word that judges and cuts with precision.

The one speaking is the risen Christ, and he speaks as judge and Lord of his church. In the verses that follow he praises her for remaining faithful in a very hostile place, but he also calls her attention to tolerating teachings that mixed faith with idolatry and immorality. That is why he presents himself with that sword: his word encourages, but it also corrects.

For today: let the Word of God examine you with sincerity. Ask him to show you where you are firm and where you have accepted things that do not please him, and respond with humility.
exp.1:16:
He who has an ear should pay attention to what the Spirit teaches the churches. To the one who overcomes, Jesus promises hidden manna to eat, a small white stone, and on it a new name that only the one who receives it knows.

Jesus speaks, through John, to the church at Pergamum. There some tolerated false teachings and lived with a mixture of faith and pagan customs. Jesus calls them to repent and promises care to the faithful. The manna recalls how God sustained Israel in the wilderness. About the small white stone there are several interpretations: acceptance, absolution, or a special entrance. The general sense is an intimate and personal relationship with Christ.

Today, when it is hard to remain faithful, remember that Jesus knows you personally and promises to sustain you. Seek his nourishment in the Word and do not settle for what the world offers.
exp.1:17:
This verse begins the letter to the church in Thyatira. Jesus presents himself as "the Son of God," with eyes like a flame of fire and feet like fine brass, a bright metal, similar to polished and refined bronze. "The angel of the church" can be understood as a messenger or a leader of that congregation; it is interpreted in several ways.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, who addresses a real church in a city known for its trades and its commerce. His eyes of fire suggest that he sees everything clearly, and his firm, shining feet speak of his authority and his just judgment. This prepares the way for the praise and the correction that come next.

For today: Christ sees our lives from within, and that is both a comfort and a reason for seriousness. We can ask him to show us where we need to change, and to continue with humility in the good we already do.
exp.1:19:
It says that Jesus rebukes the church in Thyatira because it tolerates a woman who calls herself a prophetess and teaches false things. Her teachings lead believers into sexual immorality and to eating what has been offered to idols.

Jesus himself is speaking, the Son of God, whose eyes see everything. He has just praised that church for its love, its service, its faith, and its patience, but now he corrects its tolerance.

The name Jezebel is probably a symbolic one, taken from the queen who in the Old Testament promoted idolatry in Israel. We do not know what her real name was.

For today: one can be loving and still need firmness. Love does not mean accepting every teaching. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible and, with humility, correct whatever pulls others away from God.
exp.2:0:
This verse opens the letter to the church in Sardis. Jesus presents himself as the one who has "the seven Spirits of God" and "the seven stars." Then he says that he knows what they do: they have a reputation for being alive, but in reality they are dead. The word "write" is a command given to John, and "angel" here can mean messenger or leader, though it is interpreted in several ways.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus Christ, who addresses seven churches in Revelation. The "seven Spirits" are usually understood as the Holy Spirit in his fullness, and the "seven stars" are explained in 1:20 as the angels of the churches. He rebukes Sardis because it had a good reputation but little true spiritual life.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith is real or only appearance. It is good to ask God to show us where we are asleep, and to return to what we have heard from Christ, with sincerity and obedience.
exp.2:2:
Jesus tells the church to remember what they received and heard, that is, the message of the gospel. He asks them to obey it and to change their ways. If they do not, He will come upon them unexpectedly, like a thief in the night, and they will not know when.

The one speaking is the risen Christ, who knows the works of the church in Sardis. He tells them they have a reputation for being alive, but they are spiritually dead. He does not correct them to shame them, but to wake them up. Some faithful believers still remained, and Jesus recognizes them.

For today: do not live on appearances or on memories of your past faith. Take a moment today to return to the Word you were taught, acknowledge before God where you have grown drowsy, and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.2:3:
It says that in the church of Sardis, although almost all of it was spiritually dead, there were a few people who had not dirtied their clothes, that is, who had lived with faithfulness and purity. Jesus promises that they will walk with him dressed in white, because they are worthy.

It speaks of the risen Jesus, in his letter to the church in Sardis. He had called them to wake up, repent, and return to what they had received, because they had a reputation for being alive but their works were incomplete. Even so, he sees and recognizes the faithful. White is usually understood as a symbol of purity and victory.

For today: even if you are one of the few who faithfully follow God in your surroundings, Jesus sees you. Ask him for help to stay firm and clean in heart, without letting yourself be carried along by custom or by appearances.
exp.2:6:
Jesus speaks to the church in Philadelphia, a city in Asia Minor. He presents himself with three descriptions: he is holy, pure and set apart from evil; he is true, faithful and genuine; and he is the one who holds the key of David, meaning the authority to open and to shut. What he opens, no one can shut, and what he shuts, no one can open.

The one speaking is the risen Christ, addressing a small church with little strength, yet a faithful one. The key of David calls to mind Isaiah 22:22, where the language points to royal authority. Jesus shows himself as the King who decides which doors open, and that is why the promise that follows is of an open door.

For today: if you are in a season of little strength or of closed doors, trust that Jesus is in control. Remain faithful to his word, and wait for his timing.
exp.2:7:
Jesus tells the church in Philadelphia that he knows everything they do. He lets them know that he has placed before them an open door that no one can shut. He acknowledges that they have little strength, but even so they have kept his word and have not denied his name.

The one speaking is Jesus, described as the Holy One and the True One, the one who holds the key of David and opens and shuts with authority. He writes to a small church, probably with few resources, to encourage it. The "open door" is usually understood as an opportunity to serve or to proclaim the gospel, though some also see it as access to his kingdom.

For today: even if you feel weak or short on strength, God values your faithfulness. Keep obeying and trusting him, and let him be the one who opens or closes the doors.
exp.2:17:
Jesus advises the church in Laodicea to buy from him gold refined by fire, that is, pure gold, which represents a true and tested faith. He also offers white garments to cover their shame, and eye salve so that they can see. The word "counsel" here means to advise with seriousness.

Jesus speaks in the letter to Laodicea as the risen Lord. That city was known for its wealth, its textile industry and, according to many scholars, for a school of medicine and an eye salve. They thought they had enough, but Jesus sees them as poor, blind and naked. His correction comes from his love.

For today: ask Jesus to show you honestly where you feel self-sufficient. Then come to him in prayer and with the Bible, and let him give you what you cannot give yourself.
exp.2:20:
Jesus promises that whoever overcomes, that is, whoever remains faithful in spite of trials, will receive the honor of sitting with him on his throne. He compares this to his own victory: he overcame and is now seated with his Father.

The one speaking is the risen Christ, addressing the church in Laodicea. It was a lukewarm, comfortable, self-sufficient church. He corrects it out of love and invites it to open the door to him. This promise closes his message to that church. How exactly this reign with Christ will be fulfilled is understood in several ways, but all agree that it is a great honor.

Today we can respond to Jesus' invitation: leave indifference behind, open our hearts to him, and remain faithful each day, trusting that his victory sustains us.
exp.3:1:
And immediately John was taken up in the Spirit, that is, under the guidance and power of God's Spirit. There he saw a throne set in heaven and someone sitting on it.

The speaker is John, who writes down what he saw. A voice like a trumpet had invited him to come up and be shown what would take place afterward. He does not describe the one seated with human features, but with images of light and precious stones. Almost everyone understands this to be God in his glory, although people debate how each symbol should be interpreted.

For today: even when the world seems out of control, the throne in heaven is occupied. Today you can bring your fears and your decisions to God in prayer, trusting that he rules and remains faithful.
exp.3:7:
Each of them has six wings and is full of eyes. Without rest, day and night, they proclaim: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was, who is, and who is to come."

John is recounting a vision of God's throne in heaven. The living beings are creatures that surround the throne, and their song is continuous worship. The eyes and wings are often understood as symbols of complete sight and constant service, although interpreters explain their meaning in different ways. Afterward, the twenty-four elders join in this worship.

For today: the holiness of God deserves our attention and reverence. Before you ask or speak, take a moment simply to acknowledge who God is, thank him, and worship him in simplicity, remembering that he is faithful yesterday, today, and forever.
exp.3:10:
This verse says that God is worthy to receive glory, honor, and power. The reason is simple: he created all things, and everything exists because he willed it. The word "power" here means strength or might. The verse uses the word "created" to mean that he made things, and the phrase "exist" means that they are.

The ones speaking are the twenty-four elders, who stand before the throne of God in John's vision. They fall down, worship, and cast their crowns before the throne, as a sign that all the authority they have comes from God. Exactly who the elders are is interpreted in various ways; many think they represent the people of God, but the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: remember that your life and everything you have are a gift from God. Today, before asking him for anything, take a moment to thank him and praise him simply for who he is and for having created you.
exp.4:0:
Here John tells us that he saw, in the right hand of God, who sits on the throne, a book, or scroll. It was written on the inside and the outside, and it was closed with seven seals. "Sealed" means closed with marked wax or clay, so that no one could open it without permission. The number seven usually points to something complete.

John speaks here as one who receives this vision from heaven. He is describing the scene around God's throne. What the book contains is not explained in this verse; many believe it is God's plan to judge and redeem the world, though it is understood in several different ways. The angel later asks who is worthy to open it.

For today: even when the world seems confused, the book is in God's hand, not in the hands of chance. You can rest and trust that he holds the course of history and of your life.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that John saw a powerful angel calling out with a loud voice a question: who deserves to open the book and break its seals? The word for "proclaiming" here means announcing or declaring aloud. "Worthy" means having the right and the standing to do it.

John is in a vision of heaven. God is seated on the throne and holds in his hand a book, or scroll, sealed with seven seals. Many understand it to represent God's plans for history and his kingdom, though some interpret it in other ways. The angel asks the question so that everyone can hear it, and right away it becomes clear that no one in all creation can open it. That is why John weeps. Later, Christ, the Lamb, will appear.

For today: when you feel that you do not understand what is happening in the world or in your life, remember that you are not the one who must open that book. Rest in Jesus, the only one who is worthy, and trust that He is in control.
exp.4:2:
It says that no one in the whole universe, neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth, had the authority to open the sealed book or even to look inside it. "Under the earth" probably refers to the place of the dead.

John is recounting his vision of God's throne. The book, or scroll, in God's hand is usually understood as God's plan to judge and redeem the world, although some interpret it in other ways. An angel asks who is worthy, and the silence of everyone shows that no creature is. That is why John weeps, until someone announces Christ, the Lion of Judah.

When you find yourself at a dead end or without answers, remember that you do not have to control the future. Rest in Jesus, the only one who is worthy, who holds history and your life in his hands.
exp.4:3:
John says that he wept greatly because no one was found worthy to open the book, or to read it, or even to look at it. "Worthy" means having the right and the value to do so. "Found" simply means discovered.

John, the author, is speaking during a vision of heaven. He has just seen a book with seven seals in the hand of God, and an angel asks who is able to open it. No one answers. Many understand the book to represent God's plans for history, though some interpret it in other ways. His weeping shows how much he longs for those plans to move forward. Soon after, an elder tells him not to weep, because Jesus, the Lion and the Lamb, has overcome.

When you feel sorrow because you see no way out or no justice, bring that pain honestly to God. Weeping is not a lack of faith, and Christ is worthy to hold what you cannot resolve.
exp.4:5:
And I saw, in the middle of the throne, among the four living creatures and among the elders, a Lamb that seemed to have been slain. It had seven horns and seven eyes, which are explained as the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth. Horns are usually understood as a symbol of power, and eyes as a symbol of complete knowledge.

John weeps because no one was able to open the book. One of the elders announces a Lion of Judah, but what John sees is a Lamb. In this way the text shows that Jesus conquers through His self-giving. Interpreters explain "the seven Spirits" in various ways, but they all agree that they speak of the full work of God.

For today: when you feel that nothing has a way out, remember that Christ reigns and that His self-giving love is His greatest strength. Trust in Him.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that the Lamb came forward and received the scroll from the right hand of God, who is seated on the throne. The word "scroll" refers to a written roll. The right hand usually represents power and authority.

John is recounting his vision. Before this, he was weeping because no one could open the scroll. An elder told him that the Lion of Judah had triumphed, but John saw a Lamb that looked as if it had been slain, that is, as if it had been sacrificed. Many understand that both images point to Jesus. The contents of the scroll are interpreted in several ways, but here the emphasis is that only Christ is worthy to receive it.

For today: when life or the future seems confusing, remember that history is not out of control. Jesus, who gave his life for you, holds authority. You can rest in him and trust.
exp.4:7:
Each one holds a harp and golden bowls full of incense. The text explains that this incense stands for the prayers of the saints, that is, the people of God.

Context: John describes a vision of heaven. The Lamb, who is Christ, has just received the sealed book from the hand of God. The beings around the throne respond with worship, and soon they sing that he is worthy because he was slain and redeemed people from every nation. Who exactly the elders are is interpreted in several different ways.

For today: Your prayers, even the simplest or weakest ones, are not lost. God receives them as something precious, like perfume. Pray with confidence and keep worshiping Christ.
exp.4:11:
The angels say with a loud voice that Jesus, called the Lamb that was slain (sacrificed), is worthy to receive power, riches, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and praise. The phrase "was slain" speaks of his death as a sacrifice. "Worthy" means that he has every right and all the value to receive it.

Many angels surround God's throne, together with the living creatures and the elders. Shortly before, the redeemed sang that Christ with his blood bought people for God. Now the angels join that praise. Then all creation adds its voice and worships. The Lamb is honoured precisely because he gave himself.

Today we can praise Jesus not only for what he gives us, but for who he is and for what he did on the cross. This week, set aside a few minutes to give thanks to him aloud, acknowledging that he is worthy.
exp.5:5:
Barley, which was cheaper, was given in greater quantity. And the voice asks that the wine and the oil not be harmed, since these were more luxurious products.

The voice comes from the midst of the four living creatures, near the throne of God. It appears when the third seal is opened, with the black horse and the scales. Many understand that it shows hunger and scarcity, which often follow war. Some also see economic injustice. The voice is not clearly identified, and it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: even in times of crisis, God still has control. This encourages us to trust Him and to share what we have with those who are in need.
exp.5:8:
This verse describes what John sees when the fifth seal is opened: under the altar are the souls of people who were killed for believing in the word of God and for holding firmly to their witness.

John, in his vision in Revelation, sees Jesus open the seals one after another. After the riders who bring war, famine and death, the view now turns to heaven. The verses that follow show these martyrs asking how long it will be before God brings justice. Interpreters differ on when and how this will be fulfilled, but all of them see that God does not forget his own.

For today: if you suffer for staying faithful to God, you are not forgotten. You can bring your pain to him honestly, trusting that he sees and will bring justice in his time.
exp.5:11:
John says he saw when the sixth seal was opened, and there was a great earthquake. The sun turned black like sackcloth, a rough, dark cloth made of goat hair, worn in times of mourning. The moon became completely like blood, that is, red.

John is recounting his vision from the book of Revelation. Shortly before, the martyrs were crying out for justice, and God told them to wait. Now impressive signs begin in creation. Some believe these describe the end of time; others see them as symbolic language showing God's judgment. Christians have understood them in different ways.

For today: even when it sometimes seems that injustice wins, God is not absent and does not forget his own. We can wait with patience, remain faithful to Jesus, and trust that he will bring about justice in his time.
exp.5:12:
It says the stars of heaven fall to the earth, like unripe figs dropping from a fig tree when a strong wind shakes it. The image here is of the fig tree losing its fruit before its time. The word "shaken" in the verse above is the one that means being moved by the wind.

John writes down what Jesus showed him in a vision. When the sixth seal is opened, huge signs appear in creation: an earthquake, a dark sun, a red moon. Many believe this describes God's judgment at the end of history. Others see symbolic language, like that of the prophets, speaking of the fall of human powers. People debate how to interpret it, but the tone is one of solemn judgment.

For today: nothing that seems firm in this world is eternal. Today we can place our trust in Christ, live with humility, and not put off making peace with God until tomorrow.
exp.5:14:
This verse names seven groups of people: kings, princes, the rich, commanders, the strong, slaves, and free people. All of them do the same thing: they hide in caves and among the rocks of the mountains. "Rocks" here means large boulders, and "commanders" means military leaders. The list covers everyone, from the most powerful to the most humble.

Here John speaks, recounting what he saw when the sixth seal was opened. There are earthquakes and signs in the sky, and the people feel terror before God's judgment. Some understand this as something still in the future, and others see in it images of divine judgment in general. What stands out is that no social rank protects anyone.

For today: let us not place our security in money, power, or position. Let us seek refuge in God now, trusting in Christ, and live with humility before him.
exp.5:15:
They say that the people, terrified, ask the mountains and the rocks to fall on them and hide them. They want to flee from the gaze of God, the one who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, who is Jesus Christ.

The inhabitants of the earth, from kings down to slaves, are the ones speaking, when the sixth seal is opened. They see signs in the sky and on the earth, and they recognize that the day of God's judgment has arrived. Their cry shows fear, not repentance. Some scholars see here a future event and others see symbolic language; the Bible presents it as something very serious.

For today: let us not wait until we are afraid to seek God. Today we can draw near to Christ with confidence, for in Him there is forgiveness and we do not need to hide.
exp.6:0:
John sees four angels standing at the four corners of the earth. They hold back the four winds so that no wind blows on the earth, the sea, or the trees. It is as if the world were in a pause before the storm.

John, who receives visions of Jesus in the book of Revelation, speaks here. This scene comes after the seals of judgment in chapter 6 and before God marks his servants. The winds are usually understood as judgments or calamities, though some see them differently. What is clear is that God controls the timing and protects his own.

For today: when the world seems out of control, remember that God still governs. Rest in the knowledge that He knows His people and cares for them.
exp.6:1:
Here John sees another angel rising from where the sun comes up, that is, the east. This angel carries the seal of the living God. A seal was like an official mark that showed ownership and protection. The angel cries out loudly to the four angels who had been given permission to harm the earth and the sea.

John is the one who recounts the vision. The four angels were holding back the winds, which many understand as judgments or calamities. The angel with the seal gives the command to wait, because the servants of God will be marked first. Some see in this a spiritual protection, and others debate exactly who the hundred and forty-four thousand are.

For today: even when the world seems unstable, God cares for his own and keeps track of the times. You can rest in the knowledge that you belong to him and bring him your fears with confidence.
exp.6:2:
This verse says that an angel tells four other angels not to harm the earth, the sea, or the trees. They must wait until we have sealed the servants of God on their foreheads, that is, put a mark or seal there.

The angel who comes up from the east, bearing the seal of the living God, speaks. The four angels already had permission to harm, but they are asked to pause. Before the judgments arrive, God marks his people. Interpreters debate whether this mark is literal or symbolic, and whether the 144,000 are Israelites or represent all of God's people. The text indicates that it is a mark of belonging and care.

For today: in the middle of an uncertain world, you can trust that God knows and cares for his own. Today, bring your fears to him in prayer.
exp.6:3:
John tells us that he heard the number of those who were sealed, that is, marked with a seal. There were 144,000, taken from all the tribes of Israel. Here "sealed" means being marked with a sign that shows belonging and protection.

An angel bearing the seal of the living God called for the harm upon the earth and the sea to be held back until the servants of God were marked on their foreheads. Christians understand this number in different ways: some take it as a literal group of Israelites; others, as a symbolic number representing the whole people of God. The Bible does not make this fully clear, and so it is wise to read it with humility.

Even in times of trial, God knows His own and cares for them. You can rest in the fact that you belong to Him and bring your fears to Him, knowing that He does not forget you.
exp.6:4:
It says that of three tribes of Israel, Judah, Reuben and Gad, twelve thousand were "sealed" from each one. "Sealed" means marked, like when something is marked to show that it belongs to someone. It is part of a longer list that adds up to one hundred and forty-four thousand.

John reports what he heard in his vision. An angel asks that the earth, the sea and the trees not be harmed until the servants of God are marked on the forehead. Then John hears the number. Some believe it is a literal figure and others that it is symbolic, representing the whole people of God. Christians have understood this in several ways.

For today: God knows and cares for his own, one by one, even in difficult times. You can rest knowing that you belong to him and that no one is forgotten.
exp.6:6:
This verse continues the list of the tribes of Israel. It names Simeon, Levi, and Issachar, and of each one it says that twelve thousand were sealed, meaning marked as belonging to God. Levi appears in this list, though it was not usually counted among the tribes, and Dan is missing.

John writes what he saw in a vision. Before the final judgments, God seals his servants to protect them. Many believe the number is symbolic and represents the whole people of God; others take it literally. Christians have understood it in several ways, and there is no single position.

For today: God knows and cares for his own, one by one. If you belong to Christ, you can trust that he keeps you safe in difficult times, and you can rest in that promise today.
exp.6:9:
This verse says that a great crowd was crying out with a loud voice that salvation belongs to God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb. The word "salvation" here is a shout of praise: they recognize that God rescued them. "Lamb" is a title of Jesus.

The great company of Revelation 7:9 is speaking: people from every nation, tribe, people and language, dressed in white robes and holding palm branches in their hands. It comes after the mention of the twelve tribes of Israel. Interpreters explain in various ways who the 144,000 are and how they relate to this crowd. What is clear is that they are celebrating that God saved them, and then the angels join in worship.

For today: when you feel tired or without strength, remember that your salvation does not depend on you. Take a moment to give thanks to God and to Jesus for it.
exp.6:16:
Here the verse says that Jesus, called the Lamb, cares for his people the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. He leads them to living springs of water, that is, fresh streams that never run dry. And God himself will wipe away all their tears. The word for "shepherd" here means that he will care for them, guide them, and protect them.

John writes this vision in the book of Revelation. An elder explains to him who the crowd dressed in white before the throne are: people who went through great tribulation and are now with God. The message is meant to comfort Christians who were suffering. Some scholars see here heaven and others the new creation; in both cases, the promise is of final comfort.

Today, when you are tired or hurt, you can trust that Jesus guides you and cares for you. Bring him your sorrows in prayer, knowing that God promises a day without weeping.
exp.7:2:
It says that another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, which is a vessel for burning incense. He was given a great amount of incense to add to the prayers of all the saints, that is, of the believers. All of this takes place at the golden altar, which is before the throne of God.

John recounts this vision of heaven. The seventh seal has just been opened, there was silence, and the seven angels are about to sound the trumpets. Before the judgments arrive, the text shows that God hears the prayers of his people. Some understand that this incense represents those prayers, and that God answers them, as the fire thrown to the earth shows.

For today: do not underestimate your prayer. Even when it seems small or unanswered, God receives it and keeps it before his throne. Keep praying with confidence and patience.
exp.7:3:
It says that the smoke of the incense, which the angel held in his hand, rose up into God's presence together with the prayers of the saints. "Saints" refers to the believers, the people of God. The incense is mixed with their prayers, and everything rises to God as a pleasing offering.

John describes what he saw in a vision. Before the seven trumpets sound, which announce judgments, an angel appears with a golden censer. Many understand that this shows God hears the cry of his people before he acts. Some interpret it in different ways, but the central idea is that prayers are not lost.

For today: pray with confidence, even when your prayer seems small or weak. God receives it and keeps it. Keep praying for your needs and for justice, knowing that he hears you.
exp.7:4:
It says that an angel takes the censor, that is, the vessel in which incense is burned. He fills it with coals from the altar and throws it to the earth. Then there are thunders, voices, lightnings, and an earthquake.

John is recounting a vision. In the verse before, the prayers of the saints rise up to God along with the incense. Now the same censer returns to the earth with fire, and this introduces the judgments of the seven trumpets. Many understand that God answers the prayers of his people and acts against evil. The symbolic details are interpreted in various ways.

Your prayers are not lost: God hears them and takes them seriously. You can keep praying with confidence, even if you do not yet see an answer, and leave justice and timing in his hands.
exp.7:8:
It says that, as a result of the second trumpet, a third of the living creatures in the sea died, and also a third of the ships were destroyed. "Creatures" are the beings that were created, and "ships" are vessels. The sea is an older way of saying "the sea" in this context.

John writes what God showed him in a vision. The trumpets announce judgments on the earth, and here the damage reaches the sea and commerce. That it is only "a third" shows that the judgment is serious but limited, and that there is still an opportunity to repent. Christians interpret these trumpets in different ways: as future events, as symbols of judgments throughout history, or as both.

For today: do not take for granted what seems firm, such as your economy or your plans. Trust in God, who governs over all, and respond to his patience with a humble heart willing to turn back to him.
exp.8:6:
It says that the locusts John sees in his vision look like horses ready to go to war. On their heads they wear something resembling crowns that shine like gold, and their faces look like human faces.

The verse describes what John sees through comparisons, and the wording shows that these are likenesses rather than literal things: the locusts are "like" horses, and their heads have "something like" crowns.

John is the one speaking, recounting the vision he received from Jesus Christ. It takes place at the fifth trumpet, a judgment that brings torment on people. Interpreters differ: some see spiritual or demonic forces, others human armies, and others a symbolic picture of the suffering that evil causes.

For today: Revelation shows that evil can look powerful and attractive, with crowns and strength, but God sets limits on it. Trust that God governs history, and live with humility and watchfulness, not letting yourself be fooled by appearances.
exp.8:7:
This verse continues describing the locusts that come out of the abyss when the fifth trumpet sounds. It says they had long hair, like a woman's, and strong, fierce teeth, like a lion's. It is a mixed image: something that seems human and at the same time wild and dangerous.

John recounts what he saw in his vision. These creatures are not ordinary locusts, but a symbolic picture of a painful judgment that falls on those who reject God. Christians have understood them in several ways: as evil spiritual forces, as a real punishment, or as a general symbol of evil. There is no single certain interpretation.

For today: evil often appears with an attractive appearance, but hides a destructive power. Let us ask God for discernment so that we are not deceived by what only looks good, and trust that He takes care of His own.
exp.8:8:
It says that these symbolic locusts had a kind of armor, as if they were soldiers ready to fight. Also, the sound of their wings was as loud as that of many chariots drawn by horses running into battle.

John reports what he sees in his vision when the fifth trumpet sounds. These creatures come up out of the abyss and cause suffering for five months. Christians interpret them in different ways: as demons, as a future judgment, or as symbolic images. The text does not fully explain this, so it is wise to be humble.

For today: God is still the one who sets limits on evil, even when it seems unstoppable. We can trust that nothing escapes his control, and live with hope and reverence.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that a voice speaks to the sixth angel, the one who had the trumpet, and orders him to release four angels who were bound at the great river Euphrates.

The voice comes from the four horns of the golden altar, which stands before God. For this reason, the command comes from heaven and from his presence. It is then said that those angels were prepared for an exact hour, day, month, and year. This shows that everything happens in the time that God allows. It is not known with certainty who these four angels are; many think they are fallen angels, others that they are angels serving God's judgment. It is also debated whether the Euphrates is literal or symbolic.

For today: even when evil seems to be unleashed, nothing escapes God's control. We can trust that he has times and limits, and live with humility, prayer, and faithfulness.
exp.8:16:
John describes a vision of terrible horses and riders. The riders wear breastplates (chest protection) colored fiery red, dark blue, and sulfur yellow. The heads of the horses look like lions' heads, and from their mouths come fire, smoke, and brimstone, which is a yellow stone that burns and has a strong smell.

John speaks here, relating what he sees after the sixth trumpet sounds. It is a judgment that God allows to fall on the earth, and the text says it kills a third of mankind. Christians interpret these images in different ways: as future events, as symbols of wars and punishments, or as a general message about God's judgment. There is no single explanation accepted by everyone.

For today: God is serious about sin, but He also gives time to return to Him. Do not postpone your repentance; today you can draw near to God with humility and confidence.
exp.8:20:
This verse says that, even after the terrible plagues, the people who survived did not change their hearts. They did not repent of their murders (killing others), of their sorceries (practices of magic and witchcraft, which in the original Greek are linked to drugs and secret rituals), of their fornication (sexual relations outside of marriage), or of their thefts (stealing).

John writes what Jesus showed him in a vision. These plagues belong to the sixth trumpet. Interpreters differ on whether they are literal events or symbols, but all agree on the central point: God's judgment is a warning, and even so many harden their hearts.

For today: pain and warnings do not change the heart by themselves. Ask yourself honestly whether there is something God is pointing out to you that you continue to justify. Repenting today, with humility, is opening the door to his forgiveness.
exp.9:0:
John sees another mighty angel coming down from heaven. He is surrounded by a cloud, has a rainbow over his head, his face shines like the sun, and his legs look like pillars of fire.

The speaker is John, who tells what he saw in a vision. This scene comes between the sixth and seventh trumpets, like a pause before the end. It is not certain who this angel is. Some think he is a very exalted angel; others think he represents Christ because of his glorious features. Christians have interpreted him in several ways.

For today: even when the world seems confused, God still rules with power and faithfulness. The rainbow reminds us of his promises. You can rest in the fact that he keeps what he says, and trust him this week.
exp.9:2:
This verse says that the mighty angel cried out with a powerful voice, like the roar of a lion. When he finished crying out, seven thunders answered with their own voices.

The one speaking is the mighty angel, whom John sees with the little book open, standing on the sea and on the land. His roar recalls the authority of God, since in the Bible the roar of a lion is sometimes joined with the voice of the Lord. The seven thunders speak something that John understands, but he is immediately told not to write it down. What they said, no one knows; some think it is a mystery reserved by God.

For today: we do not need to know everything in order to trust God. He reveals what is fitting and keeps the rest. We can rest in his wisdom, obey what he has shown us, and leave in his hands what we do not yet understand.
exp.9:7:
John hears the voice from heaven once more, the same voice that had spoken to him before. That voice tells him to go to the mighty angel who stands on the sea and on the land, and to take the little scroll that lies open in the angel's hand.

The one speaking is a heavenly voice, probably God's, though the text does not make this clear. This happens between the sixth and seventh trumpets, when it is announced that the mystery of God will be fulfilled. John must receive this message before he prophesies again. Some think the angel represents Christ, others that it is a very powerful angel; it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God asks us to receive his word with obedience, not just to hear it. Before sharing a message with others, let it enter your heart. Read the Bible with humility and trust, even when some truths are hard to understand.
exp.9:9:
John tells how he received the little open book from the angel and ate all of it. The first word, meaning to swallow eagerly, and the word for the stomach are explained as they appear in the verse above. In his mouth it tasted sweet like honey, but afterward it brought bitterness to his stomach.

John speaks within the vision of Revelation. A voice from heaven told him to take the little book, and the angel warned him that it would be sweet and bitter. Then he is told that he must prophesy again to many peoples. Many understand the little book to be God's message, sweet because of its truth and bitter because it includes judgment. Interpreters differ on the details of its contents.

For today: Receive the Word of God with joy, but also with seriousness. Some truths comfort and others confront. Even so, God calls us to live them out and share them with love and honesty.
exp.10:0:
It says that John was given a measuring reed, something like a rod, and was told to rise up and measure the temple of God, the altar, and the people who worship there.

John is the one who recounts a vision; the command comes from a heavenly voice, which many understand to be Christ or his angel. To measure usually means that something is placed under God's care and protection. Christians interpret the "temple" in different ways: the literal temple, the church, or the faithful people of God. There is no single agreement.

For today: God knows and cares for those who truly worship him, even in difficult times. You can trust that your faith, your prayer, and your life do not go unnoticed by him.
exp.10:1:
It says John should not measure the outer courtyard of the temple, but leave it out, because it has been given to the Gentiles, that is, to the non-Jewish nations. They will trample the holy city for forty-two months, about three and a half years.

An angel is speaking, and John writes down what he sees. Measuring the temple suggests protection and belonging to God. What is left unmeasured faces persecution. The forty-two months match the 1,260 days of the next verse. Some see this as a literal future period of time, others as a symbol of the limited time of testing for the church. Interpretations vary.

For today: even when there are times of pressure or contempt, God knows and cares for those who worship him. That suffering has a limit that he himself sets. We can remain faithful, trusting that he sustains us.
exp.10:7:
It says that the dead bodies of the two witnesses will lie in the streets of the great city. That city is called, symbolically, Sodom and Egypt, and it is also where our Lord was crucified.

John is recounting his vision. The two witnesses are prophets who gave testimony with power, and the beast kills them. The city is described with symbolic names: Sodom for its wickedness and Egypt for its oppression. Some believe it is Jerusalem, because of the mention of the cross; others think it represents every human system that opposes God. There are several interpretations.

For today: do not lose heart if being faithful to God seems to end in rejection or defeat. Jesus went through that too, and the story does not end there. Keep bearing witness with love and with confidence that God has the last word.
exp.10:8:
It says that people from all nations, tribes, and languages will look at the bodies of the two dead witnesses for three and a half days. Also, they will not allow them to be buried. Leaving a body unburied was a great dishonor.

John is writing the vision of Revelation. The two witnesses are prophets whom God sends to bear testimony. Now they seem defeated by the beast. Christians interpret this in different ways: some see literal people, others see the faithful church in general. What follows shows that God raises them up again.

For today: if being faithful to God brings you mockery or rejection, do not think that all is lost. The world may celebrate for a moment, but God has the final word. Remain firm in your testimony with confidence.
exp.10:11:
They say that the two witnesses, after being raised to life, hear a loud voice from heaven calling to them. They go up to heaven enveloped in a cloud, and their enemies see it with their own eyes. A loud voice is a powerful voice, and the call means "come up here."

This is part of John's vision of the two witnesses, who proclaim God's message and are killed by those who reject them. The one speaking from heaven is God or his heavenly authority. His call shows that God stands behind his servants. Christians interpret differently who these witnesses are, but all agree that the scene shows God has the final word.

Today, this encourages us to remain faithful even when we are rejected or misunderstood. God sees our loyalty and does not forget his own. Our task is to obey with confidence, knowing that he will bring about justice in his time.
exp.10:12:
Right when the two witnesses rise up to heaven, a strong earthquake happens. A tenth of the city collapses and seven thousand people die. The survivors are left terrified, that is, filled with fear and awe, and they gave glory to the God of heaven, meaning they acknowledged him and honored him.

John recounts this vision from Revelation. The two witnesses were killed, rose again, and were taken up to heaven. This earthquake is God's response to all of that. Many believe the city is a picture of humanity that rejects God, though others see it as Jerusalem. The numbers are probably symbolic, and interpreters do not fully agree. Then comes the sound of the seventh trumpet.

For today: God can use the shocks of life to wake us up. When something shakes us, instead of hardening ourselves, we can stop and give glory to God with humility.
exp.10:14:
It says that when the seventh angel blows his trumpet, loud voices are heard in heaven announcing that the kingdoms of this world now belong to God and to his Christ (the Messiah, the Anointed One). And that he will reign forever.

The speakers are great voices from heaven, though the text does not say exactly who they are. They come after judgments and suffering on the earth. This trumpet announces God's final victory over all human power. Christians interpret differently when and how this will be fulfilled, but all agree that God has the last word. The elders respond by worshiping.

For today: when you see injustice or feel worn down by the news, remember that the world is not outside God's control. Today you can pray with hope and live with calm, faithfulness and love, because Christ will reign.
exp.10:16:
They say that the twenty-four elders give thanks to God, whom they call Lord God Almighty, the one who is, who was, and who is to come. They thank him because he has taken his great power, that is, he has put it into action and has begun to reign openly. The word "power" here means the same as the power the verse names.

The speakers are the group of twenty-four elders, who are seated before God's throne in heaven. They have just heard that the seventh angel sounded the trumpet and that the kingdoms of the world are becoming Christ's. So they fall on their faces and worship. Scholars disagree about exactly who the elders represent, and also about when and how all of this is fulfilled, but the sense of the praise is clear.

For today: even when evil seems to be winning, we can thank God now, because he reigns and will have the last word. That confidence gives us peace and steadiness.
exp.11:1:
Here the woman of the sign in the sky is described. She is pregnant and cries out in pain because she is about to give birth. Her suffering is very intense.

The one speaking is John, who recounts a vision he received from God. This woman appears just before the arrival of the dragon, who wants to devour her child. Many believers see in her the people of God, or Israel and the church, and in the child, Christ. Others see Mary or interpret the image in other ways. What is clear is that the people of God suffer under the threat of evil.

For today: if you go through pain or trials, it does not mean that God has abandoned you. In the same chapter, God protects the woman and her child. You can cry out to God with confidence, knowing that he cares for his own.
exp.11:2:
John says he sees another sign in heaven: a huge dragon with a fiery red color. It has seven heads, ten horns, and seven crowns on its heads.

John writes this vision to encourage Christians who were under pressure and persecution. Shortly after, Revelation 12:9 identifies the dragon with the ancient serpent, the devil, and Satan. The horns and crowns speak of power and authority. Some believe the woman represents Israel, others the church, others both; interpreters do not agree on every detail.

For today: the enemy appears powerful and threatening, but the account goes on and shows the child carried safely to God. When you feel fear or pressure, remember that evil does not have the last word. Trust in Christ and stay firm in prayer.
exp.11:3:
It says that the dragon, with his tail, swept away a third of the stars of heaven and cast them down to the earth. Then he stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that he could devour her child as soon as it was born.

John writes this vision to Christians who were under pressure and persecution. Later the text identifies the dragon with Satan (12:9). Many understand the stars to be angels who followed him, though some see them as a general picture of his destructive power. The woman is interpreted in different ways: as Israel, as the church, or as both. The child points to Christ.

Even when evil seems strong and threatening, it does not have the final word. The child was taken up to God for safety, and the woman was cared for in the wilderness. When you feel fear or pressure, trust that God protects and sustains his people.
exp.11:9:
A loud voice in heaven announces a victory: salvation, power, and the kingdom of God, and the authority of Christ, are now made visible. The reason is that the accuser, Satan, has been thrown down. He was accusing believers before God all the time.

Here "power" means strength or might, and "thrown down" means cast out.

The voice is not clearly identified; some think it is the saints or heavenly beings. It comes after the vision of the woman, the child, and the dragon, and after the dragon's defeat in heaven. It celebrates that Christ already has the victory. Interpreters differ about the timing and exact form of this scene, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you feel guilty or accused, remember that your confidence is in Christ and not in your record. Confess your failings honestly, receive his forgiveness, and move forward with hope.
exp.11:10:
This verse says that believers have overcome the devil, called the accuser, for three reasons: the blood of the Lamb (Jesus, who gave his life for us), the word of their testimony (what they declared about their faith), and because they did not love their lives so much as to avoid death. The reference to overcoming points to the dragon. The word for power in the previous verse means strength.

A loud voice in heaven celebrates that the dragon has been thrown down to the earth. This is part of the vision John received, written to encourage Christians who were suffering persecution. Interpreters differ about the exact timing of this scene, but all of them see here the victory of Christ over the accuser.

Our victory does not depend on our strength or our merits, but on what Jesus has done. Today we can speak of Him with courage and faithfulness, even when it costs discomfort, mockery or loss, trusting that God sustains his own.
exp.11:16:
This verse says that the dragon, who is Satan according to Revelation 12:9, was filled with rage because he could not destroy the woman. So he went off to make war against the rest of her offspring, that is, those who keep God's commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.

John writes this vision to encourage Christians who were under pressure and persecution. The woman is interpreted in several ways: the people of God, Israel, the church, or a combination of these. What is clear is that the enemy attacks the faithful, but God has already protected the woman in surprising ways.

Today, if you follow Jesus and feel opposition or weariness, do not be surprised or discouraged. Ask God for strength, stay firm in obeying him, and bear witness to Jesus with courage where you live.
exp.12:0:
John tells how he stood on the sand of the sea and saw a beast rise up out of the sea, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon his horns ten crowns. Each horn had a crown, that is, a king's crown. Each head had a name of blasphemy, that is, words that insult God.

The apostle John speaks here, writing Revelation with symbolic images for Christians who were under pressure and persecution. Many believe the beast represents the oppressive political power of his time, such as Rome. Others see it as a future ruler. Christians have understood it in several ways.

Today, do not be impressed by human powers that think they are gods. Although they may seem strong, God remains the King. Stay faithful to Him with humility and hope.
exp.12:1:
It says John saw a beast that looked like a leopard, with feet like a bear and a mouth like a lion. These are animals that Daniel also saw in his vision (Daniel 7). Then it says the dragon gave the beast his power, his throne, and great authority.

John, who received this vision, speaks to encourage Christians who were suffering pressure and persecution. The dragon, identified in Revelation 12 with Satan, is the source of the beast's power. Many interpreters see in it a political power opposed to God; some apply it to the Roman Empire, others to a future power. Christians do not fully agree on this.

For today: do not be impressed or frightened by powers that seem enormous. Their authority is borrowed and limited. Trust that God still rules, and remain faithful to Christ.
exp.12:2:
John says he saw one of the beast's seven heads as if it had been wounded to death, yet that deadly wound was healed. Because of this, the whole earth was amazed and followed the beast.

John wrote Revelation to encourage Christians who were under pressure for refusing to worship human powers. The beast rises out of the sea and receives its authority from the dragon. Many believe it represents an oppressive political power, and it has been connected with the Roman Empire or with a future power. Interpreters do not agree on this.

Today, do not be dazzled by what seems strong, popular, or revived. The amazement of the crowd does not prove that something is true. Place your trust and your worship in Christ alone.
exp.12:9:
It says that whoever leads others into captivity will go into captivity, and whoever kills with the sword must be killed with the sword. Here the wording reads as the sword, which is the same weapon the verse names. It then states that in this we see the patience and the faith of the saints, that is, of the believers who remain faithful to God.

John writes what Jesus showed him in a vision. He speaks of the first beast, a power that persecutes believers and demands worship. Some understand the verse to announce justice for the oppressors; others take it as a call for Christians not to answer with violence. Many see both things, and the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: when you suffer injustice, do not repay evil with evil. Trust that God sees everything, and sustain your faith with patience, doing good.
exp.12:13:
It says that the second beast deceives those who dwell on the earth with miraculous signs that it is allowed to perform. It leads them to make an image of the first beast, the one that was wounded by a sword and came back to life.

John writes Revelation to encourage Christians who were under pressure to worship the political and religious power of their time. Here he describes a power that imitates God with false miracles. Interpreters see it in different ways: as Rome, as a religious system, or as something still to come.

For today: do not believe something just because it seems powerful or miraculous. Compare everything with what Jesus taught in the Bible, and keep your loyalty to God alone.
exp.12:17:
It says that whoever has understanding should count the number of the beast, because it is the number of a man, that is, human. That number is six hundred sixty-six. Some ancient manuscripts say 616, and it is not known for certain why that difference exists.

John wrote Revelation for Christians who were under pressure for refusing to give loyalty to the imperial power and its systems. The beast represents a power opposed to God. Many think that 666 points to Nero through the numerical value of the letters, but others see it as a symbol of human imperfection or of any power that presents itself as God. Christians do not agree on this, and it is good to say so with humility.

For today: instead of becoming preoccupied with guessing the number, let us ask for wisdom not to give our final loyalty to any power, money, or system. Our trust is in Christ, not in whatever promises passing security.
exp.13:1:
John tells us that he heard a sound coming from heaven. It was very loud, like the sound of many waters falling together or like a great thunder. But it was also sweet: it sounded like musicians playing their harps.

John is describing a vision. Earlier he saw the Lamb, who is Jesus, with the hundred and forty-four thousand on Mount Zion. This sound prepares the new song that follows. There are different ways to understand who the hundred and forty-four thousand are, but all of them agree that they belong to the Lamb.

For today: the worship of the redeemed is both powerful and beautiful. Take a moment to praise God with your whole heart, even if your life is full of noise or trials.
exp.13:3:
These are said to be 144,000 people who were not defiled with women and who are virgins. It also says they follow the Lamb, who is Jesus, wherever he goes. They were bought, or redeemed, from among men as the firstfruits, that is, the first part of a harvest, offered to God.

John relates what he sees and hears in a vision. The group sings a new song before the throne. Many understand the word "virgins" literally, while others take it as a symbol of faithfulness to God, not worshiping the beast or idols, since the Bible sometimes calls idolatry spiritual unfaithfulness. This cannot be stated with complete certainty; there are several interpretations.

For today: ask yourself whether you truly follow Jesus wherever he leads, even when it is hard. Today you can choose one concrete decision in which you give him first place and remain faithful to him.
exp.13:6:
This verse says that an angel proclaims with a loud voice a message for the whole world: people must respect God, give him honor, and worship him alone, because he is the Creator of everything. The reverence it calls for means taking God seriously and standing in awe of him. The phrase about the hour of his judgment having come means that the moment has arrived when God acts as judge. The springs and rivers of water are the sources of all waters.

The one speaking is an angel whom John sees flying in the sky. The angel carries the everlasting good news to all nations. This comes before the announcement of Babylon's fall and the warning about worshiping the beast. That is why the message calls people to choose the true God over other powers. Christians understand the exact timing of this judgment in different ways.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we put first in life. Take a moment each day to thank God and to put him first.
exp.13:8:
The third angel comes after the other two and announces a serious warning with a loud voice. He speaks of anyone who worships the beast and its image and receives its mark on the forehead or on the hand.

John records the vision of three angels. The first calls people to worship God, the second announces the fall of Babylon, and the third warns about the consequences of following the beast. Christians understand the mark in different ways: some see it as a literal allegiance, others as a symbol of submission to a power that opposes God. Its purpose is to call for faithfulness.

Today we can ask ourselves to whom or to what we give our deepest loyalty. Being faithful to God means not letting fear, money, or the pressure of others direct our decisions.
exp.13:16:
Here John sees another angel coming out of the heavenly temple. He carries a sharp sickle, a curved tool for cutting. The sickle is sharp, meaning it is well honed. That the angel comes out of the temple shows that his task comes directly from the presence of God.

John is describing a vision of the final judgment. Earlier, a harvesting of the earth was mentioned, and now a second scene begins: the grape harvest, the cutting of the grapes. Many understand this to speak of God's judgment on evil. Others see it in other ways, and Christians do not agree on every detail. What is clear is that God sets the timing.

For today: you can live with peace and seriousness, knowing that God is not indifferent to injustice and that he decides the right time. Trust him and seek to live in his truth.
exp.13:17:
Another angel comes out from the altar, and he has authority over the fire. With a loud voice he commands the angel who holds the sharp sickle to cut the clusters from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are already fully ripe.

We are in John's vision of the final judgment. Before this, there was a harvest like wheat; now comes a grape harvest, which leads to the winepress of God's wrath. The altar and the fire recall the prayers of the saints (Revelation 6:9-10; 8:3-5). Many read this as judgment on wickedness; others debate the details of the imagery.

For today: God does not act too late or blindly; there is a right time for everything. This invites us to trust his justice, leave vengeance in his hands, and live with humility and repentance while there is still opportunity.
exp.13:18:
This verse says that an angel swung his sharp sickle over the earth and cut the clusters from the vine of the earth. Then he threw that grape into the great winepress, which is the press where grapes are trodden to get the wine. This press is called the winepress of the wrath of God.

John relates a vision of the end. Before that, an angel called out loudly that the harvest should be gathered because the grapes were already ripe. The image of the harvest and the winepress comes from the prophets, such as Joel and Isaiah, and speaks of God's judgment on evil. Interpreters differ on the details, but they agree that God will bring an end to injustice.

For today: you can rest in the fact that God is just and does not forget evil. That frees us from seeking revenge and encourages us to live with humility, seeking peace and trusting in the mercy of Christ.
exp.13:19:
It says the winepress, the place where grapes are trodden, was trodden outside the city. From there came so much blood that it reached the bridles, the pieces of the horses' mouths. It stretched for one thousand six hundred furlongs, about 300 kilometers, though many think the number is symbolic.

John describes a vision of the final judgment. An angel harvests the earth like a ripe vineyard and throws the grapes into the winepress of God's wrath. The city may refer to Jerusalem or to God's people, and it is interpreted in several ways. The image of blood and grape harvest comes from the prophets, such as Isaiah 63 and Joel 3. It is symbolic language, and not everyone understands it in the same way.

For today: this passage reminds us that God is just and that evil will not have the last word. It invites us to live with reverence, to trust Him when we see injustice, and to share with others the hope of forgiveness in Christ.
exp.14:4:
And after this, John says, he looked again and saw the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven opened. That is, the heavenly sanctuary, which calls to mind the sacred tent where the tablets of the law were kept. The phrase "was opened" indicates that something important is about to come out of there.

John is the one speaking, in a vision. He has just heard the song of Moses and of the Lamb, which praises God's righteousness. Now heaven opens, and from that holy place seven angels come out carrying the last plagues. Many understand that this shows God's judgments are just and come from his holiness, although interpreters differ on how these scenes should be applied.

For today: you can trust that God acts with justice and truth. You do not have to take revenge or despair in the face of evil; pray, live with reverence, and hand over to God what you cannot fix.
exp.14:5:
They say seven angels come out of the temple in heaven. Each one carries a plague, that is, a blow of judgment. They are dressed in clean, white linen, and they have golden bands across their chests. The word "girded" means they are wearing them, tied securely.

John describes what he sees in his vision. Before this, the victors sing that God is holy and that his judgments are just. Now the angels come out of the place where God dwells, and this shows that his judgments come from him. Afterward they will receive seven bowls with his wrath. Some understand the linen and the gold as purity and dignity; the text only describes them, and their meaning is interpreted in several ways.

We can trust that God acts with holiness and justice. When you see wickedness that seems to go unanswered, rest in the fact that he sees everything and does not act on whim. That invites us to live with reverence and to leave vengeance in his hands.
exp.14:7:
The temple in heaven was filled with smoke, which symbolizes the powerful and glorious presence of God. While the seven angels were pouring out the seven plagues, no one could enter.

John describes what he saw in a vision. The angels had just received the bowls of God's wrath. The smoke recalls other moments in the Bible, such as the tabernacle and Solomon's temple, when the glory of God filled them (Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11). Many understand that God acts with holiness and justice, and that his judgment has a time and a limit.

For today: God is holy and powerful, but also just and faithful. We can draw near to him with respect and confidence, and rest knowing that nothing is left without his response. Today you can pray with reverence and entrust your injustices to him.
exp.15:0:
He says that John heard a very loud voice coming out of the temple in heaven. That voice orders seven angels to go and pour out their seven bowls, which represent God's punishment or anger, upon the earth. The commands are addressed to the angels as a group, so the verse is telling them to go and pour them out. The word "wrath" means righteous anger.

In the book of Revelation, John describes visions about the end of time. This voice comes from the temple, the place where God's presence is, so it is understood to be a command from God himself. The verses that follow show the first bowls falling on those who followed the beast. Christians interpret these scenes in different ways, but all of them recognize that God judges evil with justice.

Today we can trust that God does not ignore injustice. This invites us to live with humility, seek his forgiveness, and not take revenge, but leave judgment in his hands.
exp.15:1:
The first angel poured out his bowl on the earth. Then a painful and harmful sore appeared, but only on the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshipped its image.

A loud voice from the temple, understood to be the voice of God, commanded the seven angels to pour out the bowls of his wrath. This judgment falls on those who joined themselves to the beast, the power that opposes God. Christians interpret these plagues in different ways: literally, symbolically, or both. They recall the plagues of Egypt, where God judged injustice and idolatry.

For today: take care to whom you give your loyalty. Ask yourself what things compete with God in your heart, and decide to follow him with confidence, knowing that his justice is true.
exp.15:3:
It says that the third angel pours out his bowl over the rivers and the springs, and the fresh water turns to blood. This is the third of the seven final plagues. "Bowl" here is a container that represents God's judgment, and the springs are the sources from which the water flows.

John, who writes the Revelation, reports what he sees in his vision. This plague recalls the first plague of Egypt, when the Nile turned to blood. Right after, an angel declares that God is just, because those who shed the blood of the saints and the prophets now receive blood to drink. Some see figurative language here and others a literal event; Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it. We can trust that he will judge with justice, so we do not need to take revenge ourselves. Rather, let us live with humility and seek peace.
exp.15:5:
They have shed the blood of God's people, the saints and prophets, and now You have given them blood to drink, as they deserve. That is the verse's point: those who killed the saints and the prophets now receive blood to drink. The verse says God is just in doing this, because they deserve it. The wording "as they deserve" makes clear that this is the fair payment for what they did.

The angel speaking here is the angel over the waters, during the judgment of the third bowl. The rivers and springs turn to blood. He does not see this as cruelty but as justice: the blood spilled by the faithful was not forgotten. Then another voice from the altar confirms that God's judgments are true and just. Some read this judgment literally and others see it as a symbol, but the central message is the same.

We can trust that God sees every injustice and that he will judge with justice. So we do not need to take revenge; instead we can hand over to him what we cannot resolve and keep on loving.
exp.15:6:
It says that a voice comes from the altar and affirms that God is Almighty and that his judgments are true and righteous.

This happens when the third bowl is poured out on the rivers and the waters. First the angel of the waters speaks, and then another voice answers from the altar. Some think it is the voice of the martyrs, since earlier in Revelation their prayers are connected with the altar (6:9-10), but the text does not say this clearly. Both voices acknowledge that God acts with justice toward those who killed his people.

For today: when you see injustice and pain, do not lose hope. You can trust that God sees everything and will judge with perfect justice, and so you do not need to take revenge yourself.
exp.15:7:
It says that the fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and that power was given to the sun to scorch people with fire. The word "bowl" refers to a container holding God's judgment.

We are in the seven bowls of God's wrath, in the book of Revelation, written by John. Earlier, a voice from the altar declares that God's judgments are true and just. Afterward, the people suffer the heat, but they do not repent. Some interpret these scenes literally and others symbolically; the text does not fully settle the matter.

For today: the passage invites us not to harden our hearts. When difficulties come, we can ask ourselves whether we are reacting with pride or with humility, and turn to God sincerely instead of blaming him.
exp.15:9:
It says that the fifth angel poured out his bowl of God's judgment on the throne of the beast, that is, the center of its power. As a result, its kingdom was plunged into darkness, and people bit their tongues in pain. The word "throne" here refers to the seat of authority, the place from which power is exercised.

John writes this vision for Christians who were under pressure and persecution. The bowls are God's judgments on a system that opposes Him. The darkness recalls the plague in Egypt.
