The verses that follow show that people suffer, yet still do not repent. Interpreters differ on how to understand the details, but the central message is clear.

For today: pain alone does not change the heart; humility is needed. Right now we can ask God what in our lives we should acknowledge, and turn to Him without hardening ourselves.
exp.15:13:
It says that the three unclean spirits that came out of the mouth of the dragon, of the beast, and of the false prophet are spirits of demons. They perform signs, that is, miracles or deceptive wonders, and they go out to the rulers of the whole earth to gather them to a battle. That battle is the great day of God Almighty. Gathering means bringing together.

This is in the vision that Jesus gave to John about the final judgments. It describes the sixth bowl of God's wrath. The demons use deception to lead the nations to oppose God. Christians interpret the timing and exact meaning of Armageddon in different ways, but all agree that God has the final word.

For today: do not be impressed only by what is spectacular. Examine everything in the light of the Bible and stay alert in faith. Trust that God governs history.
exp.15:18:
This verse says that the great earthquake split the great city into three parts, and that the cities of the nations collapsed. God remembered great Babylon in order to make her drink the cup of the wine of his wrath. The word "remembered" in the verse above is the one the verse discusses; it means God did not forget, but now acts with justice.

This happens when the seventh angel pours out the last bowl, and a voice from the throne declares that it is done. John presents this as a vision. Many believe that the great city and Babylon represent human power that opposes God, although some identify it with Rome or with another city.

For today: God sees every injustice and does not leave it without a response. This invites us not to trust human systems that seem firm, but to place our hope in God and live with humility and justice.
exp.16:1:
It says that the rulers of the world joined themselves with the great harlot in an unfaithful relationship, and that many people were left as if drunk from the wine of that unfaithfulness. Committing fornication here speaks of joining oneself in an impure way, and being made drunk means being left without clarity to think.

An angel of the seven bowls speaks to John and shows him the judgment on this harlot, a symbol of a corrupt system that seduces the nations. The book does not clearly identify her here; some think of Rome, others of a religious or political power, and others of a worldwide system of evil. What is clear is that God condemns her.

Today we can ask ourselves what things make us drunk and take away our discernment: power, money, fame, or fashions. Let us ask God for clarity and for loyalty to him alone.
exp.16:2:
John tells that the Spirit carried him away to a deserted place, that is, a lonely and lifeless spot. There he saw a woman sitting on a beast of a scarlet color, which means bright red. The beast was covered with names of blasphemy, that is, words that insult God, and it had seven heads and ten horns.

John speaks, relating what an angel shows him. The angel promised to show him the judgment on the great harlot, an image of a system that seduces and turns people away from God. Later he calls her Babylon. Many believers see her as Rome or as a corrupt world power, and there are different interpretations.

For today: be wary of everything that glitters and promises power or pleasure but draws you away from God. Ask him to give you discernment and faithfulness.
exp.16:7:
This verse says that the beast John saw "was, and is not," but that it is going to come up out of the abyss and end in destruction. "Destruction" means total ruin. Those who live on the earth and do not have their names written in the book of life will be amazed to see the beast, which seemed finished, appear again.

An angel speaks to John and explains to him the mystery of the woman and the beast, because John had been greatly amazed. Interpreters disagree about who the beast represents: some see an empire, such as Rome, and others see a future power. What is clear is the contrast: the world marvels, but the end of the beast is already decided.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed by powers that seem invincible. Trust that God has the last word, and live firmly, knowing that those who belong to Christ are secure in Him.
exp.16:8:
It says that wise understanding is needed to grasp this message. The seven heads of the beast are seven mountains, and the woman sits upon them.

An angel speaks to John in a vision. He explains to him the mystery of the woman and the beast, because John was left astonished. Many believe the seven mountains point to Rome, the city of the seven hills, but others see a broader symbol of human power set against God. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: do not be dazzled by the power and luxury of this world, like those who marvel at it. Ask God for wisdom, and remember that your name is secure in his book of life.
exp.16:9:
It says there are seven kings in this vision. Five have fallen, one rules now, and the seventh has not yet come; when he comes, he will last only a short time. "Fallen" means they have already finished their reign.

An angel explains to John the mystery of the beast and of the woman seated on seven mountains. He writes to churches that were suffering pressure from political powers. Christians have understood these kings in different ways: as emperors of Rome, or as empires throughout history. There is no complete agreement, so it is good to read it with humility.

For today: the governments and powers of this world are temporary, and God still is in control of history. Do not place your final hope in any leader or system; trust in Christ, whose kingdom never ends.
exp.16:13:
They will wage war against Christ, the Lamb, and the Lamb will win. The reason is that He is Lord of lords and King of kings. Those who go with Him are the ones who have been called (invited by God), chosen (selected by Him), and faithful (loyal to the end).

An angel explains to John a vision full of symbols. The ten horns are ten kings who will hold power for a short time and then hand it over to the beast. Interpreters disagree about whom they represent. The central message is clear: the power of those who oppose God is brief, and Christ has the final victory. It was written to encourage persecuted Christians.

If today injustice or the powerful overwhelm you, remember that Christ reigns and will conquer. Your calling is to remain faithful to Him with hope, without letting yourself be intimidated.
exp.16:14:
Here the angel explains to John what the waters on which the prostitute sits represent. According to the text, they are "peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues," that is, people of every race, language, and country. The prostitute is an immoral woman who symbolizes a corrupt system opposed to God.

It is one of the angels who showed John the vision who speaks. Earlier it was said that the woman sits on many waters (17:1). Interpreters disagree about who she is: Rome, a false religious system, or a corrupt world power. All agree that her influence reaches many peoples, but God, in the end, judges her.

Today we can remember that no influence of the world, however great it may seem, stands above God. Let us ask him for wisdom so that we do not let ourselves be carried along by whatever dominates the culture, and so that we keep faithfully following the Lamb.
exp.16:15:
This verse says that the ten kings, represented by the ten horns of the beast, will turn against the harlot. The word "hate" means to despise with intense hostility; "desolate" means left in ruin and alone; "naked" means stripped of protection and wealth. "Eat her flesh" and "burn her with fire" are vivid images of total destruction.

The angel speaks to John and explains the vision. The harlot, called Babylon, symbolizes a corrupt system that seduces the nations and opposes God. Many believe it points to Rome or to a future world power; there are different interpretations. What is clear is that evil destroys itself, and that God, according to the following verse, directs everything until his word is fulfilled.

Today we can remember that no unjust power or deceptive luxury lasts forever. That is why it is wise to place our trust in Christ, the victorious Lamb, and not in the things the world promises but cannot sustain.
exp.16:17:
This verse says that the woman in the vision, the harlot called Babylon, represents a great city that rules over the kings of the earth.

It is spoken by one of the seven angels who had the bowls, who explains the vision to John (17:1, 7). John writes to churches that were suffering under a powerful empire. Many understand the city to be Rome, which was built on seven hills, but others see it as a broader symbol of worldwide power that opposes God. Opinions vary.

For today: the powers of this world seem great and lasting, but God is still in control and keeps his word. Live faithfully, and do not put your trust in what the world boasts of as great.
exp.17:4:
Verse 5 says that the sins of Babylon have piled up so high that it is as if they formed a heap reaching to heaven. And God has remembered them: he has not overlooked them, and the time has come to act with justice.

A voice from heaven calls God's people to come out of Babylon. This city symbolizes a system of power, wealth, and corruption that has drawn in nations, kings, and merchants. Some connect it with Rome, others with a worldwide system; it is understood in several ways. The voice explains why they must leave: the judgment is just and comes from God.

God sees everything that seems to go unnoticed, and he does not forget injustice. Today we can ask ourselves: what have I grown used to, in ideas, business, or pleasures, that pulls me away from God? With his help, we can step away from that and live with integrity.
exp.17:6:
It says that Babylon, the great city of the book, lived with pride and luxury, and for that reason she will receive torment and grief in the same measure. She feels secure: she says she sits as a queen, that she is no widow (she has not lost her protector), and that she will never suffer. "Glorified" here means that she exalted herself.

It is a voice from heaven directing the executors of judgment to give her what she deserves. Babylon represents a system of power, wealth, and wickedness that oppressed others. Many relate her to Rome, others to a world system; she is interpreted in several ways. God has not forgotten her sins.

For today: beware of the false security that success or money gives. Live with humility and trust in God, not in what you have.
exp.17:11:
This verse is part of a list of goods that Babylon used to buy. It speaks of gold, silver, precious stones and pearls. It also mentions fine fabrics: linen, silk, and colors such as scarlet and purple, which were very expensive reds. It includes fragrant woods, objects of ivory, of valuable wood, of bronze, of iron and of marble.

Here it is not God who speaks directly, but John, who describes the lament of the merchants of the earth. They weep from a distance, not so much for the city, but because no one buys their merchandise anymore. Many interpreters see in Babylon a symbol of a system of power, luxury and pride; some connect it with Rome, and others with something broader. This is interpreted in several ways.

For today: riches are not evil in themselves, but they can steal our hearts. Ask yourself what things give you security, and trust God more than what you could lose.
exp.17:18:
This verse describes the sailors and ship owners who, when they see the city burning, throw dust on their heads as a sign of mourning. They cry out in tears that the great city, which made them rich through its trade, has been destroyed in a single hour. The word "destroyed" means ruined and left empty.

These are the people who traded by sea with Babylon in John's vision. They weep more over their lost profits than over the city itself. Many interpreters see in Babylon a symbol of a system of power and wealth opposed to God, and some connect it with Rome; others understand it in a broader way. Then heaven rejoices because God brings justice.

For today: examine where you place your security. Riches can vanish quickly, so trust in God and use what you have with honesty and generosity.
exp.17:20:
A mighty angel lifts up a huge stone, something like a millstone (the large wheel once used to grind grain), and throws it into the sea. With this he announces that Babylon, the great city, will be cast down with the same force and violence, and will disappear forever. The image conveys that its ruin will be sudden and complete, leaving no trace behind.

The speaker is an angel within John's vision. It comes after the laments of kings, merchants, and sailors who grew rich through this city. Many understand Babylon to symbolize a system of power, luxury, and injustice that stands against God; some relate it to Rome, and others to a future reality. The gesture shows that God's judgment is final.

Today, this verse invites us not to place our security in riches or powers that seem firm. We can ask ourselves what things dominate our hearts, and trust in God, whose kingdom does endure.
exp.17:21:
It says that in Babylon the music of harps, flutes and trumpets will be heard no more. There will also be no craftsmen of any trade, and the sound of the millstone will not be heard. Musicians are those who play instruments; a craftsman is someone skilled in a trade; the millstone is the stone that grinds the grain.

An angel speaks in John's vision, after announcing the fall of Babylon. This city symbolizes a system of power, luxury and idolatry that oppressed God's people. Some see it as Rome, others as a worldwide system; it is interpreted in several ways. Everyday life, cheerful and busy with work, disappears completely as judgment.

For today: do not put your security in what seems permanent, such as success or comfort. All of that can pass. Put your trust in God, who does justice and remains forever.
exp.17:22:
It says that in Babylon the light of a lamp will no longer shine and the joyful voices of a wedding will no longer be heard. In other words, ordinary daily life and celebration will disappear completely. Two reasons are given: her merchants were the great men of the earth (very rich and powerful people), and by her sorceries (deceptions and hidden practices) all the nations were deceived.

The one speaking is John, who records what a mighty angel announces to him. This is the fall of Babylon, a symbol of corrupt worldly power that opposes God. Many connect her with Rome, others see her as a system that repeats itself throughout history; interpreters do not agree. The judgment comes because she deceived the peoples and persecuted the saints.

For today: do not place your trust in money, success, or whatever glitters and deceives. Ask yourself which things tempt you, and ask God to keep you faithful to Him.
exp.17:23:
It says that in Babylon, the great city of the chapter, the blood of the prophets, of the saints, and of all who were slain on the earth was found. The verse sees the image as suggesting that this city is responsible for much violence and injustice.

The apostle John reports what he sees and hears in the vision of judgment on Babylon. It closes a long lament: the city's music, commerce, and joy come to an end. Interpreters understand it in several ways: as Rome, as a worldwide system of power and corruption, or as both. The text accuses it of unjust wealth, deception, and persecution.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget those who have suffered. We can examine whether we benefit from or stay silent about something unjust, and choose truth and compassion, trusting that God will do justice.
exp.18:8:
This verse says that an angel tells John to write down a blessing: happy are those who have been invited to the supper of the Lamb, who is Jesus. "Blessed" means very happy or favored. "Invited" is the idea of being called to come. Then the angel confirms that these words come from God and are true.

Before this, heaven celebrates that the wedding of the Lamb has arrived. His bride, who represents his people, is dressed in clean linen, which stands for the righteous deeds of the saints. Many understand the bride to be the Church, although some interpret her in other ways. After this, John wants to worship the angel, but the angel stops him and tells him to worship only God.

Today we can live with hope, knowing that God invites us to a feast of joy with Christ. Respond to that invitation with trust and gratitude, and worship God alone.
exp.18:10:
John sees heaven opened, as if a curtain were pulled back. A white horse appears, and the one who rides it is called "Faithful and True." This means he always keeps his word and never deceives. He judges by deciding what is right, and he makes war in righteousness, that is, without wickedness or abuse.

John writes this vision in the book of Revelation, with images full of symbolism. Shortly before, an angel told him to worship God alone. The verses that follow show that this rider is Christ, who is called the Word of God. Many understand the scene as his final victory over evil, although Christians interpret it in several different ways.

For today: when you see injustice and wonder whether God is acting, remember that Christ is faithful and true, and that his justice is perfect. Trust him, and treat others with the same truth and justice.
exp.18:11:
It says that Jesus, the rider on the white horse, has eyes like a flame of fire, which see and examine everything clearly. He wears many crowns, that is, royal crowns, because his authority is complete. He also has a name written that no one understands, only he himself.

John the apostle describes what he sees in a vision. Shortly before, he wanted to worship an angel, and the angel corrected him: only God deserves worship. Now John sees Christ coming as the just judge, called Faithful and True. The secret name shows that Jesus is greater than we can grasp. Some believe it speaks of his divine mystery; the text does not explain it.

For today: do not reduce Jesus to a comfortable idea. He is King and he sees your heart. Trust in his justice, worship him alone, and draw near with humility, knowing there will always be more of him to know.
exp.18:12:
It says that Jesus, the rider on the white horse, is wearing clothing stained or soaked in blood. He is also given the name "the Word of God." The verse adds that a word like "dipped" means colored or soaked in something, and that "word" is another way of saying the Word.

John describes here a vision of an open heaven, where Christ appears as a King who judges with justice. This name connects him with John 1:1, where Christ is the Word. About the blood there are several interpretations: it may refer to his sacrifice on the cross, to the blood of his enemies in judgment, or to both. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: if Jesus is the Word of God, we can trust that what God says is true. Today you can read the Bible knowing that Christ speaks to you there, and that his sacrifice gives you hope.
exp.18:14:
He says that Christ, the rider on the white horse, has a sharp sword that comes out of his mouth. With it he will strike the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, that is, with firm authority, and he treads the winepress, the press where grapes are squeezed, as an image of God's judgment.

John is describing his vision of Christ's return, called the Word of God. The sword from the mouth is usually understood as his word with the power to judge, although it is interpreted in different ways. The language uses images from the prophets and the Psalms. It shows that evil will not have the last word.

For today: if Christ is the righteous Judge, I do not need to take revenge or despair in the face of injustice. I can trust God, live with humility, and seek to do good today.
exp.18:15:
He says that Jesus, the rider who comes in glory, has a name written on his robe and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords. The "thigh" is the place where a warrior carried his sword, so the name is in full view. Some think it is written on the robe at the height of the thigh; the text does not specify this.

John describes a vision of Christ's final victory over the nations that oppose God. The verses before it show him as a just judge, with heavenly armies following him. This title declares that no human ruler and no power of evil stands above him. What follows shows the judgment on those who rebelled.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus has the final word over history. When we see injustice or powers that seem unbeatable, we can keep obeying him with confidence, and not give any leader, money, or system the loyalty that belongs to him alone.
exp.18:16:
He says John saw an angel standing in the sun, who called out with a loud voice to all the birds flying in the midst of heaven. He orders them to come and gather together to the supper of the great God.

John describes a vision. Before this, Christ appears as King of kings, with a sharp sword coming from his mouth, ready to judge. This scene is the opposite of the marriage supper of the Lamb: there is a feast for the faithful, and here there is judgment on those who oppose God. Many understand the images symbolically; others, more literally. The text itself shows that the judgment is certain.

For today: there is no need to fear human power or envy the proud, because Christ is the final King. Live with humility and faithfulness, trusting that God will do justice in his time.
exp.18:19:
This verse says that the beast, a power hostile to God, was captured together with the false prophet. The false prophet had performed miraculous signs to deceive those who received the mark of the beast and worshiped his image. The two were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone.

John describes his vision of the final battle, when Christ appears riding a white horse. The beast and the kings of the earth gather to fight against Him. The book was written to encourage persecuted Christians. Many believers understand these scenes literally, and others see them as symbolic images of Christ's triumph over evil.

Today we can remember that deception and unjust power do not have the last word. When everything seems confused, let us remain faithful to Jesus and not worship anything that competes with Him.
exp.18:20:
It says that the rest of those who joined the beast in the war against Christ died by the sword that comes out of his mouth. The birds were filled with eating the flesh of the dead. The sword from the mouth represents his word, by which he judges.

John describes a vision of the end. Christ appears riding a white horse, as King and Judge. The kings of the earth join the beast to fight against Him, but they lose. Many Christians understand the image symbolically, others more literally. In either case, the message is that evil does not have the last word.

For today: if the world seems dominated by injustice, trust that Christ will reign and bring about justice. Remain faithful today, without taking revenge, and with hope.
exp.19:0:
John says he saw an angel come down from heaven. This angel held in one hand the key to the bottomless pit, which is a deep place where the powers of evil are shut away, and also a great chain.

John speaks, the one who received this vision from the Lord Jesus while he was exiled on the island of Patmos. This scene follows the defeat of the beast and his false prophet. Christians understand the thousand years in different ways: some take them literally, others as a symbol of the present time of the Church. What is clear is that God has authority over evil.

For today: even when evil sometimes seems strong, it does not have the final word. If you trust in Christ, you can live with hope and peace, knowing that God holds the key and the control of everything.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that the angel grabbed Satan and bound him for a thousand years. Seizing him means he captured or arrested him. The Devil is called the dragon and the old serpent, names that link him with deception from the beginning, as in Eden.

John recounts this vision in the book of Revelation, written to encourage Christians who were under pressure and persecution. It shows that evil has limits and that God has the final word. Christians interpret the thousand years in different ways: some see it as a literal future kingdom, others as a symbolic period that is already underway. Both views agree that Christ wins.

For today: when you feel that evil weighs too heavily, remember that Satan has chains and that God controls him. Trust in Christ and stand firm, without fear.
exp.19:5:
It says that whoever takes part in the first resurrection is blessed and set apart for God. The "second death" (according to Revelation 20:14, the final separation from God) has no power over them. They will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him a thousand years.

John writes this vision to encourage Christians who were suffering persecution for their faith. It shows that the faithful, even those who died for Jesus, do not lose in the end. Christians understand the "thousand years" in several ways: as a literal future time, as the present age of the church, or as a symbol. It is also debated what the "first resurrection" is.

For today: if your life is in the hands of Christ, death does not have the last word. That hope can give you courage to remain faithful to Jesus, even when it costs you, and to serve him as part of his priestly people.
exp.19:9:
This verse says that the devil, who deceived the nations, is thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur. The beast and the false prophet are already there. Christians understand this torment in different ways, but the text clearly shows that evil will be fully judged.

John writes this vision for Christians who were under pressure and persecution. Just before, the devil gathers the nations against God's people, and God stops them with fire from heaven. This verse marks the end of the deceiver. Then comes the judgment before the great white throne. Interpreters differ on how to understand the symbols, but all of them see God's final victory.

For today: when evil seems to be winning, trust that God has the last word. Stay faithful and do not let yourself be deceived.
exp.19:10:
John describes seeing a great white throne, with God sitting on it. Before his presence, the earth and the heaven flee away, and there is no longer any place for them. This is an image of God's holiness and power, so great that creation can no longer remain before Him.

John is writing Revelation, and here he relates a vision. He has just seen the final defeat of the devil and of those who rebelled. Now the scene of the final judgment begins, which is described in the verses that follow. Christians interpret how these events fit together in different ways, but nearly all agree that God has the last word.

For today: you can live without fear of injustice, because God will judge with perfect truth. This invites us to live with humility, trusting in the grace of Christ and treating others with justice and mercy.
exp.19:11:
John says he sees all the dead, great and small, standing before God. Books are opened in which everything each person did is written, and another book is opened, the book of life. The dead are judged according to their works.

John wrote Revelation to encourage Christians who were facing pressure and persecution. He is describing a vision of the final judgment, after the defeat of the devil. Christians have understood in various ways exactly what the books and the book of life are, but the central message is clear: God is just, and no one escapes his gaze.

Today it invites us to live with humility and honesty, knowing that God sees everything. We can trust that he will do justice, and turn to Christ for forgiveness, for life is found in him alone.
exp.20:0:
John tells that he saw a new heaven and a new earth, because the first heaven and the first earth passed away, that is, they came to an end as they were. He also says that the sea was no more, meaning that there was no longer any sea.

John, the author of Revelation, receives this vision from God. It comes after the final judgment and before the description of the new Jerusalem. In the Bible the sea sometimes symbolizes chaos, danger or separation. Some believe this is a renewal of creation, and others a total replacement; the Bible does not fully make this clear. The next verse shows what is central: God will live with his people.

For today: when the world seems broken or unsafe, remember that God promises to make all things new. That hope can give you peace and strength to remain faithful and to love today.
exp.20:1:
John says that he saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven. It was prepared like a bride dressed in her finest clothes to meet her husband. The word "adorned" means arranged, decorated with beauty.

John wrote the book of Revelation to encourage Christians who were suffering pressure and persecution. After describing the final judgment, he shows the goal of history: God makes everything new. The city is a picture; many understand that it represents God's people, while others also see a real place. What matters is that God is the one who brings it, and he will live with his people.

For today: when pain or injustice weighs on you, remember that the story does not end in chaos. God promises to be near his people and to wipe away every tear. That hope helps you live today with patience, faithfulness, and comfort.
exp.20:3:
This verse promises that God himself will comfort his people with tenderness, like someone drying the tears of a child. It announces that there will be no more death, no more crying, no more outcry (cries of anguish), and no more pain. "The former things" are the world marked by suffering and sin, which has already passed away.

The one speaking is a great voice from heaven, and John writes it down as part of a vision. The voice announces that God will dwell with people in the new Jerusalem. Then the one seated on the throne confirms that his words are faithful and true. Many believers understand this as the final hope of Christians.

For today: if you are going through pain or loss, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. You can bring your tears to God, trusting that he sees them and that one day he will wipe them away completely.
exp.20:6:
This verse promises that whoever overcomes will inherit all things. God himself says that he will be their God, and that the person will be his son.

The speaker is the one seated on the throne, who is God, and he says this at the end of John's vision, when he promises to make all things new. Shortly before, he offers the water of life freely to the one who is thirsty. Then he warns those who reject God. Many understand overcoming as remaining faithful to Christ to the end, trusting in him, though some explain it with more emphasis on perseverance.

For today: when you feel tired of struggling, remember that your hope does not depend on your own strength, but on God's promise. Today you can draw near to him with confidence, as a child, and keep moving forward in faith.
exp.20:9:
John tells how the Spirit carried him away to a great and high mountain, and from there he saw the great holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. "Carried me" means that the Spirit took him there. This vision was not a physical journey, but something John saw while under the power of the Spirit.

John is speaking, the one who receives the revelation of Jesus Christ. An angel has just invited him to see the bride, the wife of the Lamb. Earlier the final judgment was described; now the destiny of God's people is shown. Many understand the city as an image of the redeemed people and of God's presence with them. Others also see a real place. Christians interpret it in several ways.

God has prepared a secure and pure future for those who trust in Him. If today you are going through pain or injustice, remember that the story does not end in chaos. Live with hope, faithfulness and peace, because the city comes from God.
exp.20:10:
It says that the new Jerusalem shone with the glory of God. The word "glory" here means splendor, or radiance. Its light was like a very precious stone, like jasper, and it was clear as crystal. Jasper is used for a precious stone; scholars debate whether it was clear or of another color, but the text describes it as shining and pure.

John speaks, recounting a vision. An angel carries him in the Spirit to a high mountain to show him the city, called the bride of the Lamb. This is part of the ending of the book, where God renews all things and lives forever with his people. Many understand the image as a symbol of God's people in their glorified state.

For today: If the future of the children of God is a life full of his glory, pure and transparent, we can live with hope and ask him to make us more sincere and pure from now on. His light hides nothing; it gives us peace.
exp.20:11:
It says the holy city, the New Jerusalem, has a wall that is great and high. It has twelve gates, and at each gate there is an angel. Written on the gates are the names of the twelve tribes of Israel. "Wall" is the barrier that surrounds the city, and "tribes" are the families that came down from the sons of Jacob.

John writes what God showed him in a vision near the end of the book. An angel carried him to a high mountain to see the city coming down out of heaven. The walls and gates speak of security and of entrance. The names of the tribes and, in the verse that follows, the names of the apostles, join God's people of all times together. Many see in this a symbol; others take it in a more literal way.

For today: God gives you security and a place among his people. Rest in the knowledge that you belong to a family far larger than yourself.
exp.20:12:
It says that the holy city, the new Jerusalem, has twelve gates, three on each side: to the east, to the north, to the south and to the west.

John describes what he sees in a vision of the new creation. An angel shows him the city, and the gates bear the names of the twelve tribes of Israel. Many understand that the gates opening toward the four directions signify that people from all over the world can enter. Others see here a symbol of the whole people of God. The text does not explain further, so it is wise to speak with humility.

For today: God has a place for people from everywhere. We can ask ourselves whom we have left out of our friendships or our church, and offer them today a kind invitation, just as God opens his gates.
exp.20:13:
It says that the wall of the New Jerusalem rests on twelve foundations, and that on them are written the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. "Foundations" are the bases or footings. "The Lamb" is Jesus, who gave himself up for his people.

John is describing the vision God gave him of the heavenly city. Earlier, the gates bear the names of the twelve tribes of Israel. Now the foundations bear the names of the apostles. Many understand that this joins the people of God from the Old and New Testaments together, although the details are interpreted in several ways.

For today: our faith rests on a foundation that God laid, the message of Jesus that the apostles passed on to us. Read the Bible regularly and build your life on that teaching, not on passing fashions or opinions.
exp.20:15:
It says the holy city is shaped like a square, with the same length and width. The angel measured it with a golden measuring rod and gave it twelve thousand furlongs. A furlong was an ancient unit of about 185 meters, so that comes to roughly 2,200 kilometers. Also, the height is equal to the length and the width, so it forms a perfect cube.

John speaks, recounting what he sees in the vision. The angel measures the city to show that God has designed it with exactness and that it is secure. Many see in the numbers a symbol of fullness and perfection. Others take them in a more literal way. The Bible does not fully clarify this.

For today: if God prepared the home of his people with such care, we can trust that he also takes care of the details of your life. Rest in his plan and wait with hope.
exp.20:16:
It says that the angel measured the wall of the holy city and found it to be one hundred and forty-four cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of length, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 centimeters. The phrase "according to the measure of a man, that is, of the angel" means that the angel used the same measure that people use, so that John could understand it.

John is seeing the New Jerusalem, and the angel who speaks with him is measuring it with a golden reed. Interpreters differ: many see in the number 144 (12 times 12) a symbol of God's people, made up of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles. Others take it as a literal measurement.

For today: God cares for His people with security and order. You can trust that your future with Him is well kept, and live with hope.
exp.20:18:
The verse says that the foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of precious stone. It names the first four: jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, and emerald. "Foundations" are the bases that hold up the wall. The ancient names of some stones may not match exactly the gems we know today.

John writes down what the angel shows him in a vision of the end of time. Shortly before, the angel measured the wall, and John describes the shining city as pure gold. Many understand these images as symbols of the beauty, security, and glory of God with his people, though some see them in a more literal way.

For today: God prepares something beautiful and firm for those who trust him. When you feel tired or discouraged, remember that your hope has a secure foundation. Live today with patience and joy.
exp.20:19:
This verse completes the list of the twelve precious stones that adorn the foundations of the wall of the New Jerusalem. Here appear the sardonyx, the sardius, the chrysolite, the beryl, the topaz, the chrysoprase, the jacinth, and the amethyst. Ancient names do not always match the gems we today know by those same names, so it is not certain to identify each stone exactly.

John speaks, recounting what the angel shows him in his vision of the holy city. He describes the final home of God's people with images of beauty and glory. Many see an echo of the stones on the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28), and the foundations are connected with the apostles (v. 14), although this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God is preparing a future full of beauty and variety. This encourages us to remain steadfast in the midst of difficulties, trusting that the best is still to come.
exp.20:20:
It says that the holy city has twelve gates, and each one is a single enormous pearl. The main street, or plaza, is pure gold so clear that it looks like transparent glass.

John speaks, describing what he saw in a vision of the new Jerusalem at the end of the book. Many understand these images as symbols of beauty, purity, and the value of life with God. Some see them in a more literal way; Christians do not always agree. What follows clarifies the central point: God himself and the Lamb are its temple and its light.

For today: if the future God is preparing is so beautiful and clean, we can live with hope and not be discouraged by the trials of now. Today you can ask him to help you value his presence more than the shining things of this world.
exp.20:21:
It says that John, in his vision of the new city, saw no temple in it. The reason is that the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb, who is Jesus, are the temple of the city. "It" refers to the city, the New Jerusalem.

The one speaking is John, who tells what an angel showed him at the end of Revelation. In the Old Testament, the temple was the place where people could draw near to God, but with limits. Here it is shown that there is no longer any distance: God's presence fills everything. Some see this in a more symbolic way, others more literally, but the central message is the same.

For today: you do not need a special place to meet with God. Right now you can speak to him simply, at home, at work, or on the road, and live with the hope of always being close to him.
exp.20:23:
It says that the nations that have been saved will walk guided by the light of the city, which is the new Jerusalem. The kings of the earth will bring their glory and their honor into it.

The one speaking is John, who recounts the vision he received of the holy city. He has just said that God and the Lamb are its temple and its light. That is why the nations do not walk by their own light, but by God's. Interpreters explain in various ways exactly who the "kings" are, but all agree that they place their riches and honors before God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we do with our achievements, talents, and recognitions. This vision encourages us to offer them to God with humility and to live, from now on, guided by his light.
exp.20:24:
It says that the gates of the New Jerusalem will always stand open during the day, and that there will be no night there. In ancient times the gates of a city were shut at night for safety. Here, since there is no night, there is no danger and no need to close them.

John writes down what God showed him about the final city, where God and the Lamb (Jesus) are the light. The open gates speak of complete peace and safety. The next verse makes clear that nothing unclean will enter, so the openness does not mean carelessness; rather, evil no longer exists there. Some understand these images symbolically and others more literally.

For today: if God promises us a place without fear or darkness, we can live with hope and confidence, even in difficult times. Today, hand over to God one worry that is taking away your peace.
exp.20:26:
It says that in the holy city, the New Jerusalem, nothing impure will enter, nor anyone who practices detestable things or deceit. Only those whose names are written in the book of life of the Lamb, who is Jesus, will enter. The word "abomination" refers to things that God hates.

John writes what God showed him in a vision. Shortly before, he describes a city with gates always open, without night, where the nations bring their glory. This phrase clarifies that this openness is not for everything, since the city is pure. Christians often understand that entrance depends on belonging to the Lamb, not on one's own merits, though some interpret it with different nuances.

Today, this invites us to rest in the grace of Christ and, at the same time, to live with sincerity. You might today give up a small lie and ask God for help to speak the truth.
exp.21:0:
John describes a vision of the new heaven. An angel shows him a river of the water of life, pure and bright as crystal. This river flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, who is Jesus. The word "clear" in the verse means that it shines with great light, so the river is bright and transparent. The water of life represents the full and eternal life that God gives.

The apostle John is the speaker, writing the Revelation to encourage Christians who were suffering persecution. We are near the very end of the Bible, in the vision of the new Jerusalem. Many see here a return to Eden, but now without the curse. Some understand the river symbolically, and others literally; the text does not fully clarify this.

For today: true life comes from God, not from ourselves. Each day you can draw near to Him in prayer and in His Word, with the hope that one day everything will be restored.
exp.21:1:
In the city of heaven, in the middle of its main street and on both sides of the river of life, stands the tree of life. It bears twelve kinds of fruit, one each month, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations. The word "street" here refers to a wide road or avenue, and "healing" means cure or wholeness.

John writes what the angel showed him in a vision, near the end of Revelation. After describing judgment and the victory of Christ, the Bible shows the final state of the restored creation. The tree of life reminds us of Eden (Genesis 2), now open again. Some understand the leaves for healing literally, and others as a picture of the fullness of peace among the peoples.

For today: God promises a complete restoration, not just a partial one. If you carry pain, division, or weariness today, you can wait with confidence, and in the meantime be someone who brings healing and peace to those around you.
exp.21:2:
It says that in the new city there will no longer be a curse, that is, the consequences of sin and the separation from God that began in Genesis 3. Instead, the throne of God and of the Lamb (Jesus) will be there, and God's servants will serve him. Serving here also includes worship.

Context: John writes what an angel showed him in a vision, near the end of the book. He addresses Christians who were under pressure and persecution, to encourage them with the promise that God will restore everything. Many see here a return to Eden, but now with God living in the midst of his people. Scholars interpret in various ways how literal the images are, but they agree on the central hope.

For today: When pain or mistakes weigh you down, remember that the story does not end in the curse. Today you can practice that hope by serving God with joy and helping others.
exp.21:3:
It says the servants of God will see his face. This means standing face to face with God, something that was not possible before for sinful human beings. Also, his name will be on their foreheads, a sign that they belong to him and that he recognizes them as his own.

Here John speaks, describing the final vision of the new Jerusalem. There is no longer any curse, and the throne of God and of the Lamb is in the midst of his people. It was written to encourage believers who were suffering and waiting. Some understand the marked forehead as an image of identity and closeness; the text presents it as a symbol, not as something to be explained in detail.

Today you can live knowing whom you belong to. When you feel tired or ignored, remember that God knows you by name and that your hope is to see him face to face. That encourages you to be faithful today.
exp.21:4:
This verse says that in the new creation there will be no more darkness. God's people will not depend on lamps or on the sun, because God himself will be their light. And they will reign with him forever.

The speaker is John, who describes the vision Jesus gave him at the end of the book. He writes to Christians who were under pressure and persecution, to encourage them. He shows them that the end of the story is the full presence of God, without curse, without darkness, and without fear. Some see symbolic language here and others a more literal meaning, but the central message is the same.

For today: when you are in a night of pain or doubt, remember that God is your light and your final hope. Today you can ask him to guide you through his Word while that day comes.
exp.21:5:
Here the angel tells John that everything he has seen in this book is trustworthy and true. Being "faithful" means that these words can be believed, and being "true" means they are not false. God, who spoke earlier through the prophets, has now sent his angel to show his servants what must happen soon, quickly, or without delay.

The one speaking is one of the angels who guided John through the visions. We are at the end of Revelation, after the description of eternal life with God. The message serves as a seal: what is written comes from God himself. How the words about what must happen soon are understood varies among readers, but all agree that it calls us to take the message seriously.

For today: when the world seems confusing or unjust, rest in the fact that God's promises are true. Read his Word with confidence and live with hope and faithfulness.
exp.21:6:
Here Jesus is the one speaking, saying that he is coming soon. Right after, he declares blessed, that is, happy and favored, the one who keeps the sayings of this prophecy, meaning the one who obeys them and holds them carefully in the heart.

The book of Revelation comes to its end. Just before this, the angel confirmed that these words are faithful and true, and that God showed his servants things that must happen soon. Here Jesus takes up the word to encourage believers. Christians understand "coming soon" in different ways: as something about to happen, or as a sure promise that could be fulfilled suddenly.

For today: it is not enough to read or study this book; the blessing belongs to the one who lives it. Today you can choose one teaching from the Bible and put it into practice faithfully, waiting for Christ with hope.
exp.21:11:
He says that Jesus is coming soon. Jesus says that he brings with him what he will give to each person according to what they did, that is, according to the way they lived.

The one speaking is Jesus, in the final words of the book of Revelation. Earlier he said that the time is near and that the message should not be kept hidden. Then he presents himself as the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. Some understand "soon" as closeness in time; others understand it as something that will arrive suddenly. Christians have interpreted it in several ways.

Today we can live each day with our eyes fixed on Christ. This is not about living in fear, but about doing good with sincerity, trusting that God sees everything and is just.
exp.21:13:
It says that those who obey the commandments of Jesus are happy and blessed. "Blessed" here means very richly blessed. The word translated "right" means permission or authority: they will be able to eat from the tree of life and enter through the gates of the holy city, the New Jerusalem.

Jesus is the one speaking, and he has just said that he is coming soon and that he will give to each person according to what they have done. He presents himself as the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. He writes to the churches to encourage them to remain faithful. Some manuscripts have a different wording for this verse, one about those who wash their robes, instead of the wording about keeping his commandments; scholars debate this, but the underlying meaning is similar: a clean and faithful life.

For today: obeying Jesus is not a burden but the path to true blessing. Today you can choose one concrete action, such as forgiving someone or being honest, and do it out of love for him.
exp.21:14:
This verse says that outside the city of God will be the "dogs," which here is a harsh way of speaking about people who are impure or shameless. Also left outside are the sorcerers (those who practice witchcraft), the whoremongers (those who live without restraint sexually, to use the word of this version), the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices a lie.

Jesus is speaking, near the end of the book. He has just blessed those who keep his commandments and enter through the gates of the city. This verse shows the other side: whoever clings to evil without repenting does not enter. But right away Jesus invites: "whosoever will, let him take the water of life."

For today: ask yourself whether there is some lie or habit you are protecting. Bring it honestly to Jesus, for his invitation remains open to whoever comes to him.
exp.13:11:
In the middle of these hard times, the perseverance of the saints is on display. The saints are the believers who belong to God. Here "perseverance" means holding on firmly and not giving up. These believers are described as people who keep the commandments of God and hold to the faith of Jesus, which can be understood as faith placed in Jesus or the faith that Jesus taught.

John relates his vision. Just before, there is a warning about punishment for those who worship the beast and receive its mark. This verse contrasts those people with the faithful, who resist the pressure to follow the beast. Then a voice from heaven promises rest to those who die in the Lord. Interpreters explain the details of this vision in several ways.

For today: even when faithfulness costs something, keep obeying God and trusting in Jesus, even in small things, because God sees your perseverance.
exp.5:6:
Here John reports that the Lamb opens the fourth seal, and then he hears the fourth living creature. Its voice says: "Come!" It is the same call that was heard with the other three seals.

The fourth living creature speaks, one of those surrounding God's throne. Its call introduces the pale (or greenish) horse, whose rider is named Death. Interpreters understand this in different ways: some as real judgments in history, others as symbols of what happens in every age. It is seen that everything happens under God's control, since the power was given to him.

For today: when the suffering and injustice of the world frighten us, we can look on calmly, remembering that Christ has control and sustains his people.
exp.2:1:
The verse calls the church to wake up and stay alert. "Wake up" means to be on guard, not to stay asleep. What remains of their faith is still worth keeping but is about to die out, so it must be strengthened. The reason is that Jesus has not found their deeds complete in the sight of God.

The one speaking is Jesus, who holds "the seven Spirits of God" and "the seven stars." He addresses the church in Sardis, which had a good reputation but was spiritually dead inside. His correction aims to lead them to change their hearts before it is too late. About Sardis, it is best not to say more than the text states.

For today: do not settle for having a good reputation or for doing religious things out of habit. Honestly ask yourself which area of your faith is growing cold, and take one concrete step today, such as praying, reading the Bible, or reconciling with someone.
exp.20:14:
This verse says that the angel who was speaking with John carried a golden measuring rod. The measuring rod was a long staff used for taking measurements. With it he was going to measure three things: the city, its gates, and its walls.

John is describing his vision of the New Jerusalem, the city of God at the end of time. The angel is the one who shows him everything. Measuring in the Bible usually indicates that something belongs to God and is under his care. That the rod is made of gold suggests that everything in that city is pure and precious. Interpreters explain the measurements in different ways, and they do not all agree.

For today: God knows exactly what is his, and you are part of it. You can rest in the knowledge that your life is not neglected or forgotten. Today, bring to him in prayer what worries you, trusting that he has it measured and under control.
exp.17:0:
John tells us that, after these things, he saw another angel coming down from heaven with great authority. The earth was illuminated by his glory. The point of the verse is that the earth was made bright by the angel's brilliance.

John speaks here, recounting his vision in the book of Revelation. This angel comes to announce the fall of Babylon, a symbol of the system of pride, wealth and idolatry that opposes God. Interpreters disagree about whether it represents Rome, a future power, or something broader. What is clear is that God acts with authority and judges evil.

For today: do not let yourself be dazzled by the power or the money of this world, because they do not last. Place your trust in God, whose light and justice do endure.
exp.1:14:
The passage says that in the church at Pergamum there were some who held to the teaching of the Nicolaitans, and Jesus says he hates this. The words "in the same way" connect this teaching to what was said about Balaam just before. Calling it something Jesus hates means he firmly rejects it.

Jesus, the risen one, speaks to the church, praising Pergamum for staying faithful in a hostile city where Antipas was killed. But he also corrects them, because they tolerated teachings that encouraged mixing with idolatry and immorality. We do not know for certain who the Nicolaitans were. They are linked to this kind of teaching, but there are different views about where they came from.

For today: being faithful in serious moments is not enough if we tolerate teachings that contradict Christ. Test what you hear against the Bible, and if something pulls you away from purity or faithfulness, repent and return to Jesus.
exp.2:13:
Jesus speaks to the church in Laodicea, the last of the seven letters in Revelation. He presents himself with three titles: "the Amen," meaning the one who is firm and true; "the faithful and true witness," who always tells the truth; and "the Originator of God's creation," which many understand as the source of all creation, the one who stands above it. The word "angel" here may refer to the messenger or the person responsible for that church.

Christ, risen, speaks to a comfortable church that has lost its fervor. Before rebuking it, he presents himself as someone trustworthy. What he will say next is a truth spoken with love, though it will hurt.

For today: if Jesus is the faithful witness, we can let him tell us the truth about our spiritual life, without excuses. Today you can ask him to show you where you have grown cold or settled in, and answer him with honesty.
exp.15:10:
This verse says that the people, while suffering pains and sores, cursed and spoke against God, whom it calls "the God of heaven." Yet they did not turn from their wrongdoing or change their hearts. To curse God is to speak against Him with contempt, and to repent is to turn away from one's wrong course and be sorry for what one has done.

John writes what he saw in his vision. This is the fifth bowl of God's judgment, poured out on the throne of the beast, whose kingdom was plunged into darkness. Many understand that the text shows the hardness of the human heart, although there is debate about how these scenes will be fulfilled. The passage emphasizes that even their pain did not lead them to God.

For today: suffering can soften us or harden us. When trials come, instead of blaming God, we can humbly ask Him what we should correct and draw near to Him with sincerity.
exp.5:10:
Each of the martyrs was given a white robe. They were also told to rest a little while longer, until the full number of their fellow servants and brothers, who would be killed just as they had been, was complete.

"Each one" means one for every person. To rest means to take a break from struggle. "Fellow servants" are those who serve the same Lord.

Context: at the fifth seal, John sees under the altar those who were killed for their faith, and they ask God how long it will be before justice comes. God answers with comfort and with a call to wait. Many understand the white robes as a symbol of victory and purity, though their exact meaning is debated. Then comes the sixth seal, with signs of judgment.

For today: if you are waiting for justice and the delay wears you down, you can bring your cry to God honestly. He sees his own, cares for them, and comforts them. Trust that his timing is perfect.
exp.16:6:
Here the angel asks John why he is so amazed. He promises to tell him the hidden meaning of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The word "mystery" here means something hidden that God makes known.

One of the angels of the seven bowls is speaking. John has just seen a woman drunk with the blood of the saints, and he was deeply struck by it. The angel does not leave him confused but is going to explain the vision to him. Interpreters disagree about who the woman is: many see Rome or a world system opposed to God, and others propose other readings.

For today: when evil seems powerful and leaves us puzzled, let us not stay only amazed. Let us ask God for understanding through his Word, and trust that he is in control.
exp.9:1:
Here John describes that the strong angel held in his hand a small scroll that lay open. He placed his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land. The verse of the words "small scroll" and "lay open" is this: a small scroll is a little roll of writing, and "lay open" shows that it could be read.

John, the author of Revelation, tells what he saw between the sixth and seventh trumpets. The angel with feet on sea and land shows authority over all creation. Some believe this angel is Christ, others that he is a mighty angel sent by God; the Bible does not make this clear. There is also no agreement about what the small scroll contains.

For today: God has authority over the whole world, even when the news seems chaotic. You can rest in the knowledge that He guides history, and trust what He has revealed without being anxious about what He has not explained.
exp.1:7:
Jesus tells John to write a letter to the angel of the church in Smyrna, that is, to the messenger or leader of the church there. Jesus presents himself as the First and the Last, meaning the one who was there before all things and will remain at the end. He also says that he died and returned to life.

The one speaking is the risen Christ. Smyrna was a city in Asia Minor, and this church was suffering poverty and opposition. That is why Jesus presents himself as the one who conquered death: in this way he prepares his readers to receive words of encouragement in the face of the suffering that was coming.

For today: when you are afraid or go through a trial, remember that Jesus has already passed through death and came out victorious. You can trust that he has the last word over your life.
exp.5:4:
It says that Jesus, the Lamb, opens the third seal, and one of the living creatures says to John, "Come!" John looks and sees a black horse. The rider holds a pair of scales in his hand, the kind used to weigh and sell food.

John recounts his vision of heaven. The four riders show sufferings that strike the world. After the war of the red horse comes the black one, which is usually understood as hunger and scarcity, since the following verse speaks of food at very high prices. Some interpret it as future events and others as realities throughout all of history. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: when you see injustice or scarcity, do not remain indifferent. Share what you have with someone who needs it, and trust that Christ, who opens the seals, still has control.
exp.12:6:
It says the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints, that is, the believers, and to conquer them. It was also given authority over every tribe, people, tongue, and nation. "Was given" means "was granted": its power is not its own. "Authority" means the right and ability to rule.

John writes this vision to churches that were under pressure and persecution. The beast represents a political power hostile to God; interpreters relate it to Rome, to a future antichrist, or to both. What matters most is that God sets limits: forty-two months, and everything "was given" to it. The following passage reminds us that the Lamb already has the names of his own written down.

For today: if you suffer pressure because of your faith, do not confuse an apparent defeat with the end. Remain faithful and steadfast, trusting that God is still in control and knows your name.
exp.1:25:
The writer says that Jesus promises something special to the one who overcomes, meaning the one who stays faithful and keeps living out what He taught until the end of life or until His return. To that person He will give authority over the nations. The phrase "continues in My work" points to a life of following Him, not to earning salvation through effort.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, in His letter to the church in Thyatira. Some believers there were under pressure to accept false teaching and immoral conduct. Jesus encourages the faithful to hold firm. How this authority will be fulfilled is understood in several ways: some see it in the future kingdom, others as sharing in the rule of Christ.

For today: be steady in small things. This week, choose one faithful decision, such as telling the truth or refusing something that dishonors God, and trust that He sees and rewards your perseverance.
exp.18:7:
She is described as the bride of the Lamb, who is God's people, and she was given clothing of fine linen, bright and pure. "Was given" shows that it is a gift. The fine linen represents a life that pleases God.

John writes what he hears in his vision: a great multitude praises God because the marriage of the Lamb, that is, Christ, has come. It is celebrated that God reigns and that his people are ready. Some see here works that God himself produces in believers; others place more emphasis on their faithfulness. Both ideas fit the text.

Today: live your faith through righteous acts and love, knowing that God is the one who gives you the grace and strength to do them.
exp.12:5:
It says the beast opened its mouth to speak against God, insulting his name, his dwelling place, and those who live in heaven. To blaspheme is to speak with contempt and mockery toward what is sacred.

John writes this vision to Christians who were under pressure and persecution. The beast represents an oppressive power that opposes God and receives authority for a limited time: forty-two months. Interpreters understand it in different ways: as Rome, as a future political system, or as a general symbol of evil. What is clear is that its power is permitted, not eternal.

When evil seems to speak loudly and win, do not be impressed or intimidated. Its time is limited, and God still reigns. Stay faithful, speak with respect toward what is sacred, and trust that your name is in the hands of the Lamb.
exp.11:15:
The verse says that the earth helped the woman. The earth opened its mouth and swallowed up the river that the dragon had poured out of his mouth to sweep her away.

John writes this vision in Revelation to encourage believers who were being persecuted. The woman is usually understood as the people of God, and the dragon as Satan (12:9). The river may represent persecution or deception, but interpreters explain it in several ways, just as they do the way the earth helps her. What is clear is that God protects his people in unexpected ways.

When you feel that an attack or a pressure is sweeping you away, remember that God can care for you with resources you did not imagine. Trust in him, stay faithful, and ask for eyes to see his help.
exp.18:2:
It says that the crowd in heaven shouts "Hallelujah" a second time, which means "praise God." Also, the smoke of the judged city rises forever and ever. The smoke is an image that God's judgment is complete and final.

The great crowd in heaven speaks, celebrating that God has judged the great harlot, a symbol of Babylon, the city and the system that corrupted the earth and killed God's servants. Interpreters understand her in different ways: Rome, a world power, or any system opposed to God. They praise because God did justice and avenged the blood of his people.

Today we can trust that God sees every injustice and will resolve it in his time. That lets us wait without bitterness and praise him, even when evil seems to win.
exp.16:4:
The verse says that the woman had a name written on her forehead: "A mysterious name: Babylon the Great, the Mother of Prostitutes and of the Abominations of the Earth." The word "prostitutes" here refers to unfaithfulness to God, and "abominations" are things that are deeply detestable to God. That name shows that she is the source and model of all that corruption.

John relates what an angel shows him in a vision. Babylon was an ancient city, a symbol of pride and opposition to God. For that reason, here it is a symbol. Interpreters differ: some see Rome, others a corrupt religious or political system, others the world opposed to God. The angel says he will explain the "mystery," that is, a hidden meaning.

Today we can examine which bright things in the world attract us and draw us away from God. Let us ask for wisdom so that we are not dazzled by luxury, power, or false religion, and so that we remain faithful to Christ.
exp.10:13:
The verse says the second woe is now over and the third woe is coming soon. A "woe" is an expression of grief or misfortune. In this verse, "shortly" means soon or swiftly.

The text does not say clearly who is speaking, but it seems to be the voice that accompanies John's vision, perhaps the angel or the eagle that announced the three woes earlier. It comes after the story of the two witnesses, their ascent to heaven, and the earthquake. Interpreters differ on how to understand these symbols. The verse marks a transition toward the seventh trumpet, where it is proclaimed that the kingdom of the world becomes that of Christ.

For today: even though there are times of pain and judgment, God leads history toward its goal. We can live with patience, faithfulness, and hope, trusting that Christ will reign.
exp.13:4:
It says that no lie was found in the mouths of these people, and that they are blameless. "Lie" means a false statement made on purpose. A "blameless" person is one who cannot rightly be charged with wrongdoing. They are described as people of integrity, whose words and lives are clean.

John describes a vision of heaven. He speaks of the group of the 144,000, who follow the Lamb (Christ) and were bought for God. Some understand them to be a literal number, and others take them to symbolize the whole faithful people of God. Their honesty stands in contrast to the lies of the deceiver and of the beast that appear in nearby chapters. Then an angel calls everyone to fear God.

For today: watch your words. Strive to speak the truth even when it costs you, and ask God to cleanse you and help you live with integrity, knowing that Christ has already bought you with his blood.
exp.18:13:
This verse describes the armies of heaven who follow Christ, riding on white horses. They are dressed in fine linen, white and pure. The fine linen is cloth of very high quality. Notice that their clothing is pure and unstained, unlike the clothing of Christ, which is stained with blood.

John, the author, recounts a vision he received. It shows Jesus, called "the Word of God," coming as King and Judge. Many believe these armies are the faithful believers and the angels, though the text does not fully make this clear. Later in this same book, the fine linen is connected with the righteous deeds of the saints (19:8). Notice also that the armies do not fight with weapons: the sword comes out of Christ's mouth.

Today we can live with hope, knowing that Christ will triumph. And we can follow him with a pure life, trusting in his victory and not in our own strength.
exp.7:12:
He says that John saw and heard an angel flying through the middle of heaven. In a loud voice the angel announced woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because the remaining three trumpet blasts were about to sound. The word "woe" appears in the verse itself, so no separate explanation is needed here.

John recounts his vision. Four trumpets have already sounded, with judgments that strike one part of creation. This angel makes a solemn pause before the last three, which will be harsher. Many understand it as a merciful warning. Interpreters differ on whether these events are literal, symbolic, or still future.

For today: God warns before he judges and gives time to return to him. Let us not take his patience lightly. Today is a good day to examine your heart, ask for forgiveness, and live with humility and hope in Christ.
exp.7:1:
John says that he saw seven angels who stand before God, and that they were given seven trumpets. "Standing before God" means that they are in his presence, ready to serve him. The trumpets were given to them, meaning they do not act on their own.

John, who receives this vision while on the island of Patmos, speaks here. After the solemn silence that follows the seventh seal, a new series of judgments announced with trumpets begins. Some scholars think this series continues what has already been seen, and others think it repeats it from another angle; the Bible does not fully make this clear. What is clear is that everything happens under God's authority.

For today: even when the world seems confused, God remains in control and nothing falls outside his plan. You can rest in him and pray with confidence, knowing that he hears and governs history.
exp.4:4:
One of the elders comforts John, who is crying. He tells him to stop weeping, because there is already someone who can open the scroll and break its seven seals. This one is called "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" and "the Root of David." "Has triumphed" means that he won the victory, and for that reason he has the right to open the scroll.

John is in a vision of heaven. He weeps because no one was found worthy to open the scroll, which many understand as God's plan to judge and redeem. The titles recall Old Testament promises about a king who would come from Judah and from David. What is surprising is that, when John looks, he sees a Lamb as if it had been slain. Many understand that both images speak of Jesus: power and sacrifice.

For today: when you feel that everything is without a way out, do not weep without hope. Bring your anguish to Jesus, who has already overcome and still holds control of history.
exp.21:19:
He who testifies to all these things says, "Yes, I am coming soon." This verse says that Jesus, who bears witness to everything written in this book, affirms this with certainty. "Soon" means without delay. John responds with a prayer: "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!" That is, he sincerely longs for Christ to return.

Here Jesus speaks, and then John responds, the one who received this revelation. It comes after a serious warning not to add or take away anything from the words of the book. It is the closing of the whole Bible. Many believers understand "soon" as the certainty that his coming is sure and could happen at any moment. Others interpret it in different ways.

Today we can live with hope and without fear, praying "Come, Lord Jesus!" while remaining faithful to his Word, treating others well, and joyfully doing what he has entrusted to us.
exp.19:3:
John says he saw thrones, and that those seated on them had been given authority to judge. He also saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for their testimony about Jesus and for the word of God. These were people who had not worshiped the beast or its image, and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. The phrase "had been given" means "they were granted" authority.

John writes Revelation to encourage Christians who were under pressure and persecution. It comes right after Satan is bound for a thousand years. Christians have understood this thousand-year period in different ways: as something literal and future, as something happening now, or as a symbol. The Bible does not settle every detail here, so humility is appropriate.

For today: stay faithful to Christ even when it costs you, because God does not forget those who are loyal to him. His faithfulness is rewarded, and their suffering is not in vain.
exp.0:1:
Here John says that he is a faithful witness to three things: the word of God, the testimony of Jesus Christ, and everything he saw in the vision. To testify means to truthfully declare what one has received and seen. "Saw" refers to the visions he received.

The speaker is John, who writes the book and presents himself as a servant of Christ. The verses before this explain that the revelation comes from God, passes to Jesus Christ, then to an angel, and finally to John. With this, he assures his readers that he is not writing his own ideas. Traditionally it is thought to be the apostle John, although some scholars debate his identity.

For today: we too are called to be witnesses. We can honestly share what God has shown us in His Word and in our lives, without adding to or exaggerating it, and trust that He sustains the message.
exp.0:3:
John writes a letter to seven churches in the province of Asia, a region of what is today Turkey. He wishes them grace and peace. That blessing comes from God, described as the One who is and was and is to come, and also from the seven spirits before his throne. As the text continues, it also comes from Jesus Christ.

The one speaking is John, who receives this revelation and writes it down for real Christian communities, some of them under pressure or hardship. About the seven spirits, there are several interpretations: many believe they refer to the Holy Spirit in his fullness, since seven often signifies perfection; others think of seven angels. It is a point that is debated.

For today: when you feel uncertain about the future, remember that peace comes from God, who rules over the past, the present, and what is to come. Ask him for that peace today.
exp.8:3:
It says that the locusts that came out of the smoke were given an order: they were not to harm the grass of the earth, or any plant or tree. They could only harm the people who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads.

It is part of the fifth trumpet in Revelation. John reports what he sees in a vision. These locusts are not ordinary ones, since they act under limits placed on them. Some believe they are spiritual or demonic forces, others see a symbol of judgment; it is interpreted in several ways. The seal on the forehead recalls Revelation 7, where God marks his servants.

For today: even in dark times, God sets limits on evil and cares for his own. We can rest in the fact that he still has control and belong to him with confidence.
exp.4:8:
They sing a new song to the Lamb, who is Jesus. They say that he is worthy to take the scroll and open its seals, because he was slain, that is, given up as a sacrifice. By his blood he purchased people for God, that is, paid the price to bring them to God. These people come from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation.

The ones singing are the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders, who stand before God's throne. They have just seen the Lamb take the scroll, which holds God's plans for the world. They praise him because only he, through his death and victory, can bring those plans to fulfillment. Scholars interpret in different ways who the elders are.

For today: Jesus' salvation is for all peoples, without exception. We can receive with humility people of other cultures and languages, and pray or support the gospel reaching everyone.
exp.6:15:
They say that those who stand before God's throne will no longer suffer the hardest needs of life. They will never again hunger or thirst, and the sun will not beat down on them, nor any scorching heat. It is a promise of complete care. The phrase "never again will they hunger" means that nothing will wear them down or strike them again.

One of the elders around the throne speaks, answering John, who did not know who this multitude was.
