He explains that they are those who came out of a great tribulation and were washed clean by the blood of the Lamb, who is Jesus. The verses that follow present the Lamb as a shepherd who leads them to springs of living water. Interpreters disagree about exactly who they are, but all of them see comfort for faithful people who suffer.

For today: when you go through pain or lack, remember that God has not forgotten you. You can bring your weariness to him in prayer and wait patiently for his final comfort.
exp.21:15:
Here Jesus says that He Himself sent His angel to give the churches this testimony about everything written in the book. Then He presents Himself with three titles: "the Root and the Offspring of David" (both a descendant of that king and the source of him) and "the bright Morning Star," the one that shines just before dawn.

The one speaking is Jesus, near the very end of Revelation. He has just warned that some remain outside the city and others enter it. With these titles He confirms that the promises made to David are fulfilled in Him, and that this message comes with His authority. Many see in the morning star an image of hope in the face of a new day.

For today: when the night feels long, look to Jesus as your sure hope. Read this with confidence, and let His promise hold you up and encourage you to live faithfully for Him.
exp.2:10:
He says that Jesus is coming soon. The word "soon" here means that his coming will not be delayed. Jesus tells his church to hold firmly to what they already have, so that no one takes away their crown, which stands for the reward of those who keep going in faith.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, in his letter to the church in Philadelphia. It was a church with little strength, yet faithful to the word of Christ, even under opposition. He encourages them to stay firm. Some believe "soon" refers to his return; others, to a coming in judgment or help. In both cases, the call is to perseverance.

For today: do not lose heart if your strength is small. Choose one simple practice of faith, such as praying or reading the Bible each day, and be steady in it.
exp.19:2:
Here it says that an angel threw him into the Abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him. So Satan cannot deceive the nations until the thousand years are complete. Afterward, he must be released for a brief period of time, and the verse makes clear that this release is something that must happen.

The apostle John writes what he saw in a vision, to encourage Christians who were suffering persecution. The message is that God has the last word over evil. Christians understand the "thousand years" in different ways: some as a literal future period of time, others as a symbolic stage that is already underway. All agree that Satan's power has limits.

For today: when you feel that evil is advancing without restraint, remember that it is under God's authority. Trust in Christ and stand firm in the truth.
exp.8:4:
These creatures, called locusts, were allowed to torment people, but not to kill them, for five months. The pain they caused is compared to the sting of a scorpion. "Were not given power" means they were not permitted, and "stinging" describes what a scorpion does.

John recounts a vision that Jesus showed him. It is the fifth trumpet, a judgment on those who do not have God's seal. Notice that the power of these creatures is limited: it was given to them, and they have a fixed time. Interpreters differ: some see something literal and future, others a symbol of destructive spiritual forces. The five months are also explained in several ways.

Even when evil seems unleashed, God still keeps control and sets limits on it. If you are going through a painful trial today, trust that it does not escape his hand, and seek refuge in him.
exp.8:19:
It says that the people who survived these terrible plagues still did not change their hearts. They kept worshiping demons and idols made of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood. These idols cannot see, hear or walk. "Repent" means to change direction and turn back to God. "Bronze" here is the metal the verse names.

John writes down what he saw in a vision, in the book of Revelation. This happens at the sounding of the sixth trumpet, when judgments come upon the earth. The text shows that punishment, by itself, does not always transform a person. Some interpret these plagues literally and others symbolically; Christians understand them in several ways.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your life, such as money, success or fear. Do not wait for a crisis to come before you turn back to Him; God invites you today to change.
exp.3:2:
John describes God seated on his throne. He does not say that he saw a face or a human figure, but flashes of light like precious stones. The One seated there looked like jasper and carnelian, and a rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne. Jasper and carnelian are bright stones; jasper can come in several colors, and carnelian is reddish.

John writes this vision to churches that were under pressure and hardship. After hearing the voice say "Come up here," he is carried in the Spirit into heaven. Before seeing future things, he first sees who rules: God. Some think the rainbow recalls God's faithfulness after the flood, but the text does not explain this.

For today: when life feels uncertain, remember that the throne is not empty. Spend a few minutes praying quietly, acknowledging that God reigns and that you can entrust your worries to him.
exp.13:14:
Then another angel comes out of the temple in heaven, calling out in a loud voice to the one sitting on the cloud: "Swing your sickle and reap, because the time has come to harvest; the crop of the earth is ripe." A "sickle" is a curved tool for cutting wheat, and "harvest" here means gathering in the grain. "Ripe" means the crop is ready to be gathered.

The angel speaks with a message from the presence of God, since he comes out of the temple. He addresses the one seated on the cloud, who is usually understood to be like the Son of Man, and is commonly identified with Jesus. The angel does not decide the moment; he announces that it has arrived. Many see here the final judgment, others a gathering of the faithful, and others both. Christians have debated the exact meaning.

For today: God has his time and is neither late nor early. We can live with patience and faithfulness, trusting that he knows when to act.
exp.5:0:
John tells that he watched as the Lamb, who is Jesus Christ, opened the first of the seven seals on the scroll. Then he heard one of the four living creatures call out in a voice like thunder, "Come!" The creature was inviting John to come and look closely at what was about to happen.

John is the one telling this vision. Earlier, in chapters 4 and 5, he saw God's throne and the Lamb, the only one worthy to open the scroll. Now he begins to be shown what is inside. The four living creatures surround the throne, and one of them invites John to look. Scholars interpret the riders that follow in various ways, but all agree that the Lamb is in control.

For today: when the world seems confusing or threatening, remember that the Lamb is the one who opens the seals. Rest in the fact that nothing escapes his hand, and pray with confidence.
exp.3:3:
Around God's throne, John sees twenty-four other thrones, and sitting on them are twenty-four elders. They are dressed in white and wear golden crowns on their heads.

John receives this vision in heaven while he is exiled, according to the book. He wants to encourage churches that are suffering, showing them that God reigns. Who the elders are is understood in several ways: some see the people of God represented, others see heavenly beings who serve him. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: even when the world seems disordered, God remains on his throne. You can rest in that and worship him with confidence, knowing that those who belong to him have a place and a hope in him.
exp.2:21:
It says that whoever has ears should listen carefully to what the Holy Spirit says to the churches. "Hear" here means more than catching sounds: it means paying attention and obeying. The phrase "to the churches" is worded in the verse as "to the churches."

The one speaking is Jesus, and this phrase closes his letter to the church of Laodicea, the last of the seven letters in Revelation. That church was lukewarm and felt self-sufficient, but Jesus lovingly calls it to repent. The same phrase is repeated at the end of each letter, which is why the message is for all the churches, not just one.

For today: it is not enough to just listen to sermons or read the Bible out of habit. This week, set aside a few minutes to ask the Spirit to show you one concrete step of obedience, and give it to him as your response to his voice.
exp.14:0:
This verse says that John saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing: seven angels with the seven final plagues. The word "final" here is the word that the verse uses, and it marks these as the last of the plagues. With these plagues the wrath of God is completed, meaning God's anger reaches its full and final end.

John speaks here, recounting a vision he received from Jesus Christ. Before this, he has described the beast's opposition against God's people. Here a new scene begins, announcing the final judgment on evil. The verses that follow show those who have overcome praising God for his righteous ways. Scholars interpret in various ways how and when these plagues take place, but all agree that God brings injustice to an end.

For today: you can trust that God does not forget evil or injustice. If you are suffering today or seeing abuse, wait with patience and remain faithful, knowing that God is just.
exp.8:17:
It says that a third of mankind was killed by three plagues: fire, smoke, and sulfur, which proceeded from the mouths of the horses in the vision. "Was killed" means "died"; "plagues" are punishing blows.

John recounts what he saw when the sixth trumpet sounded. A huge army of riders brings judgment on the earth. Many understand this as a warning from God so that people will repent, although interpreters disagree about whether these are literal events, symbols, or both. The verses that follow show the underlying problem: the survivors did not repent.

For today: let us not wait for life to shake us before turning back to God. If today you feel that He is calling you to change something, respond with humility and without delay.
exp.6:12:
This verse tells how one of the elders who surround the throne speaks to John with a question: who are these in white robes, and where have they come from. The word "addressed" here does not mean that he replied to something John said, but that he began to speak to him. It is a question meant to teach, since the elder himself will give the answer.

John is seeing in a vision a huge crowd before the throne of God, after the worship of the angels. The elder asks so that John will pay attention and understand. John replies with humility: "Lord, you know." Then it is explained that they are those who came out of the great tribulation and were washed by the blood of the Lamb. Interpreters differ about when that tribulation takes place, but the text stresses that God cares for his people.

Today we can learn to recognize what we do not know and to ask God to teach us. And if we go through trials, we can trust that Christ cleanses and sustains us.
exp.1:26:
It says that the one who overcomes will receive authority to rule over the nations "with an iron scepter." The word "rule" means to govern or to shepherd; the "iron scepter" is a symbol of firm, unbreakable power; the "pottery" is clay pots; and "shatter them" means to break them into pieces. Jesus adds that this authority was given to him by his Father.

Jesus speaks in his letter to the church in Thyatira. The believers there were under pressure from false teaching and corrupt practices. He encourages them to remain faithful until his coming. The image comes from Psalm 2, where the Messiah reigns over rebellious nations. Interpreters debate whether the image speaks of destruction or of firm government; both ideas have been proposed.

For today: do not lose heart when faith is costly. Keep obeying Christ with steadiness, trusting that the future is in the hands of the one who reigns with justice.
exp.9:3:
This verse tells us that, after the seven thunders spoke their messages, John was about to write them down. But a voice from heaven told him to seal up what the thunders said and not to write it down. In other words, that message was to be kept hidden.

John is recounting his vision. A mighty angel, holding a small open book, called out like a lion, and the seven thunders answered. What they said is not revealed to us. Some think it was a judgment that God chose to keep in reserve; others think it is simply not our place to know. The Bible does not make this clear.

For today: God does not tell us everything, and that is good. We can trust that what He has revealed is enough to follow Him, and leave in His hands what He has kept silent, without worrying or speculating.
exp.0:11:
John hears a loud voice behind him and turns to see who is speaking to him. When he turns around, he sees seven golden lampstands. The word "lampstand" in this verse refers to a stand for holding lamps, much like a candelabra.

John is on the island of Patmos, and the voice is that of Jesus, who tells him to write to seven churches in Asia. Later, in verse 20, it is explained that the seven lampstands represent those seven churches. And in the middle of them appears Christ, which shows that he is present among his people.

For today: Jesus is not far from his church, but in the midst of it. If today you feel small or alone in your community of faith, remember that Christ walks among his own. Seek him with confidence and let his voice guide you, just as John turned to listen to it.
exp.7:5:
It says that the seven angels with the seven trumpets got ready to sound them. The idea of "prepared" here is that they got themselves set and in position. It is a moment of pause, like when everything is in place just before something begins.

John records what he saw in his vision. Just before this, the prayers of the saints rose up to God along with the incense, and the fire from the altar was thrown down to the earth. Then come the judgments of the trumpets. Many understand that God answers the prayers of his people, although Christians interpret in different ways how and when these scenes are fulfilled.

For today: our prayers are not lost; God hears them and acts in his own time. We can keep praying with patience and confidence, even when we do not yet see an answer.
exp.11:7:
This verse says the dragon and his angels did not win the battle in heaven. "Not strong enough" means they could not overcome or hold their ground. "No longer any place for him in heaven" means they no longer had room there; they were driven out completely.

John is the one speaking, recounting a vision he received. Just before this, a war is described between Michael and his angels against the dragon. The verses that follow explain that the dragon is Satan, the accuser, and that he is cast down to the earth. Interpreters differ on whether this scene is a future event, a past one, or a symbolic picture of Christ's victory. Even so, the central message is the same: God has the victory.

For today: when you feel that evil or guilt is accusing you, remember that its power has limits. Rest in Christ, who already holds the victory, and keep trusting Him with a steadfast faith.
exp.13:7:
A second angel follows, announcing the fall of Babylon, the great city. The message is repeated, "Fallen, fallen," to give emphasis and certainty. The charge is that Babylon has made all the nations drink the wine of her immorality, that is, a spiritual and moral unfaithfulness that swept the peoples along, like someone who makes others drunk and leaves them without judgment. The word "passion" here speaks of an unrestrained desire.

The speaker is an angel within a vision given to John. He comes after the angel who proclaims the eternal gospel and God's judgment, and before the warning of the third angel. Babylon represents a human power opposed to God; some relate her to Rome and others to a worldwide system of all times. It is interpreted in several ways.

Today, examine what things seduce you into living far from God, and decide to place your trust in Him, not in what the world promises.
exp.6:14:
This verse says that the crowd dressed in white stands before God's throne and serves him day and night in his temple. The word "tabernacle" here means a dwelling or shelter; God himself will spread his tent over them, that is, he will cover them, protect them, and live with them. The phrase "for this reason" points back to what was just said: they have been washed in the blood of the Lamb.

One of the heavenly elders speaks, explaining to John who these people dressed in white are. They are the ones who come out of the great tribulation. Interpreters disagree about whether this refers to a specific final time or to the persecution that believers suffer in every age. What is clear is that the passage aims to comfort those who suffer for their faith.

For today: if Christ has cleansed you, you can draw near to God without fear. In your trials, remember that his care covers you like a protecting tent. Today you can serve him with gratitude in everyday life, trusting that he sustains you.
exp.13:15:
He says that the one sitting on the cloud, like the Son of Man, swung his sickle over the earth, and the earth was harvested. The word "harvested" here simply means the crop was gathered in. A sickle is a curved tool used for cutting grain.

John is describing a vision. An angel came out of the temple and told this figure that the time had come to harvest, because the crop was ripe. Many understand that this is Christ and that it refers to the final harvest at the end of time. Some think it speaks of judgment, others of the gathering of believers, and others of both. What is certain is that God decides the moment.

For today: God holds time and the end in his hands. You can live with peace rather than fear, trusting in Christ, and keep doing good with patience.
exp.10:18:
It says that the temple of God was opened in heaven, and that the ark of his covenant appeared inside it. The word "covenant" means an agreement or promise. Then there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and a great hailstorm.

The twenty-four elders have just worshiped God, because he has taken his power and reigns, judges the nations, and rewards his servants. This verse closes that scene. The ark was the symbol of God's presence and of his faithfulness to his covenant. Interpreters differ on details, but almost all see here a sign that God keeps his promises and that his judgment is real.

For today: when the world seems unjust or out of control, remember that God is faithful to his covenant. You can rest in the fact that he will fulfill what he promised, and live with confidence and reverence.
exp.3:8:
He is described as the one who lives forever and ever, that is, the one who has no end and never dies. The word "glory" speaks of his greatness, "honor" of his worth, and "thanks" of our gratitude for who he is.

John describes a vision of heaven. The four living creatures give glory, honor, and thanks without rest, and what follows shows that the twenty-four elders respond with worship. They fall down and cast their crowns before the one on the throne. The one seated there is said to have created all things, and for that reason he deserves this worship. There are different interpretations of what the creatures and the elders represent, and the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: before asking something of God, take a moment to thank him for who he is. Recognizing that he lives forever and governs all things can give you peace in the midst of your worries.
exp.8:10:
These creatures, resembling locusts, are ruled by a king: the angel of the Abyss. His name is Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek. Both names mean "destruction" or "destroyer." The Abyss is a deep, dark place, associated with the confinement of evil beings. "Hebrew" refers to the Hebrew language.

John reports what he saw in a vision, during the fifth trumpet. These creatures torment people for five months. Interpreters debate who this angel is: many think he is Satan or one of his agents; others, an angel under God's control. The text does not fully clarify this. What is clear is that his power has limits, since everything happens within a fixed time.

For today: evil may seem enormous and destructive, but it has a name, limits, and an end. You can entrust your fears to God, for He reigns over all power.
exp.5:2:
This verse says that the Lamb, that is, Jesus Christ, opens the second seal of the scroll that John saw. Then John hears the second of the four living creatures say to him, "Come!" It is an invitation to look at what is about to appear.

The second living creature, who stands near the throne of God, speaks. Just like the first, it calls John to watch. What follows is a red horse, whose rider receives power to take away peace and bring about violence. Interpreters explain these visions in various ways, but nearly all of them see in them war and conflict. Note that it is the Lamb who opens the seals.

For today: when you see violence or news that troubles you, remember that Christ still is in control of history. Rest in him, and seek to be a person who promotes peace.
exp.4:13:
This verse says that the four living creatures answered "Amen," which means "so be it" or "it is true." The elders fell down and worshiped God, the one who lives forever and ever.

In this scene in heaven, all of creation has just praised the one sitting on the throne and the Lamb, who is Jesus, the one who was slain, that is, given up as a sacrifice. The four living creatures and the elders close that praise with their agreement and their worship. Interpreters explain who the elders are in several different ways, but they all agree that the elders represent those who worship God.

For today: when you come near to God, do not only ask. Pause for a moment, acknowledge who He is, and say "amen" from the heart, with humility and gratitude for what Christ has done.
exp.13:0:
John sees a scene different from the ones before it: the Lamb, who is Jesus Christ, is standing on Mount Zion, and with him are 144,000 people. All of them have his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads, as a sign that they belong to him.

John wrote Revelation in a setting of persecution. Just before this, the book showed the beast marking its followers. Now comes the contrast: others bear the mark of God. Christians interpret in various ways whether the number is literal or symbolic, and whether Zion is the earthly Jerusalem or the heavenly one. In any case, the message is one of comfort for the faithful.

Today we can remember that our deepest identity comes from belonging to God, not from what the world says about us. When you feel pressure to fit in, remember whose you are.
exp.16:0:
One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls comes to John and says, "Come here." He promises to show him the punishment of the great prostitute, who sits on many waters. A prostitute is a woman who sells her body; here she is a symbolic image.

The one speaking is an angel, and John writes it down. The earlier bowls spoke of God's judgment. Now the angel explains, in a vision, who this woman is. The same book later says that the waters represent peoples (17:15). Interpreters disagree about whom the prostitute represents: some think of Rome, others of a worldwide system of power and idolatry.

For today: God does not leave deception and unfaithfulness unanswered. Ask yourself which attractive things in the world compete for your loyalty to God, and ask Him to help you remain faithful to Him.
exp.11:11:
This verse has two messages: joy for heaven and sorrow for the earth. The heavens and those who live in them are called to celebrate. But the earth and the sea receive a "woe," a warning of suffering, because the devil has come down to them in great fury. He knows that he has only a short time left.

A loud voice in heaven speaks right after announcing that the accuser has been thrown down and that the believers overcame him by the blood of the Lamb and by their testimony. Many understand that the devil's anger is seen at once when he pursues the woman. Interpreters differ on how and when this is fulfilled.

For today: if you face opposition or trials, do not lose heart. Your enemy has already been defeated, and his time is limited. Hold fast to Christ and to your testimony with faithfulness.
exp.11:5:
The passage says the woman fled into the wilderness, to a place that God had prepared for her. There she would be nourished for 1,260 days.

"Prepared" means made ready in advance, set in place beforehand. "Nourished" means that she would be cared for and given what she needed to live.

John writes this vision in Revelation to encourage believers who were suffering. The woman is often understood as the people of God, though she is interpreted in several ways. The dragon is Satan, who pursues the child and the woman. The 1,260 days equal three and a half years, a limited period that appears elsewhere in the book. Its exact meaning is debated.

God does not abandon his people in difficult times. Even when you feel you are in a "wilderness," such as a season of scarcity, loneliness, or trial, he may have a place of care prepared for you. Trust that his provision arrives and that every trial has a limit in his hands.
exp.17:1:
This verse says that a powerful angel cried out in a loud voice that great Babylon has fallen. Now she has become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird, and every detestable beast. "Lair" means a hiding place for wild animals; "haunt" is a place someone visits or lives in, often one that is avoided by others; "detestable" means something that causes strong disgust.

The angel speaking came down from heaven with great authority, and his glory lit up the earth. He announces the judgment of Babylon, which in Revelation represents a system of power, wealth, and sin that deceives the nations. Interpreters connect her with ancient Rome, with a corrupt worldwide system, or with both. Then comes the call: "Come out of her, my people."

For today: God is not impressed by the glitter of power or money. Examine which things in the world attract you and pull you away from God, and ask him for help to separate yourself from them and live faithfully.
exp.17:13:
It says that everything Babylon longed for with her whole being, her luxuries and pleasures, has slipped out of her hands. "The fruit of your soul's desire" refers to the things she so eagerly wanted. The phrase "luxury and splendor" refers to the wealth and glory she has lost, and she will never see them again.

This is part of the announcement of Babylon's fall, the great city that symbolizes power, wealth, and rebellion against God. An angel proclaims her judgment, and the earlier list of merchandise shows her luxury. Interpreters connect her with Rome or with a world system; not all agree. The merchants weep afterward because they have lost their business.

For today: riches can vanish in a moment. It is worth asking what our soul truly desires and placing our hope in God, not in things that do not last.
exp.1:8:
Jesus tells the church in Smyrna that he knows everything they go through: their hardships, their suffering, and their material poverty. Even so, he calls them "rich." He also knows the slander of those who falsely claim to be Jews but are in fact a synagogue of Satan.

The message comes from the risen Christ, "the first and the last, who was dead and came to life." Smyrna was a city under social and religious pressure, and the believers faced opposition. Some understand that these opponents were Jews who accused them; others, that they were people who claimed to belong to God's people without actually doing so. The text gives no further details.

For today: when you feel poor, overlooked, or criticized, remember that Jesus sees everything and measures your riches by your faith in him. Hand your pain over to him and remain faithful with confidence.
exp.12:15:
The passage says that the second beast, the one that performs signs and deceives, requires every person, regardless of social standing, to receive a mark on the right hand or on the forehead. Here "slave" refers to a person who is owned by another, and "mark" is a sign placed on the body. All are included: the small and the great, the rich and the poor.

John writes this vision to Christians who were under pressure for refusing to worship the power of the empire. The mark imitates the seal that God places on his servants. It shows to whom a person belongs and to whom they give their loyalty. Interpreters disagree about whether it is something literal, symbolic, or both, but all see a warning against false loyalty.

Ask yourself: what things compete for my loyalty today, such as money, fear, or the approval of others? Decide, in prayer, to remain faithful to Christ, even when it costs you.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that the Lord is the Alpha and the Omega, that is, the first and the last letters of the Greek alphabet. With this he declares himself the first and the last: everything begins and ends in him. It also says that he is the one who is, who was, and who is to come, meaning that he is present now, has always been, and will come. "The Almighty" means that nothing escapes his power.

Here the Lord himself is speaking, in the middle of the introduction to the book. John has just spoken of Christ's coming with the clouds. Some understand that the one speaking is God the Father and others that it is Jesus; the context allows both readings. John was writing to Christians who were suffering hardship, and this declaration reminded them who has control.

For today: when you feel that your life or the world is out of control, remember that the Lord is already in your beginning, in your today, and in your ending. Rest in him and trust.
exp.0:0:
This verse presents the book as "the revelation of Jesus Christ," meaning something Jesus makes known. God gave it to Jesus to show his servants what must soon come to pass. Jesus made it known by sending his angel to his servant John.

The one writing is John, who presents himself as a messenger rather than the owner of the message. Traditionally he is identified with the apostle John, though some scholars dispute this. The book is addressed to Christians who faced pressure and persecution. The verses that follow promise a blessing to the one who reads, hears, and obeys. There are different ways of interpreting the events the book describes.

For today: read Revelation not to frighten yourself or to calculate dates, but to trust that Christ is in control and to obey faithfully what God has already shown you.
exp.0:15:
He says that Jesus, whom John sees in a vision, holds seven stars in his right hand. A sharp sword with two edges, meaning one that cuts on both sides, comes out of his mouth. His face shines like the sun at its brightest.

John writes from the island of Patmos and tells what he saw of the risen Christ. Later, Jesus himself explains that the stars are the angels of the seven churches (1:20); some understand the "angels" as messengers or leaders. The sword is usually understood as the power of his word. John falls down as if dead, and Jesus lays his right hand on him, saying: "Do not be afraid."

For today: Jesus holds in his hand those who belong to him, and his word has authority. You can draw near to him with reverence and confidence, and read his Word, letting it correct you and also comfort you.
exp.5:3:
It says that another horse came out, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace away from the earth and to make people slay one another. He was also given a great sword.

This is the opening of the second seal in John's vision. Christ, the Lamb, opens the seals, and one of the four living creatures says "Come and see." Red is usually understood to stand for war and violence. Some read it as historical events and others as a pattern that repeats until the end. Notice that the rider was "granted permission" and "was given" the sword: there are limits, and God remains in control.

For today: when you see violence and division, do not lose hope. Ask God to make you a peacemaker in your home, your work, and your church, and trust that Christ reigns over history.
exp.9:4:
This verse describes the mighty angel whom John saw standing with one foot on the sea and the other on the land. Now he lifts his right hand toward heaven, the gesture made when taking an oath. What follows is the oath itself.

John is recounting his vision. Earlier, seven thunders spoke, and John was forbidden to write down their message. Now the angel prepares to swear by God, the Creator of all things. His stance over sea and land suggests that what he says affects all of creation. Some understand the words "there would be no more delay" to mean that there will be no further waiting; others understand them differently.

God has the final word, and He will fulfill what He promised. Even when we do not understand everything, we can trust that He is bringing history to its goal. Today, give your doubts to God and receive His peace.
exp.21:10:
This verse says that each person continues on their path: the unrighteous keeps on being unrighteous, the vile keeps on being vile, the righteous keeps on practicing righteousness, and the holy keeps on being holy.

The word "continue" in the verse means to keep on or remain as one already is.

The angel speaks, and then Jesus, at the close of the book. The message is not sealed because the time is near and Christ is coming to reward each person according to his works. Some see this as a solemn warning: soon it will be too late to change. Others see it as a description of how character becomes firmly set over time.

Today we are called not to delay. If God speaks to you, respond now, and keep growing in a clean and righteous life, for our daily choices shape who we become.
exp.11:14:
This verse says that the serpent, which is the dragon, spewed water from its mouth like a river after the woman. Its aim was for the torrent to overtake her and sweep her away. The phrase "sweep her away" here means carried off by force, and "to overtake" means to catch up with her.

John writes this vision in Revelation. The dragon, identified in this same chapter with Satan, was thrown down to the earth and pursues the woman. She received the wings of an eagle to flee into the wilderness, where God sustains her. Many see in the woman the people of God, though this is interpreted in several ways. The river may represent deception, persecution, or pressure, but this is not known with certainty.

For today: when pressures or lies overwhelm you, remember that God knows how to sustain you. Trust in Him, seek His help, and do not think that His care depends on your own strength.
exp.6:11:
This verse says that the angels answer the praise of the crowd with an "Amen," and then list seven things that belong to God: blessing, glory, wisdom, thanks, honor, power, and strength. The word "honor" in the verse refers to respect and dignity, while "power" and "strength" speak of might and authority. The verse ends by saying that all of this belongs to our God forever and ever. It closes with another "Amen."

The speakers are the angels who stand around the throne, together with the elders and the four living creatures. They have just heard a great multitude from every nation declare that salvation comes from God and from the Lamb. They fall down and worship. Many understand the Lamb to be Jesus. Next, one of the elders explains who the ones clothed in white are: those who came out of the great tribulation.

For today: before you ask for something in prayer, take a moment to give thanks to God and honor Him for who He is. This reminds us that salvation and power belong to Him, not to us.
exp.2:12:
He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. This verse is an invitation to listen carefully. "He who has an ear" refers to the person who is willing to pay attention. "Let him hear" means that it is not enough to merely hear sounds; one must take in the message and act on it. What is heard is what "the Spirit says to the churches."

Jesus speaks to the church in Philadelphia, within the letters to seven churches in Revelation. He has just encouraged them to remain firm and promised a reward to the one who overcomes. This same phrase appears at the end of each letter, showing that the message is meant for other churches as well, not only for the first one that received it.

For today: do not read the Bible only out of habit. Before reading, ask God for a willing heart, and then choose one specific thing you will put into practice this week.
exp.16:11:
This verse says that the ten horns of the beast are ten kings. They have not yet received a kingdom, but they will receive authority as kings for a very short time, "one hour," along with the beast. The word "authority" here means the right and power to rule.

Here an angel speaks to John, explaining the vision of the woman and the beast. Christians interpret these kings in various ways: some see future governments, others see historical powers, and others see them as symbols of human opposition against God. What is clear is that their power is brief, and it ends when they make war against the Lamb and He overcomes them.

For today: do not lose heart or be overawed by human powers that seem strong. Their authority is passing, but Christ reigns forever. Remain faithful to Him, trusting that His victory is certain.
exp.1:12:
Jesus says he knows very well the situation of the church in Pergamum. They lived where the throne of Satan sits, that is, where evil held great power. Even so, they stayed faithful: they held fast to the name of Jesus, and they did not deny their faith in him. Antipas, his faithful witness, was killed among them, in the place where Satan dwells. The word "where" refers to the place they lived.

Jesus himself is speaking, the one with the sharp two-edged sword, which represents his word that judges with truth. He writes to encourage them for their firmness amid pressure and persecution. Interpreters do not agree on exactly what the throne of Satan was: perhaps the worship of the emperor, the pagan temples, or both.

For today: even if your surroundings pressure you to stay silent or give in, Jesus sees your faithfulness. Stand firm in him, knowing that you are not alone.
exp.17:5:
It says that Babylon should be paid back in kind for what she has done, and that the payment should be double what she deserves. The cup she mixed for others is now to be mixed for her, in a double portion.

A voice from heaven speaks and calls God's people to leave that city so that they will not share in its sins or its plagues. Babylon stands for a system of pride, luxury, and injustice against others. Some readers see it as Rome, and others as a wider world power; it is understood in several ways. The central message is that God sees evil and judges it with justice.

Today, this text encourages us not to take revenge, because God is the judge. It also invites us to examine whether we are caught up in attitudes of pride, ambition, or injustice, and to turn away from them with trust in God.
exp.12:14:
This verse says that the second beast, later called "the false prophet," was permitted to give breath to the image of the first beast, so that the image could speak. It also says that the image would cause everyone who refused to worship it to be killed. The phrase "was permitted" shows that God allowed this to happen. The "inhabitants" are the people who live on the earth.

John writes to Christians who were under pressure to worship the emperor and the powers of their time. This vision shows a religious power that deceives with false miracles and forces people to worship. There are several interpretations: some see Rome, others see future events, and others see a constant struggle between God and the powers of the world.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed by what seems powerful or miraculous. Compare everything with Jesus and his Word, and remain faithful to him even when it costs you.
exp.10:6:
It says that when the two witnesses have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up from the Abyss will wage war against them. It will overpower them and kill them. "When the two witnesses have finished their testimony" means they have completed the task God gave them. "The Abyss" refers to a place of darkness, connected with the forces of evil.

John speaks here, relating the vision Jesus gave him. The two witnesses prophesy with power for a time set by God, and no one can stop them before they complete their mission. Who they are and when this takes place is understood in various ways among Christians, so it is wise to hold these details with humility. The central message is clear: evil seems to triumph, but only after God has protected them until the end of their task.

For today: trust that God sustains you while you carry out your calling. If you suffer opposition for being faithful, it does not mean God has abandoned you; He has the final word.
exp.7:11:
When the fourth angel blew his trumpet, a third of the sun, the moon, and the stars was struck. As a result, a third of them grew dark, and a third of the day was without light, and a third of the night as well.

John writes what he saw in a vision. The trumpets are warnings of judgment that grow stronger, somewhat like the plagues of Egypt (the darkness, Exodus 10). Interpreters differ: some see it as literal future events, others as symbolic language about judgments throughout history. Here the harm is partial, only a third, like an urgent call to turn back to God before the end.

Today we can remember that God reigns even when everything seems to grow dark. We should not wait to turn to Him; let us live with sincerity and trust, knowing that Christ is the light that no darkness can put out (John 1:5).
exp.11:6:
This verse tells that a war broke out in heaven. Michael, who is a chief angel, and the angels with him fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back. The verse uses the word "fought," which means to battle or struggle against an opponent.

John wrote this, and he received this vision from Jesus Christ. The book speaks in symbols to encourage believers who were suffering persecution. The following verses say that the dragon is Satan and that he was defeated and thrown out. Christians understand in different ways when and how this scene is placed in time, but all agree on its central message: evil does not win.

When you feel that evil is stronger than you, remember that the great battle is already in God's hands. Rest in Him, pray, and keep doing good with confidence.
exp.10:2:
God says he will empower two of his witnesses so that they can speak on his behalf. They will prophesy for 1,260 days, which is about three and a half years. During that time they will go about clothed in sackcloth, a rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning and repentance. The phrase "I will empower" shows that God himself entrusts them with this task.

The one speaking is Jesus, who gives the vision to John. This comes after the measuring of the temple, and the forty-two months of the trampled city line up with these same 1,260 days. Who the two witnesses are is understood in several ways: some see specific individuals, while others see the faithful Church. The text does not fully settle the question.

For today: God sustains those who bear witness to him, even in difficult times. You can remain faithful and sincere in your faith, trusting that God cares for your witness even when the surroundings are not in your favor.
exp.3:5:
Before the throne, John sees something like a sea of glass, as clear as crystal. In the center, around the throne, are four living creatures, covered with eyes in front and in back.

John is the one speaking, describing a vision he received from heaven. He writes to churches that were under pressure and persecution, to remind them that God reigns. Many understand the sea of glass as a sign of God's holiness and calm, and the eyes as his complete knowledge, but scholars do not fully agree on the exact meaning of these symbols.

When the world seems confused and out of control, remember that there is a firm and peaceful throne. God sees everything and continues to reign. You can rest in him and worship him with confidence.
exp.20:25:
It says that the nations will bring the best they have into the holy city, the New Jerusalem: their glory and their honor. Here "honor" means what is valuable and worthy of respect.

John is describing what he saw in a vision of the new heaven and the new earth. The city is lit by the glory of God and of the Lamb, and its gates are open. The next verse makes clear that only those written in the book of life enter. Christians understand in different ways exactly what this richness of the nations means, but they all agree that all honor ends in God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we do with what we have: talents, culture, work and recognition. We can use them as an offering to honor God and serve others, instead of seeking our own glory.
exp.14:1:
John sees something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal and mixed with fire. Beside it stand those who have won the battle against the beast, against its image, against its mark, and against the number of its name. They are holding harps given by God, which are instruments for praising him.

The word "conquered" means that they came out as the winners.

John is the one who receives this vision in the book of Revelation. Before the last seven plagues, the faithful people are shown already safe, and then they sing praise. The sea of glass recalls the Red Sea and the song of Moses. Some see the fire as a symbol of judgment or of testing; this is understood in several ways.

For today: even when the pressure of the world is strong, faithfulness to God is not in vain. Remain firm in Christ and let the hope of his victory lead you to praise him, even in difficult times.
exp.13:12:
John says he heard a voice from heaven telling him to write: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, from this moment on. The Spirit answers, yes, they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them. The rest described is from their efforts and sufferings, and the words about their deeds mean that what they did in faith is not lost; God remembers it.

Before this, the text shows the punishment of those who worship the beast and have no rest. After it, the final harvest is described. This voice comforts believers who suffer or are persecuted for their faith. It contrasts their rest with the restlessness of the others. Some understand "from this moment on" as referring to the martyrs of that time; others, as all believers.

If you serve God today with weariness or without seeing results, take heart: nothing you do in faith is in vain, and those who die in Christ rest in Him.
exp.13:2:
It says that before the throne of God they sang a new song. They sang it in front of the four living creatures and the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth. The phrase "redeemed from the earth" means ransomed, bought back at a price.

John is describing a vision he saw. He has just seen the Lamb, who is Christ, standing on Mount Zion with this group, who bear the name of the Father. The scene in heaven encourages believers who are under pressure and persecution. Some understand the number literally and others as a symbol of God's faithful people, and Christians interpret it in several ways.

For today: God has redeemed us, and that redeemed life produces a praise of its own. You can thank him sincerely for what he has done in you, and keep following Christ faithfully even when it costs you.
exp.10:9:
This verse says that the people of the world will gloat over the death of God's two witnesses. They will throw a celebration and send gifts to one another, because those prophets had been a torment to them. "Dwell" refers to those who live in a place, "gloat" means to take open pleasure in someone's misfortune, and "gifts" are presents. Here "tormented" speaks of troubling people and making them suffer through the message they bring.

John writes this vision in Revelation. The two witnesses announced God's truth, and for that reason they were rejected and killed. Their bodies are left exposed in the city. There are several ways to interpret who the witnesses are and which city this is, and Christians do not agree on everything. But the text shows the world's contempt for God's message, before God raises them up.

For today: do not be discouraged if the truth you live by troubles others. The world's applause is not the measure of your faithfulness, and God has the last word.
exp.15:16:
Then the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came from the throne in the temple, saying, "It is done!" The word "loud" here carries the sense of "strong" or "mighty," and "poured out" means that he emptied the contents of his bowl.

We are at the last of the seven judgments that John sees in his vision. The one speaking is God himself, or someone speaking from his throne with his authority. With these words it is announced that the judgment is coming to its end. What follows, with thunder, earthquake, and the fall of Babylon, shows the result. Christians interpret in different ways when and how all of this will be fulfilled, but they agree that God has the final word.

For today: you can trust that evil will not last forever. When injustice weighs on you, remember that God sees, and that one day he will say, "It is done." In the meantime, live awake and faithful.
exp.1:27:
He says Jesus will give the one who overcomes "the morning star." It is a short promise, but a very rich one. The word "overcomes" refers to the one who remains faithful to Christ to the end, despite pressures.

Jesus, the risen one, speaks in his letter to the church in Thyatira. He writes to encourage those who did not become defiled by false teaching and immorality. In Revelation 22:16, Jesus himself says: "I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star." That is why many understand the promise to mean receiving Christ himself, in full fellowship. Others add the idea of a new age dawning, but the text does not fully explain this.

For today: when faithfulness costs you, remember that the greatest reward is not a thing, but Jesus himself. Ask him today for strength to follow him with steadiness.
exp.15:12:
It says that John saw three evil spirits come out of the mouths of three figures: the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. These spirits looked like frogs.

John is speaking, relating the vision Jesus gave him. This happens when the sixth angel pours out his bowl, during the final judgments. Many understand the dragon as Satan, and the beast and the false prophet as powers that deceive the nations. Christians interpret in different ways how this will be fulfilled. The spirits come out of the mouths because their weapon is lies.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away by deceptive messages, even when they sound convincing. Compare what you hear with the Bible and stay watchful in prayer, as Jesus advises: "Blessed is the one who stays awake."
exp.18:5:
John says he heard a sound like a huge crowd, like the rushing of many waters, and like a mighty rumbling of thunder. Everyone was crying out, "Hallelujah!", which means "praise the Lord." The reason is that the Lord our God, the Almighty, reigns: he has taken his place as King and rules with full authority.

Before this, the elders and the living creatures worship, and a voice from the throne calls all of God's servants, small and great, to praise him. Now a heavenly multitude answers. The text does not say exactly who they are, but they fit with God's people and the heavenly beings. They rejoice because God acts with justice, and the wedding of the Lamb is drawing near.

Today we can remember that, even when the world seems out of control, God is still the King. This week, in the middle of some worry, pray a short prayer of praise and entrust your situation to his rule.
exp.2:14:
Jesus tells the church in Laodicea that he knows very well what they do. They are neither cold nor hot, that is, they are neither clearly distant nor sincerely passionate. He says, "How I wish you were one or the other!" because he would prefer a clear position.

The one speaking is the risen Christ, who presents himself as the Amen, the faithful and true witness. Laodicea was a prosperous city, and its church felt self-sufficient. Many think the idea of being lukewarm points to a lack of commitment; some also connect it to the lukewarm water of the region, although this is debated.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: is my faith real, or only comfortable? Take a few minutes to pray and ask Jesus to renew your love for him, and take one concrete step of obedience or service today.
exp.20:8:
One of the seven angels who had carried the seven bowls full of the final plagues came to John. He invited him, "Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb." The Lamb is a title for Jesus Christ.

The one speaking is an angel, and John is the one who writes down what he sees. This same kind of angel had appeared earlier, showing the judgment on Babylon (chapter 17). Now the contrast is clear: after the judgment, the bride is presented. The verses that follow show that the bride is the holy city, the New Jerusalem, an image of God's people. Many understand that she represents the Church; the image is symbolic.

For today: if your life belongs to Christ, your future is not fear but a promise of union and joy with Him. Today you can live with hope and faithfulness, remembering that God brings his story to an end with restoration.
exp.4:12:
John hears all of creation praising together. When he says "every creature," he means every created being: in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, and in the sea. "Praise" is what is given, "honor" is recognition of worth, "glory" is splendor, and "power" is authority. All of this is given to God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, that is, Jesus. He is praised forever and ever, without end.

Earlier, the angels, the elders, and the living creatures had praised the Lamb who was slain, that is, sacrificed. Now the praise grows and takes in all of creation. Interpreters differ on exactly what "under the earth" means, but the clear idea is that nothing is left out. Then the four living creatures say "Amen," and the elders worship.

Today we can remember that Jesus deserves the first place. Before asking him for anything, take a few minutes to praise him for who he is and for what he has done.
exp.11:8:
This verse says that the great dragon was hurled down from heaven. He is identified as that ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels were hurled down with him. The words "hurled down" and "hurled to the earth" show that he did not leave on his own: he was driven out. "Devil" means accuser or slanderer.

This is part of a vision that John receives, full of symbols. It follows the battle in heaven, where Michael and his angels prevail. Then a voice from heaven announces that salvation has come, because the accuser has been brought down. Believers overcome him by the blood of the Lamb and by their testimony. Interpreters disagree about when and how this is fulfilled.

For today: when you feel accused or deceived, remember that the enemy has already been defeated by Christ. Rest in his forgiveness and stand firm in the truth of his word.
exp.18:9:
John tells how he fell at the feet of the angel to worship him. The angel stopped him at once: "Do not do that!" He explained that he is a servant just like John and like John's brothers, those who rely on the testimony of Jesus. The command is clear: worship God. At the end he says that the testimony of Jesus is "the spirit of prophecy," meaning that all prophecy at its root points to Jesus and bears witness to him.

John has just heard the invitation to the wedding supper of the Lamb and the words "these are the true words of God." Moved, he bows down before the messenger. The angel corrects John because only God deserves worship. That same correction appears again in Revelation 22:8-9.

For today: admire and thank those whom God uses to bless you, but do not put them in God's place. Direct your worship to him alone, and let everything you read in the Bible lead you to Jesus.
exp.21:7:
John says that he himself is a witness to everything that was shown to him in this vision. After hearing and seeing it, he falls down to worship at the feet of the angel who had shown him these things. "Quickly" means soon or swiftly, and "fell down" means he bowed low to the ground.

John speaks at the end of the book of Revelation. He has just heard that these words are faithful and true. He is so moved that he worships the messenger instead of God. The angel immediately corrects him: he is only a servant, just like John, and only God deserves worship. Some think John did it out of amazement, and the Bible does not explain further.

We can admire the people God uses, but worship belongs only to God. Today it is worth asking ourselves: do I admire the messenger more than the Lord who sends the message?
exp.15:8:
It says that during the fourth plague, people suffered a terrible heat, but instead of turning to God, they cursed him. "Cursed" means speaking with contempt against God. "Authority" in the verse means having the right to rule or command. "Repent" means changing one's course with humility. "Give Him glory" means acknowledging Him as God.

We are in the vision of the seven bowls, where John describes judgments upon the earth. Before this, a voice from the altar declares that God's judgments are true and just. Those who suffer know where the plague comes from, but they harden their hearts. The fifth angel brings more pain, and once again there is no repentance. Interpreters differ on whether these events are literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: pain can soften us or harden us. When difficulties come, instead of complaining with bitterness, we can pray with humility and ask, "Lord, what do you want to teach me?"
exp.20:22:
This verse says that the heavenly city does not need the sun or the moon to shine on it. "Glory" means the radiance and brightness of God himself, and "lamp" means the light source. God's glory fills the city with light, and Jesus, called "the Lamb," is its lamp.

John writes what he saw in a vision about the new Jerusalem, at the end of Revelation. He speaks to Christians who were under pressure and persecution, to give them hope. Shortly before, he says there is no temple, because God and the Lamb are present directly. Many understand the city symbolically and others more literally; in both cases the center is the presence of God.

Today you can remember that God is the source of all true light. When you feel confused or weary, ask Jesus to guide you, and live with the hope that one day you will be in his presence.
exp.10:17:
The nations were enraged, and God's wrath has come. This is the time to judge the dead and to reward God's servants, the prophets, the saints, and all who fear his name, whether they are small or great. It is also the time for God to destroy those who destroy the earth.

Here the twenty-four elders speak, the ones who worship God in heaven after the seventh trumpet. They give thanks because God has taken his great power and reigns. Interpreters differ on how to understand the exact timing of these events, but all agree that it is a declaration of God's victory over evil.

For today: although we see injustice and harm in the world, we can live with hope and faithfulness. God sees each one of his own, however small they may seem in the eyes of others, and he does not forget their service.
exp.11:13:
It says that the woman was given two wings of a great eagle, so that she could fly from the presence of the serpent to a place prepared for her in the wilderness. There she is nourished during "a time, and times, and half a time," an expression that is usually understood to mean three and a half years.

John relates this vision in symbolic language. The dragon, who is Satan, has already been thrown out of heaven and pursues the woman. Many see her as God's people, others as Israel or the Church; there are several interpretations. The eagle's wings call to mind God's care in Exodus 19:4. The message is that God protects his own in the middle of persecution.

For today: when you go through seasons of trial or loneliness, trust that God knows how to sustain you. His care does not always spare you from the wilderness, but it accompanies you and feeds you there.
exp.6:5:
This verse continues the list of the tribes of Israel. It names Asher, Naphtali and Manasseh, and for each one it says that 12,000 were "sealed," meaning marked as belonging to God. The word points to a mark showing that someone belongs to God and is protected.

John reports what he saw in his vision. Before more trials come upon the earth, God marks his servants as his own. Some read this as a literal number of Israelites, while others understand it as a picture of the whole people of God. It is worth noticing that Manasseh appears in the list, while Dan and Ephraim are not named, and the Bible does not clearly explain why.

For today: God knows each of his own by name and cares for them. When you feel afraid, remember that you belong to him and that he holds you up.
exp.2:18:
Jesus says that he rebukes and disciplines those he loves. Here "discipline" means correcting and teaching, like a loving parent who guides a child with care. That is why he tells them to be "earnest," that is, to take things seriously and with real commitment, and to repent, or in other words, to change course.

Jesus speaks to the church of Laodicea, in a letter from the book of Revelation. They believed themselves rich and in need of nothing, but Jesus sees them as spiritually poor, blind, and naked. His rebuke does not reject them: right away he invites them to open the door to him so they can share a meal with him.

For today: when someone or something corrects you, do not take it as rejection. If God shows you a mistake, respond with humility, change, and draw close to him again.
exp.3:0:
John says that, after what he had just seen, he looked and saw a door standing open in heaven. He heard again the voice that had spoken to him before, sounding like a trumpet, and it was saying, "Come up here." It promised to show him what must happen after these things. John is inviting the reader to pay close attention to what he is about to describe, and the phrase about being "in the Spirit" means that he was carried away in a vision.

John wrote the book of Revelation. Earlier, in chapters 2 and 3, Christ spoke to seven churches. Now the vision turns toward heaven. Many understand that the voice is Christ's, since it sounds like the voice John heard in 1:10. Christians interpret the order of the events that follow in different ways, but all of them see that God reigns and that John received this vision to encourage his people.

When life seems confusing or painful, God invites us to look higher. Today you can spend a few minutes praying and remembering that God still sits on his throne and that your life is in his hands.
exp.15:17:
When the seventh angel pours out his bowl, flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder appear, and there is a great earthquake, stronger than any since people have lived on the earth.

John recounts his vision from Revelation. The voice from the throne had said "It is done": God's judgment reaches its final point. The lightning and thunder recall God's presence on the throne. Christians understand in different ways whether this earthquake is literal, symbolic, or both. What is clear is that God judges Babylon, the symbol of human power that opposes Him.

For today: do not place your security in what can be shaken, such as money, power, or prestige. Trust in God, whose kingdom cannot fall, and live with hope and faithfulness.
exp.21:12:
He says that Jesus is "the Alpha and the Omega," the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. It is a way of saying that He is the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End of all things.

Jesus is speaking in this final passage of the book, announcing that He is coming soon. He has just said that He will repay each person according to their works. By declaring Himself the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End, He makes clear that He has authority over all of history and can judge with justice. The words that follow invite us to live faithfully, with the promise of the tree of life.

Today we can live with calm and seriousness, knowing that our lives are in the hands of the One who began and will finish everything. Today you can choose to be honest and to obey Him in small things, trusting in His justice and His mercy.
exp.17:2:
It says that all the nations have drunk the wine of Babylon's immorality, like someone who gets drunk and loses their judgment. The kings were immoral with her, and that word speaks of unfaithful alliances, idolatry and corruption. The merchants, or traders, grew wealthy from her extravagance and luxury.

A mighty angel is announcing the fall of Babylon, a symbol of worldwide power that opposes God. It is debated whether this represents Rome, a future system, or both. Then another voice from heaven calls God's people to come out of her so that they will not share in her sins or her punishment.

For today: examine which things in the world attract you, such as easy money, luxury or approval, and ask God to help you not depend on them or be swept along by them.
exp.1:18:
Jesus tells the church in Thyatira that he knows their life well. He recognizes five good things: their deeds, their love (here "charity" means practical love), their service, their faith, and their perseverance, that is, their endurance through hardships. Furthermore, what they are doing now is greater than what they did at the beginning. It is a church that keeps growing.

The one speaking is the Son of God, with eyes like a flame of fire, who see everything thoroughly. Before correcting the church for tolerating the woman called Jezebel, he first acknowledges what is good. His gaze is true: he sees what pleases him and also what is lacking.

For today: God notices our effort and our growth. Take heart, because nothing you do with love goes unnoticed. But also let him correct you with kindness where it is needed.
exp.5:13:
It says that the sky recedes, or rolls up, like a scroll being wrapped up and put away. Also, every mountain and island is moved from its place. The word "receded" carries the sense of pulling back or drawing away. It is an image of everything that seemed firm being shaken.

John speaks, relating a vision that Jesus gave him. The sixth seal shows God's judgment shaking creation. Christians interpret this in several ways: as a literal scene of the end, or as symbolic language expressing God's power. The verses that follow show that people, from kings to slaves, tremble before the Lamb.

For today: if even the mountains move, it is not wise to place our security in passing things such as money, power, or prestige. We can rest in Christ, who remains firm.
exp.3:6:
In this verse John describes four living creatures around the throne of God. Here, the word for these beings means living creatures, not common animals. The first is like a lion, the second like a calf (a young bull), the third has a face like a man, and the fourth is like an eagle in flight.

The one speaking is John, who recounts a vision of heaven. He describes the scene of worship that surrounds God. The four beings appear praising him without rest. Interpreters understand them in several ways: some see in them all of creation worshiping God, others see high-ranking angels. Ezekiel 1 and 10 have similar images. The Bible does not explain this with precision.

For today: if all of creation and the beings of heaven live worshiping God, we too can begin the day by recognizing his greatness with a simple prayer of gratitude and praise.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that the fallen star was given the key and opened the Abyss, a deep pit that stands for a dark, enclosed place. From it rose a great deal of smoke, like the smoke of a huge furnace, and the smoke darkened the sun and the air. The smoke is what makes the sun and the air grow dark.

John writes what he saw in a vision, during the sounding of the fifth trumpet. These trumpets announce judgments that warn a world that rejects God. Some believe the star is an angel and others that it is a figure of evil; the text does not fully make this clear. What is clear is that the pit opens only because permission is given, and that the locusts come out right after.

For today: evil can darken life and confuse us, but it never escapes God's control. When everything seems dark, trust that he still governs, and seek his light in prayer and in his Word.
exp.21:9:
Here the angel tells John not to seal up the words of prophecy in this book, meaning not to keep them hidden. The angel gives the reason: the time is near, so what is announced matters now.

The speaker is the angel who accompanied John through the whole vision. He has just corrected John when John fell down to worship him: only God deserves worship. In Daniel 12:4 the prophecy was commanded to be sealed; here the opposite happens, since the message is meant to be read and obeyed. Christians understand in different ways how soon "near" is fulfilled, but all of them see in this an urgent call.

Today, do not leave the Bible closed. Read it carefully, obey it, and share it with someone, knowing that every day counts before God.
exp.8:5:
It says that during the torment of the locusts, people will suffer so much that they will long to die, but they will not be able to. The words "seek" and "flee" are explained as follows: "seek" means that they will keep looking for death, and "flee" means that death will escape them, as if moving away from them.

John writes down what he saw in a vision, at the fifth trumpet. The locusts torment only those who do not have the mark of God, that is, the seal that protects his people. Some believe it is a literal future judgment; others see it as a picture of spiritual forces or of evils that afflict the world. The text shows that the suffering has a fixed limit: five months.

For today: God takes care of his own even in difficult times. If you feel anguish today, remember that you are not alone. Seek God and trustworthy people, because despair does not have the final word.
exp.10:15:
This verse says that the twenty-four elders, who sit on thrones before God, fell on their faces and worshiped God. "Sit" here means they are seated on thrones, and "fell on their faces" is a gesture of humility and complete respect.

The seventh trumpet sounds, and in heaven it is announced that the kingdoms of the world now belong to God and to his Christ. The elders respond with worship and thanksgiving. Who exactly they are is understood in several ways: some think they represent God's people, others think they are heavenly beings. The text does not fully clarify this.

When God acts, the right response is to worship him. Today we can do the same: before asking or questioning, we can pause to give thanks and acknowledge that God reigns, even when the world seems confused.
exp.8:15:
The verse says the number of mounted troops was two hundred million, a vast figure meant to convey an enormous army. John adds that he heard their number, which means he did not count them himself but was told how many there were.

John, the writer, recounts what he sees and hears in a vision. This takes place when the sixth trumpet sounds, part of the judgments that announce the end. The four angels are released to punish humanity. Some believe the numbers are literal, while others read them as symbolic and pointing to a devastating power. The Bible does not fully clarify this, so it is wise to be humble when interpreting it.

For today: God has complete control, even over what seems overwhelming. The angels are released at the exact time appointed for them, and nothing happens outside his timing. We can trust him and turn to him with humility.
exp.8:18:
The verse says that the power of these horses was in two places: in their mouths, from which came fire, smoke and sulfur, and in their tails. The tails were like snakes, having heads, and with them the horses inflicted harm. The wording "with which to inflict harm" in this reader's verse makes plain that the tails were the means of the damage.

John recounts what he saw in a vision, during the sixth trumpet. It is a judgment upon the earth. Christians interpret these images in different ways: as future events, as symbols of armies, or as signs of judgments in general. What the text makes clear is that, even after so much suffering, many did not repent.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our heart softens or hardens when trials come. God invites us to turn back to Him with humility, without waiting for the pain to become greater.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that a powerful angel made a solemn oath in the name of the one who lives forever and ever, God the Creator of everything: the heavens, the earth, and the sea, along with all that is in them. The angel's words, "There will be no more delay," mean that the waiting is coming to an end and God's plan is about to move forward.

The angel speaking is the one John saw standing on the sea and on the land. John had just heard the seven thunders, but he was told not to write them down. After the oath, the angel announces that when the seventh trumpet sounds, God's secret plan will be fulfilled, just as he announced to his prophets.

For today: even when it sometimes feels as though God is slow, he holds control of history and will keep his word. We can trust him and wait with patience, without needing to understand everything.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that grace and peace also come from Jesus Christ. John describes him with three titles: "the faithful witness," because he tells the truth about God and stayed faithful even to death; "the firstborn from the dead," because he was the first to rise and will never die again; and "the ruler of the kings of the earth," because his authority is above every human ruler. The verse also says that he loves us and has released us from our sins by his blood. Being released from sin speaks of cleansing and forgiveness.

The one speaking is John, who is writing to seven churches in Asia, probably in times of pressure and difficulty. At the beginning of his letter, he wants believers to see first who Jesus is and what he has done for them. This gives them firmness before they read difficult visions.

For today: when you feel guilty, insecure, or troubled by what is happening in the world, remember that Jesus loves you, has cleansed you, and rules over all things. Rest in his forgiveness and trust in his authority.
exp.18:18:
It says that John saw the beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies assembled to wage war against the One seated on the horse, and against His army. The phrase "assembled" is the key idea here: the enemies have come together for one final battle. It is the great last battle between evil and Jesus.

John writes this vision to encourage Christians who were under pressure and persecution. Just before, an angel invites the birds to the great supper of God, a picture of judgment. Just after, the beast and the false prophet are defeated by the word of Christ, the sword from his mouth. Christians understand this moment in different ways: as a future event, or as a symbol of Christ's triumph over all evil.

For today: even when evil seems strong and well organized, it does not have the last word. We can remain faithful to Jesus with hope, knowing that he wins.
exp.15:4:
This verse says that John heard the angel in charge of the waters praising God. The angel tells him that God is righteous and holy, the one who is and was, because he has brought these judgments. "Judgments" here means that God pronounced sentence and carried it out.

The angel of the waters speaks right after the rivers and springs turn to blood. The next verse explains the reason: those who poured out the blood of the saints and the prophets now receive blood to drink. Some see here a literal punishment and others a symbolic image; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when injustice hurts us or confuses us, we can trust that God sees everything and judges with perfect justice. In this way we can hand over our desire for revenge and keep doing good with patience.
exp.17:12:
This verse continues the list of goods that merchants sold to Babylon. It names spices and incense (cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense), foods and drink (wine, olive oil, fine flour, wheat), animals (cattle, sheep), and means of transport (horses, carriages), and at the end, the bodies and souls of slaves, that is, people who were bought and sold as merchandise.

Context: John describes in his vision the fall of "Babylon," a powerful, rich, and corrupt city. Many understand it as Rome, and others as a symbol of any system that lives off luxury and injustice. The merchants weep, but not for her, but because their business is over. The list ends with human beings, which reveals the gravest thing about that wealth.

For today: examine whether you value people more than things. Try to buy, work, and earn fairly, without taking advantage of anyone.
exp.2:9:
It says that the church of Philadelphia was faithful and kept Christ's command to persevere. Because of this, Jesus promises to keep it from the "hour of testing," a time of trial that is about to come upon the whole world. "Testing" means putting people to the test, and "those who dwell on the earth" are those who live clinging to this world.

Here Jesus, risen, speaks in his letter to a small church, with little strength, but faithful and persecuted. He encourages it with promises. Christians interpret in different ways what that hour is and how he will keep them: whether he will deliver them from it or sustain them in the midst of it.

For today: even if you feel weak, remain faithful to Christ with patience. He sees your steadfastness and promises to sustain you in difficult times.
exp.15:2:
This verse says that the second angel poured out his bowl into the sea. The water turned to blood, the kind of blood that belongs to a dead person, and every living thing in the sea died. The verse uses plain wording here, so the point is simply that the sea itself was changed and its living creatures were destroyed.
