A voice from the temple, understood to be God's, commanded seven angels to pour out the bowls of his wrath on the earth. These are judgments on a world that opposes God and follows the beast. This recalls the plagues of Egypt, when the water also turned to blood. Some take this literally and others as a symbol. Then the angel over the waters declares that God is just.

For today: God takes evil and the life he created seriously. This invites us to live with humility, not to take his patience lightly, and to trust that he will do justice. Today you might pray for those who suffer injustice and ask him to keep you faithful.
exp.12:8:
He who has an ear, let him hear. This is an invitation to listen carefully. It does not speak of the physical ear, but of a disposition of the heart to receive and obey what God says.

These words come from Jesus, who uses them in the Gospels and in the letters to the seven churches. Here they appear after the description of the first beast, which persecutes the saints and receives worship from many. Many understand it to be an oppressive power; there are several interpretations about its exact identity. The warning calls the church not to be distracted or to surrender, and to remain faithful.

For today: do not be content with hearing the Word of God only in passing. Read it with attention and ask for help to obey it, especially when the pressure of the environment pushes you to give in. Patient faithfulness is the response God expects.
exp.17:15:
This verse says that the merchants weep over the great city, Babylon, because it once looked very luxurious. It was clothed in fine linen (a delicate and expensive cloth), in purple and scarlet (cloths dyed in costly colors), and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls. Its beauty was outward and showy.

The merchants speak as people who grew rich through her. They do not mourn the city so much as their own lost business. In Revelation, Babylon is a symbol of the power and luxury of a world that turns away from God; some connect her with Rome, and others understand her in a broader way. Her fall comes suddenly, "in one hour."

For today: let us take care that our hearts do not depend on money or appearances. All of that can disappear quickly. Let us seek first what does not end: a life with God and with the people we love.
exp.8:11:
It says that the first great calamity has already passed, but that two more are still to follow. The word "woe" is a cry of grief and warning. "Passed" means that it has already happened. With this, the scene of the locusts that torment the people comes to an end.

The one speaking is John, who recounts what he sees in his vision. In Revelation, the trumpets announce God's judgments, and the two woes that remain correspond to the last two. Interpreters explain these images in different ways, but they agree that they show the seriousness of judgment and that God controls the timing and order of events.

For today: do not take God's warnings lightly. If He warns us clearly, it is because He wants to lead us to repentance. Today you can respond with humility and return to Him with confidence.
exp.2:5:
It says that whoever has ears should listen carefully to what the Spirit says to the churches. It is not only about hearing sounds, but about paying attention and obeying.

The one speaking is Jesus, who dictates letters to seven churches in the book of Revelation. This is the closing phrase of the letter to Sardis, just after his promise of white garments for the faithful. This same invitation is repeated in every letter. It shows that the message, though addressed to one church, is meant for all.

For today: when you read the Bible or hear a teaching, do not be satisfied with just hearing. Ask the Spirit to show you what you need to change or believe, and take one concrete step of obedience this week.
exp.17:7:
It says that Babylon's punishment will come suddenly, all in one day. Her "plagues" are calamities: death, grief, and famine. In the end she will be consumed by fire, because the Lord God is mighty to judge her. "Mighty" here means that no one can stop her judgment.

It is a voice from heaven speaking to God's people, asking them to come out of Babylon. This city symbolizes a system of pride, luxury, and oppression. Many connect it with Rome, and others see it as a broader symbol of the world in rebellion against God. She used to say, "I sit as a queen," confident that nothing would bring her down.

For today: do not place your security in success, money, or power, because all of that is temporary. Trust in God, who is just, and ask him for help to live with humility and not be carried away by the world's pride.
exp.3:4:
From the throne came flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder, like a storm full of power. Before the throne burned seven torches of fire, and the text itself explains that these are the seven Spirits of God.

John, who describes a vision of heaven, speaks here. Earlier he saw God seated on the throne, surrounded by elders who worshiped Him. The lightning and thunder recall God's presence on Mount Sinai. Many understand the seven Spirits as the Holy Spirit in His fullness, although some interpret it in other ways. The central message is that God reigns with holiness and power.

For today: when the world feels chaotic, remember that God's throne remains firm. Draw near to Him with reverence and confidence, and pray for the guidance of His Spirit.
exp.20:17:
The verse says that the wall of the city was made of jasper, and that the city itself was pure gold, as pure as glass. Jasper is a precious stone, and here it is pictured as bright and clear. The gold is pure and transparent, like clean glass, which is an image of purity and light, without stain or shadow.

John, the author, recounts what an angel showed him in a vision at the end of Revelation. After describing the new heaven and the new earth, the angel measures the city. The images are symbolic, and scholars interpret them in different ways, but all of them point to the glory, the security, and the holiness of God's people with Him.

For today: God promises a future that is clean and transparent, without deceit or corruption. You can ask Him to help you now to live with sincerity, hiding nothing, trusting that He finishes what He has begun.
exp.21:18:
And if anyone takes away from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city, which are described in this book. This verse says that if anyone takes away from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away his part in the tree of life, in the holy city, and in the promises written here. To take away means to remove or cut back, and a "part" is the portion or share that someone would have.

Jesus speaks, through John, at the end of Revelation. Just before this, he invites everyone to come and take freely of the water of life. This warning, similar to Deuteronomy 4:2, protects the message so that no one trims it or changes it. Interpreters debate whether it speaks of losing salvation or of a judgment on the one who falsifies the book; the text stresses the seriousness of being faithful to the Word.

For today: read the Bible with humility, without hiding what makes you uncomfortable or bending it to fit your preferences. Ask God to teach you to obey all of it.
exp.12:11:
This passage says that the second beast, the one that rises out of the earth, uses all the authority of the first beast, acting in its presence. It uses that power to make everyone who lives on the earth worship the first beast, the one whose mortal wound had been healed. A mortal wound is a wound that would cause death, and "had been healed" means it was made well again.

John writes this vision for Christians who were under pressure because of their faith. Here a second beast appears, one that seems gentle like a lamb but speaks like a dragon. Many understand it as a religious or propaganda power that supports the political power of the first beast. Interpreters differ on the details, but the central message is clear: deception serves idolatry.

For today: do not give your final worship to any power, leader, or system, however attractive it may seem. Compare what you hear with the Word of God, and remain faithful to Christ with patience.
exp.9:6:
When the seventh angel is about to sound his trumpet, God will bring his hidden plan to full completion. A "mystery" is something God kept secret and later reveals. "Fulfilled" means brought to its intended end and fully carried out. God had already announced this plan to his prophets.

John describes a vision here. A mighty angel has just sworn by God the Creator that there will be no more delay. Between the sixth and seventh trumpets, this announcement assures that God's plan will not fail. Interpreters differ on how and when this is fulfilled in detail.

For today: if you find it hard to understand why God takes his time, remember that he has a plan and will carry it out. You can wait with patience and keep trusting him.
exp.15:19:
This verse says that every island fled, and no mountain could be found. "Fled" means that they went away or moved far off; "no mountain could be found" means that they were no longer in their place. It is a picture of an earthquake so enormous that it changes the whole earth.

This happens at the seventh bowl of God's wrath, the end of the judgments in Revelation. John describes what he saw in a vision. Some believe it is a literal future event; others read it as symbolic language for the end of the power of evil. Christians understand it in different ways. What is clear is that God judges Babylon, a symbol of the pride and injustice of the world.

For today: what seems most solid, like mountains and islands, can fall. Place your trust in God, not in money, power, or the things of this world. He endures and cares for his own.
exp.11:0:
John says he saw a great sign in heaven, meaning a symbolic image: a woman wrapped in the light of the sun, with the moon beneath her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head. "Clothed in the sun" means covered in its brightness. It is a scene of glory and dignity.

John, who received this vision from Jesus Christ to encourage the churches that were suffering, is the one speaking. Interpreters explain the woman in several ways: as Israel, as the people of God, as the church, or with some reference to Mary. The twelve stars may recall the twelve tribes or the apostles. The text that follows shows her giving birth while a dragon threatens her.

For today: even when evil seems strong, God cares for his people and has the final word. When you go through trials, trust that your life is in God's hands.
exp.14:2:
They sing of those who did not give in to the beast, the victors, who sing two songs at once: the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb. In their song they praise God for his great and wonderful works, and they declare that his ways are just and true. The word "last" is used here for the final plagues, and God is described as King of his people.

The speakers are the group of faithful believers standing beside the sea of glass, with harps in their hands. The song of Moses recalls Israel's deliverance at the sea (Exodus 15). Here a similar deliverance is celebrated, just before the final plagues. Interpreters disagree about how and when this is fulfilled, but the theme is clear: God rescues and judges with justice.

Today we can praise God even in the midst of difficulty, trusting that his ways are just, even when we do not always understand them.
exp.6:10:
All the angels stood around the throne, together with the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell facedown before the throne and worshiped God.

John is describing a vision. He has just seen a huge crowd from every nation praising God and the Lamb for salvation. Now the whole of heaven answers with worship. The angels were not saved as human beings were, but they join in the song. Then they say "Amen" and give God seven expressions of honor.

For today: when life fills you with noise and worries, take a few minutes to worship God for who he is, not only for what he gives you. Bowing your heart before him brings your perspective back.
exp.2:19:
He says Jesus is standing outside the door and knocking. If anyone hears his voice and opens the door, he will come into their home and they will eat together, like friends. "I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me" speaks of closeness and fellowship. The word "hears" here means to listen and pay attention.

These words are spoken by the risen Jesus in his letter to the church in Laodicea. That community felt rich and self-sufficient, but he saw it as lukewarm and in need. So he speaks to them with firmness, but also with love: "As many as I love, I rebuke and discipline." Many believe the invitation was addressed to believers who had shut Christ out, although it also applies to anyone.

For today, do not wait until you feel perfect. Set aside a few minutes for quiet prayer, listen to his voice in the Bible, and honestly open to him the areas of your life you have kept closed.
exp.1:3:
He says that Jesus, although he recognizes the good in this church, has a serious complaint: they no longer love as they did at the beginning. The phrase "you have abandoned" means that they let go of something they once had. The "first love" is the initial love toward Christ, that sincere and fervent devotion from the start. It can be understood as love for God, love for people, or both.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, in a letter to the church in Ephesus, sent through John. He praises their work, their patience, and their firmness against false apostles. But he warns them that doing things rightly does not replace the heart. For this reason he invites them to remember, repent, and return to the first works.

For today: set aside a few minutes to speak with Jesus honestly, without a to-do list. Ask him to renew your love, and do one concrete act of affection today toward him or toward someone close to you.
exp.2:11:
Jesus promises those who "overcome," meaning those who stay faithful to the end, that he will make them a pillar in the temple of God. That person will never again leave it. He will also write on them the name of God, the name of the city of God, the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from God, and his new name.

Here Jesus speaks to the church in Philadelphia, a community with little strength but a faithful heart. He encourages them to hold firm, because he is coming soon. A pillar suggests stability, permanence, and honor. Written names suggest belonging and security. Philadelphia suffered earthquakes, so the image of a firm pillar carried great weight for its readers. Interpreters differ on the symbolic details.

Today, even if you feel weak or tired, you can remain faithful with confidence. Your place with God does not depend on your strength but on his promise. Today, keep obeying in the small things.
exp.11:12:
It says that when the dragon realized he had been thrown down to the earth, he set out to pursue the woman who gave birth to the male child. The words "saw" and "thrown" in the verse above are the ones the verse refers to, and "gave birth to" is the wording used in the verse itself.

John is recounting a vision. The dragon is Satan, according to Revelation 12:9. The woman has been understood in several ways: as Israel, as the church, or as God's people in general. The dragon, defeated in heaven, vents his fury against God's people. This passage aims to comfort believers who were suffering persecution.

For today: if you face opposition or trials, remember that the enemy has already been defeated and has a limited time. Stand firm, trusting in Christ, because God cares for his people, even in the wilderness.
exp.1:4:
Revelation 2:5 calls the church to remember how far it has fallen, to turn back, and to do the deeds it did at first. The verse says that if they do not repent, Jesus will come to them quickly and remove their lampstand from its place. The lampstand is a lamp stand, and the call to do the first deeds means returning to the actions that came from their first love.

The risen Jesus speaks to the church in Ephesus. They worked hard, endured, and rejected what was false, but they had left their first love. Jesus does not reject them: he recognizes what is good and calls them to return. The lampstand represents the church as a light; removing it is commonly understood as losing its place of witness, though it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: it is not enough to serve much; check whether you do it out of love for Christ. Spend a few minutes today praying sincerely and doing something simple that shows that love.
exp.13:10:
It says that the punishment of those who worship the beast and its image will be continuous and without end. The smoke of their torment that rises forever and ever shows that God's judgment is real and final. "No rest" means there is no relief from the suffering, day or night. The phrase "receives the mark" refers to receiving the beast's mark, which stands for loyalty to it.

Here an angel, the third, speaks within the vision that God gave to John. It is a serious warning that no one should join the power that opposes God. Christians interpret the beast and its mark in different ways, but all see a clear contrast. The faithful who persevere find rest in the Lord, while those who reject God have no rest.

Today it invites us to examine to whom we give our loyalty. We can ask ourselves what things compete with God in our hearts, and renew our trust in Christ, with perseverance and hope.
exp.10:5:
These verses say that the two witnesses have the power to shut the sky so that no rain falls while they prophesy. They also have the power to turn the waters into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish. The word "power" here means the ability or authority to act. "Strike" means to hit or punish.

John is writing down the vision that Jesus gave him. The two witnesses speak on behalf of God, and God protects their message. Their powers bring to mind Elijah, who shut the sky, and Moses, who sent plagues. Christians understand them in different ways: as two real people, or as the Church bearing witness. There is no single interpretation that is certain.

For today: God cares for those who are faithful to him, even when the world rejects them. We can bear witness with courage and humility, trusting that the power comes from him and not from ourselves.
exp.11:4:
She gave birth to a son, a male child, who would rule all the nations with an iron scepter, that is, with firm and just authority. Before the dragon could devour him, the child was quickly taken up to God and to his throne.

John is describing a vision full of symbols. The dragon, which in the same chapter is identified with Satan, tries to destroy the child. Many Christians see in the child Jesus, since the "iron scepter" language echoes Psalm 2 about the Messiah. Interpretations differ about who the woman is: Israel, the Church, or Mary. John writes to encourage believers who were suffering persecution.

For today: although evil may seem powerful, God cares for his people and his plan does not fail. When you face trials, trust that Christ reigns and rest in that hope.
exp.12:4:
The verse says that the beast was given a mouth to speak arrogant and blasphemous words against God. It was also given authority to act for forty-two months, which is three and a half years.

The word "authority" in the verse refers to the right to act. The phrase "was given" shows that the beast did not have this authority on its own, but only what was permitted to it.

John writes this vision to Christians who were under pressure and persecution. The beast represents an oppressive political power that receives its strength from the dragon. Many interpreters see in this Rome or a future power, and others see a symbol of every government that rises against God. The forty-two months recall Daniel and show a limited time.

Today we can remember that evil never has the last word. Even when it seems strong and speaks with pride, God sets its limits. This invites us to remain faithful with patience and to trust in Christ.
exp.0:10:
The voice John hears identifies itself as "the Alpha and Omega, the first and the last." Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. Then it tells John to write down what he sees in a scroll and send it to seven churches, naming them one by one: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Those cities were in the region of Asia, which today is part of Turkey.

John is on the island of Patmos because he was preaching the word of God. The voice sounds like a trumpet, and the verses that follow show that the one speaking is Jesus. He gives the command so that his message will reach communities that were facing hardship.

For today: if Jesus is the first and the last, we can trust him with our beginning and our end. When you are going through a difficult season, read this as a reminder that he is still in control.
exp.15:11:
It says that the sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and that its water dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East. In this way the path was cleared for rulers coming from the lands east of the river. "To prepare the way" means to make a clear path.

John reports what he sees in his vision of the seven bowls, which show God's judgment on a world that refuses to repent. The Euphrates was a historic boundary of the biblical world. Interpreters disagree: some take it literally, others as a symbol. What follows shows that a great final conflict is being prepared.

For today: God is in control of history, even when the nations are restless. Trust in Him, and keep a heart ready to repent while there is still time.
exp.12:7:
The verse says that all the people who live on the earth will worship the beast, except those whose names have been written in the Book of Life that belongs to the Lamb. The Lamb is Jesus, the one who was sacrificed. The phrase "from the foundation of the world" can be read in two ways: it can go with the Lamb who was slain, or with the names being written. Scholars understand it both ways. Some take it to mean that Christ's sacrifice was planned from eternity, and others take it to mean that the names were written from the creation of the world.

John writes this book to Christians who were persecuted by a power that demanded worship. He shows that evil seems to triumph and to dominate everyone, but the destiny of the faithful is kept safe by Christ himself. The verses that follow call for patience and faith.

Today, when the pressure of our surroundings pushes us to go along with the crowd, we can rest in the fact that our security depends on the Lamb and not on the approval of the majority. Remain faithful, even when you walk against the current.
exp.16:10:
The beast that once existed and now does not, appears again as an eighth king. At the same time, it belongs to the seven kings before it, meaning it shares their same nature. Its end is destruction, which means total ruin.

Here an angel speaks to John, explaining the vision of the woman seated on the beast. Interpreters do not agree on who the seven kings are: some think of Roman emperors, others of successive empires, and others see symbolic language. What is clear is that the message aims to comfort Christians who were being persecuted: the power that opposes God has an expiration date.

For today: when the powers of the world seem invincible, remember that they do not have the final word. Remain faithful to Christ with patience and trust, knowing that He reigns and that all injustice will come to an end.
exp.6:8:
John says that, after he saw the 144,000 who were sealed, he saw a multitude too large to count. They came from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue. They stood before the throne of God and before the Lamb, who is Jesus. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands. The words "tribe" and "crowds" in this passage refer to groups of people from every background and any gathering of people.

The one speaking is John, who tells what he saw in a vision. Before this, he heard the number of those sealed from the tribes of Israel. Now he sees a multitude from all peoples. Many believe these are the same people of God seen in two ways, while others think they are two separate groups. The white robes speak of purity and celebration, and the palm branches of victory and joy. The purpose is to encourage believers who were suffering.

For today: the church of Christ is far larger and more diverse than we can see. We can welcome believers from other cultures and languages with joy, knowing that one day we will worship together.
exp.0:17:
Here Jesus says that he is the Living One. He was dead on the cross, but he rose again and is alive forever and ever. The word translated "Hades" in this verse refers to the place of the dead, not necessarily the place of final punishment. "Keys" signify authority and control: Jesus holds power over death and over the place of the dead.

The one speaking is the glorified Jesus, who appears to John on the island of Patmos. John falls down as if dead from fear, and Jesus places his hand on him and says: "Do not be afraid." He reminds John who he is, the first and the last, to give him confidence before commissioning him to write down what he will see.

For today: if Christ holds the keys of death, we do not have to live dominated by the fear of dying or of losing those we love. When you feel fear, repeat his word: "Do not be afraid," and place yourself in his hands.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that Jesus, the Lamb, has made his people a kingdom and priests to serve God. "They will reign upon the earth" announces that the redeemed will share in God's rule.

The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures sing a new song before the throne. They praise the Lamb because he was slain, that is, sacrificed, and with his blood he purchased people from every tribe and nation. Their song prepares the praise of the angels that follows. How and when that reign will happen is understood in different ways among Christians.

For today: if God has called you a priest, you can come to him in prayer without fear and pray for others. Today, intercede for someone who needs it and treat them with humility and service.
exp.1:22:
Jesus says that he will strike the children of the woman called Jezebel with death, meaning those who follow her teaching. "Strike dead" here refers to the judgment that falls on them. To "search" means to examine thoroughly. "Minds" and "hearts" point to the innermost parts of a person: thoughts and desires. So all the churches will know that Christ sees the heart and will repay each person according to their deeds.

Jesus speaks to the church in Thyatira. He praises its love and its service, but rebukes it for tolerating a false prophetess who led others into sexual immorality and idolatry. He gave her time to repent, and she refused. Many understand "Jezebel" as a symbolic name, though this is not known with certainty.

For today: do not be satisfied with looking good on the outside. Ask God to examine your heart, and confess soon whatever is drawing you away from him, because his patience is an invitation to return.
exp.13:9:
Whoever worships the beast and receives its mark will drink the wine of God's wrath. The phrase "poured out undiluted" means it is poured out with nothing mixed in, that is, at full strength. That judgment is described as torment with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb, who is Christ.

The third angel speaks, giving a warning in a loud voice. This comes after the fall of Babylon, which led the nations astray. John writes to believers who are under pressure to submit to a power that opposes God. The language is symbolic and is interpreted in various ways, but the central message is that God is just and does not ignore evil.

For today: do not give in to what demands a loyalty that belongs only to God, even when it costs you. Remain faithful to Jesus with patience, trusting that God will bring about justice.
exp.9:10:
The verse tells John that he must prophesy again, that is, speak a message from God to many peoples, nations, languages, and kings. The word translated "must" means that this is necessary, not optional. The word "again" shows that John had already prophesied and now has to keep going.

In this chapter, the strong angel is the one who gives the message, and John is the one who receives it. John has just eaten the little book, which was sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach. Many understand this as a picture that God's word is sweet to receive but painful to announce, since it includes judgment. Others interpret it differently, and not everyone agrees on the details.

For today: if God gives you a truth, do not keep it only for yourself. Share it with humility and love, even when it is not easy, and trust that He sustains you.
exp.18:17:
It tells that an angel calls the birds to eat the flesh of all who oppose Christ: kings, commanders, mighty men, horses and their riders, everyone whether slave or free, and the small and the great. "Commanders" are the military leaders, and "mighty men" are the strong and powerful. The image is very strong on purpose.

The one speaking is an angel standing in the sun, and John sees him in his vision. This comes right after Christ appears as "King of kings and Lord of lords." This "great supper of God" contrasts with the marriage supper of the Lamb. Many understand the scene as symbolic language of the final judgment on evil; others see it as more literal. The Bible uses similar images in Ezekiel 39.

For today: no power, rank, or wealth can be compared with Christ. Today you can choose to trust in Him rather than in your own strength or position, and live with the hope that God's justice will prevail in the end.
exp.12:12:
It says that the second beast, the one that comes up out of the earth, performs great signs before the people. It even causes fire to come down from heaven to earth. The words "signs" and "causing fire from heaven" mean that it does astonishing and visible deeds, to impress everyone.

John writes this vision to encourage Christians who were under pressure to worship the political and religious power of his time. This second beast supports the first and deceives people with miraculous displays. Many see in it a symbol of false religious propaganda, although interpreters differ on how to understand it. It recalls the fire from heaven of Elijah, but here it is used to deceive.

For today: do not take a miracle or something impressive as proof that something comes from God. Test everything against the teachings of Jesus and against the Bible, and ask God for wisdom so that you are not deceived.
exp.16:16:
God allowed the ten kings, represented by the horns, to share one purpose and hand their power over to the beast. The wording of this verse shows that God has placed this purpose in their hearts, so that they carry out his plan by uniting to give their kingdom to the beast. Everything happens only until the words of God are fulfilled.

An angel speaks to John, explaining the vision of the harlot and the beast. The kings will turn against the harlot and destroy her, but the angel makes clear that even this wickedness does not escape God's control. Interpreters disagree about who these kings and the city are; some think of Rome, others of a future power. What is clear is the message: God governs history.

For today: when the world seems chaotic or unjust, rest in the knowledge that God is still in control. Remain faithful and pray with confidence, because his words will be fulfilled.
exp.1:20:
God gave "that woman Jezebel" a period of time to change her course. Here "immorality" refers to sexual sin, and it may also include spiritual unfaithfulness to God. To "repent" means to change one's mind and way of living. Even with the time given, she is unwilling to do so.

Jesus, risen, speaks in his letter to the church in Thyatira. He praises their love, their service, and their endurance, but rebukes them for tolerating a false prophetess who taught people to do wrong. Calling her "Jezebel" probably recalls the queen of the Old Testament who led Israel into idolatry. We do not know her real name. Christ shows patience before acting in judgment.

Today, God's patience is not permission to keep living in sin, but an invitation to return. If you sense that God is calling you to change something, do not put it off for later. Respond today with humility and sincerity.
exp.19:14:
In the final judgment, anyone whose name was not found written in the Book of Life was thrown into the lake of fire. The Berean Standard Bible describes this as a person "found" without a name in that book, so the verse makes clear that judgment is based on whether a name is recorded there. The "lake of fire" is an image of final judgment, and it is called "the second death."

John writes this vision in Revelation to encourage Christians who were under pressure and persecution. It shows that God is just and will have the last word over evil and death. Christians interpret the fire in different ways, as literal punishment or as a symbolic image, but all agree that it means a serious separation from God.

Today, this verse invites us to trust in Christ, not in our own merits, and to live with hope and without fear. It also encourages us to share the message of salvation with others in love.
exp.16:5:
John sees a woman who appears drunk, though not on wine but on blood: the blood of the saints and the witnesses for Jesus, that is, believers who were killed for their faith. When John sees her, he is utterly amazed. He was stunned and bewildered by what he saw.

John is writing down the vision that Jesus gave him in Revelation. The woman, called "Babylon the great," represents a system of power, luxury, and wickedness that persecutes God's people. Many believe it points to Rome, while others see a broader symbol. The angel will later explain the mystery to him, so that he will not be left alone with his amazement.

For today: do not be impressed by the power or the glitter of this world. God sees those who suffer for Christ and does not forget them. Ask him for faithfulness to follow him with firmness.
exp.17:14:
The merchants who sold these things and gained their wealth from her stand at a distance, afraid of sharing her suffering. They weep and mourn because they fear what will happen to them as well.

John describes a vision of God's judgment on the great city, a city that stands for a system of power, luxury, and injustice. Many believe it points to Rome, while others see a broader symbol. The merchants are not grieving for her; they are grieving for their own lost wealth. The list just before this verse even includes the souls of men, that is, people bought and sold as slaves.

Today we can ask ourselves what we depend on more: riches or God. It is wise to work honestly and not to get rich at the expense of others, because what rests on money can vanish in a single hour.
exp.5:7:
When the fourth seal is opened, John sees a horse that is pale green, the color of a corpse. Its rider is named Death, and Hades, the place of the dead, follows close behind. They are given authority over a fourth of the earth to kill with the sword, with famine, with plague, and with the wild beasts of the earth.

John records this vision of the Lamb who opens the seals. It is the fourth of the four horsemen, and it continues what war and scarcity bring. Important: the authority was given to them, which means it has a limit. Interpreters differ on whether this is future, present, or symbolic.

For today: even when suffering and death seem out of control, they do not have the final word. You can trust that God still reigns and sets the limits.
exp.2:16:
The church of Laodicea thought of itself as rich and in need of nothing. But Jesus shows them their true condition: they were wretched (people to be pitied), pitiful, poor, blind, and naked. What they thought of themselves did not match reality.

The one speaking is Jesus, in his letter to the church of Laodicea. That city was known for its wealth, and many scholars think Jesus uses images from its surroundings, such as money, clothing, and eye medicine. He speaks to them firmly because their faith was lukewarm, but also because he loves them and calls them to change.

Today, this invites us to ask ourselves with humility: do I feel secure because of what I have or do, without realizing that I need Christ? Today you can pray: "Lord, show me the truth about my heart."
exp.13:13:
John sees a white cloud, and seated on the cloud is someone like the Son of Man. He has a golden crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand. The sickle is a curved tool for cutting grain at harvest time. "Sharp" means well honed.

John speaks here, telling what was shown to him in a vision. It comes right after the promise of rest for those who die faithful to the Lord. Then a harvest is announced, that is, a time of judgment or final gathering. Many believe this figure is Christ; others think he is an angel, because the text says "One like the Son of Man." Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: you can live with patience and hope, trusting that God has the final word and that he decides the right moment. Meanwhile, stay faithful, because your works are not lost before him.
exp.15:14:
It says Jesus will come unexpectedly, like a thief who arrives without warning. He calls happy and favored the one who stays awake and keeps his clothing on, so as not to be left naked and exposed in shame. To remain awake means to stay attentive and alert. Clothing is what covers a person.

The one speaking is Jesus, who interrupts the scene of the final judgment with a warning. Around him, deceiving spirits gather the kings for battle. Many believe the clothing represents a faithful and clean life before God, but the text does not fully explain this, and there are different interpretations.

For today: do not live distracted or put your faith off until later. Every day, seek to be ready, praying, reading the Bible, and obeying God simply, not living in fear but with hope and attention.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that Jesus Christ has made us a kingdom and priests to God, who is also his Father. In other words, he has given us a place of honor and of service before God. The word "power" in the verse means rule or authority, and "forever and ever" means that it lasts without end. The verse closes by praising Christ: to him belong the glory and the power.

The writer is John, addressing seven churches in Asia, in the region of what is today Turkey. He has just spoken of Christ's love and of how he freed us from our sins by his blood. For that reason, this praise flows out with gratitude. He then announces that Christ will come with the clouds. Scholars understand in several ways how the promise of being a "kingdom" and "priests" is fulfilled, but they all agree that it is a gift, not something earned.

For today: as a priest, you can approach God in prayer without fear. Today, thank Christ for that access and serve someone with humility.
exp.20:7:
It says that those who keep rejecting God and do not repent will have their place in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is called the second death, a permanent separation from God. The first word in the list, "cowardly," here refers to people who, out of fear, deny the faith. The "abominable" are those who do detestable things, and the "sorcerers" practice witchcraft or poisoning. The "sexually immoral" are those who live in sexual sin.

God himself is speaking, the one who sits on the throne, within the vision that John receives. Just before this, he promises the water of life freely to the thirsty and an inheritance to those who overcome. This list is the contrast: it shows how serious it is to reject that invitation. Afterward John sees the holy city, the new Jerusalem. Some understand the lake of fire literally, others as a symbol; all agree that it is very serious.

For today: if you are tired of your failures, come to Christ thirsty and sincere. His forgiveness is free, and he helps you leave behind what keeps you away from God.
exp.1:15:
It says Jesus calls the church to change direction. "Repent" means to turn around. "Soon" means in the near future, and "I will come to you" is a visit to correct. The "sword of my mouth" is his word, which judges and uncovers the truth. He will wage war "against them," those who follow those false teachings.

Here Jesus, risen, speaks to the church in Pergamum. He commends them for holding firm to the faith, but rebukes them for tolerating those who mixed faith with idolatry and immorality, as in the case of Balaam. About the Nicolaitans, it is not known with certainty who they were; we only see that their teaching was harmful.

For today: being faithful in one's personal life is not enough. If we tolerate what harms the community, Jesus calls us to address it with humility, using his word and not our own opinions.
exp.21:17:
It says that whoever hears the words of this prophecy receives a solemn warning: if anyone adds anything to them, God will send the plagues described in this book. Here the word "testify" means "warn with seriousness" or "declare solemnly." The word "add" means to put something more onto the message.

The one speaking is Jesus, who in the verses before presents himself as the root and offspring of David, and as the bright morning star. This is the closing of the book of Revelation. Many understand that the warning protects the message from being altered. Some see here a reference only to this book; others see it as a principle for all of Scripture.

For today: read the Bible with humility. Do not add your own ideas to it or bend it to what suits you; let it speak to you and correct you.
exp.6:13:
Here one of the elders asks John who the people dressed in white are. John answers humbly: "Sir, you know." Then the elder explains that they are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation, that is, out of a great distress or trial. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Their robes, which stand for their life and their cleanness before God, were made clean through what Jesus, the Lamb, has done. Being made white means they were made clean.

The one speaking is one of the elders of heaven, within John's vision. He asks the question to teach. Some believe the "great tribulation" is a specific time at the end; others believe it refers to the persecution of God's people in every age. Both views see here the faithful people of God.

For today: when you go through trials, do not trust in your own cleanness. Rest in what Christ has done for you, and keep standing firm with hope.
exp.19:12:
It says that all the dead will be handed over for judgment: those who died in the sea, and also those who were in Death and Hades. In this version, Hades refers to the place or state of the dead, not the lake of fire. Each person is judged according to their deeds.

John writes what he saw in a vision, near the end of Revelation. It is the scene of the great white throne, where God judges the dead. The books show what each one did, and the book of life decides who belongs to God. Afterward, Death and Hades are destroyed. Christians interpret some details differently.

For today: live with the confidence that God sees everything and is just. Trust in Christ, not in your own merits, and let that faith show in the way you live.
exp.7:0:
It says that when the Lamb opened the seventh seal of the scroll, there was silence in heaven for "about half an hour." The idea is that everything suddenly goes quiet. After so many voices and songs in the earlier chapters, the scene falls into a deep stillness.

John writes what he sees in his vision to encourage the churches that were suffering. The earlier seals showed judgments and sufferings, along with the worship of the redeemed. This silence makes way for the seven trumpets and for the prayers of the saints that rise before God. It is understood in several ways: as solemnity before judgment, as reverent waiting, or as God attentive to the prayers of his people. The Bible does not explain it precisely.

For today: set aside a few minutes of silence before God, without asking or speaking. Leave the noise aside, trust that He hears your prayers, and wait reverently for whatever He wants to say to you.
exp.6:7:
This verse completes the list of the twelve tribes of Israel, with twelve thousand people "sealed" from each one. To be "sealed" means to be marked as belonging to God. Here the tribe of Joseph is listed, and the list includes Manasseh, Joseph's son.

John describes what he saw in a vision. Before the final judgments, God seals his servants to protect them. Interpreters disagree: some believe they are literal Israelites; others believe they represent all of God's people. The number twelve thousand per tribe is usually understood as symbolic, a sign of completeness. Soon after, John sees a countless multitude from every nation praising the Lamb.

For today: God knows his own and cares for them one by one. If you trust in Christ, you can face difficult times with calm, because you belong to him and you are not forgotten.
exp.20:4:
He who sits on the throne says, "Behold, I am making all things new." Then he tells John to write down these words, because they are faithful and true. It is a promise of renewal made by God himself.

This is the first time in Revelation that the one on the throne speaks directly. Before this, a loud voice had announced that God would live among his people, with no more tears or death. Now God himself confirms that promise and asks John to put it in writing, to encourage believers who were suffering. Many understand this to refer to a new heaven and a new earth, though Christians discuss how exactly this will look.

For today: when pain or failure makes you think nothing will ever change, remember that God is faithful. You can bring him your weariness and wait with confidence, because his work of renewal has already begun, and he will finish it.
exp.16:3:
She was dressed in purple and scarlet, colors of wealth and royalty, and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls. But in her hand she held a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality, an image of spiritual unfaithfulness.

John recounts what an angel shows him in a vision. The woman, called "Great Babylon," represents a system of power, wealth, and seduction that draws people away from God and pursues his people. Interpreters connect her with Rome, with a worldwide system, or with other ideas; there is no single agreement.

For today: do not let yourself be deceived by what looks beautiful on the outside. Examine what is inside the cup, and seek to keep your loyalty with Christ, not with the glitter of the world.
exp.21:16:
It says that the Holy Spirit and the bride, who is the church, invite Jesus: "Come!" Whoever hears must also say "Come!" Furthermore, it invites everyone who is thirsty to come, and anyone who desires the water of life to drink freely, that is, at no cost, without paying anything.

Jesus himself has just presented himself as the bright morning star, and his angel gives this testimony to the churches. We are at the close of the book of Revelation. After speaking of judgment, the text ends with an open invitation. Many understand that the "Come!" is addressed to Christ, asking him to return, and also to the thirsty, asking them to come to him.

For today: if you feel thirst for peace, forgiveness, or meaning, do not wait to make yourself presentable first. Come to Jesus just as you are, ask him sincerely, and then invite others through your life and your words.
exp.18:6:
It calls for joy and celebration, and for giving glory to God, because the wedding of the Lamb, who is Jesus, has now arrived. The phrase "let us rejoice and be glad" is a call to great joy, and "his bride has made herself ready" means that she is now prepared. Her preparation is already complete.

Here a great multitude in heaven speaks, with a sound like rushing waters and mighty thunder. They praise God because he reigns and his justice has triumphed. Many understand the bride to represent the church, the people of God. The next verse explains that her fine linen clothing stands for the righteous deeds of the saints.

For today: live with hope and joy, not with fear. Guard your faith and your daily actions, trusting that God completes what he promises.
exp.13:5:
John sees another angel flying high in the sky, in a place where everyone can see it. The angel carries the eternal gospel, the good news from God that never changes, to announce to those who live on the earth. It is meant for every nation, tribe, tongue, and people.

John writes this vision in Revelation. Earlier he saw the faithful followers of the Lamb, and now he sees God's message going out to the whole world before the judgment. The verses that follow say this angel calls people to fear and worship God. Some see here a final opportunity to repent; others interpret it in other ways.

Today we can remember that the gospel is for all people, without exception. We can pray for those who share it in other places and, simply, speak of Jesus to someone close to us this week.
exp.3:9:
The twenty-four elders fall down before God, who sits on the throne. They worship him because he lives forever. They also take off their crowns and lay them before the throne. The word translated "fall down" describes kneeling or bowing low in reverence. The phrase "forever and ever" means without end. At the end of the verse, the elders begin to speak.

John describes a scene in heaven. The four living creatures praise God without rest, and the elders answer with worship. Who the elders are is understood in different ways: some see representatives of God's people, others see heavenly beings. Their crowns suggest honor received, and by casting them down they acknowledge that all glory belongs to God. They say so in the next verse: he created all things.

Today we can imitate the elders by recognizing that what we are and what we have comes from God. Offer him your achievements and your plans with gratitude.
exp.17:16:
In one hour, it says, such great wealth was brought to ruin. Then those who made their living from trade by sea stood watching from a distance: the shipmaster (the captain or owner of the ship), the passengers, the sailors, and everyone who depended on the sea for their livelihood. The phrase "destroyed" means wiped out and gone.

In his vision, John describes the fall of Babylon, a great city that stands as a symbol of power, luxury, and pride. Those who speak are the ones who grew rich from her. They are grieving, but more for their own lost business than for the city itself. Many believe Babylon represents Rome or a worldwide system opposed to God, and it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: wealth can disappear very quickly. Place your trust in God and not in money, and use what you have with generosity and honesty.
exp.1:28:
He who has an ear should listen carefully to what the Holy Spirit says to the churches. It does not speak of hearing with the body, but of paying attention and obeying.

Here Jesus, risen, is speaking in his letter to the church in Thyatira, the fourth of the seven letters in Revelation. Earlier in that letter he promised the faithful who overcome that they will share in his authority and receive the morning star. This final phrase appears at the close of each letter. It is an invitation to all the churches, not only to Thyatira, to take the message seriously.

Today, do not read the Bible only out of habit. Before you read, ask God to help you listen, and then write down one concrete thing you can obey this week.
exp.2:8:
Jesus says that he will bring some people from the "synagogue of Satan" to a place of submission. These are people who claim to be Jews but are not, because they are liars. They will come, bow down at the feet of the believers in Philadelphia, and come to know that Christ has loved them. The phrase "bow down at your feet" here expresses bowing in recognition, not worshiping a person.

Jesus, risen, speaks to the church in Philadelphia, a small congregation with little strength, but faithful. Some, who presented themselves as God's people, rejected it and probably accused it. Scholars do not agree on the details of who they were. The message is one of comfort: Christ defends his own.

For today: if others look down on you for being faithful to Jesus, you do not need to defend yourself with resentment. Keep his word with humility, trusting that he himself will show, in his time, who are the ones he loves.
exp.17:17:
This verse describes the sailors and sea traders who watch the smoke rising from the city as it burns. In shock and grief, they cry out: "What city was ever like this great city?" The verse says the city is on fire, and the cries are loud calls of distress.

It is the ship captains, the sailors, and everyone who made their living from sea trade who speak. They mourn because the fall of "Babylon," a symbolic name for a powerful and proud system, destroys their source of income. Interpreters connect it to Rome, to a corrupt world system, or to both. They grieve over what they are losing, not out of repentance. In the end, heaven rejoices because God brings justice.

Today we can ask ourselves where we have placed our security. Money, status, and the power of this world can vanish in a single hour. Only what is anchored in God remains firm.
exp.4:10:
John sees and hears a vast crowd of angels surrounding God's throne, along with the living creatures and the elders. Their number is described as myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, a way of saying they were too many to count.

Earlier, the elders and the living creatures sang that the Lamb is worthy to open the sealed book because he was slain, that is, given up as a sacrifice, and with his blood he redeemed people from every nation. Now the angels join the song. Many understand the Lamb to be Jesus Christ, and the passage shows that all of heaven worships him for what he has done.

For today: when you feel alone or small in your faith, remember that your praise joins an immense chorus. Take a moment today to thank Jesus for his sacrifice, unhurried and from the heart.
exp.17:9:
The kings of the earth, seeing Babylon fall, stand at a distance because they fear suffering the same punishment. From afar they cry out "Woe, woe," an expression of grief and dread. They acknowledge that the city seemed great and mighty, but her judgment came in a single hour, that is, very suddenly. Here "torment" means suffering and punishment.

John describes a vision of the fall of Babylon, a symbol of a system of power, wealth and pride that opposes God. The ones who mourn are the kings who grew rich through her. They weep over their own loss, not out of repentance. Many interpret Babylon as Rome; others see a broader symbol of all corrupt power.

For today: let us not place our security in money, power or prestige, for these can vanish quickly. Let us trust in God, whose kingdom endures, and examine which things dominate our hearts.
exp.1:0:
Jesus tells John to write a letter to the "angel" of the church in Ephesus. He introduces himself as the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands. The "lampstands" are the stands or supports where the lamps are placed.

The one speaking is the risen Christ. In Revelation 1:20 he himself explains that the stars are the "angels" of the seven churches and the lampstands are the churches. There are several interpretations of the "angel": some think it is a messenger or pastor, others a heavenly being. Christ presents himself as the one who cares for and is present in the midst of his church, before he praises and corrects Ephesus.

For today: Jesus is not far from his church, but in the midst of it, and he sustains it. You can serve with encouragement and also receive his correction with confidence, because he knows you and cares for you.
exp.18:1:
This verse says that God's judgments are true and just. He has judged the great prostitute, who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and he has avenged the blood of his servants that she had spilled. "Immorality" here speaks of unfaithfulness and moral corruption; "avenged" means that God brought about justice.

A great multitude in heaven speaks and praises God, calling out words of praise to the Lord. They celebrate that God has acted against evil. The "great prostitute" is usually understood as Babylon, an image of corrupt power opposed to God, although interpreters disagree about exactly what it refers to.

For today: when you see injustice and grow tired of waiting, remember that God sees everything and judges with justice. You can trust that he will do what is right, and you do not need to take revenge on your own.
exp.19:13:
This verse says that Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, and that this lake of fire is the second death. Hades refers to the realm of the dead, not to the lake of fire itself. In other words, death itself and the realm of the dead are destroyed.

John records a vision of the final judgment, right after the dead are judged before God. This was written to encourage Christians who were being persecuted: in the end, death will not have the last word. Some understand the language literally and others symbolically.

Today we can live with hope and without fear of death, trusting in Christ, because God promises to put an end to it. That invites us to live by faith and to speak of that hope with others.
exp.0:18:
Jesus tells John to write down three things: what he has already seen, what is now happening, and what will happen after this. The phrase "after this" points to the events that follow the present. These are the things that are going to take place.

The one speaking is the risen Christ, the first and the last, who holds the keys of death and of the grave (the place of the dead). John had fallen down as if dead from fear, and Jesus placed his hand on him, lifted him up, and calmed him. Christians understand these three parts in different ways: some see the vision, the seven churches, and the future; others see them differently. Even so, the command is clear: John must put everything in writing.

For today: if Jesus holds the keys of death, we can face the future without fear. Today, when something troubles you, repeat his word: "Do not be afraid," and entrust your day to him.
exp.21:8:
Here an angel stops John when he falls down before him. He says, "Do not do that!" The angel describes himself as a fellow servant with John, the prophets, and those who keep the words of this book. His final command is clear: worship God.

It is the angel who showed John the visions of Revelation. John, impressed by what he saw and heard, bows down to worship him. Something similar happens in Revelation 19:10. The angel corrects John to make clear that only God deserves worship, not the messengers.

For today: honor those who have taught you the faith, but do not place any person, leader, or spiritual experience in the place of God. Let all your admiration end in worshiping Him.
exp.17:10:
And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because there is no one left to buy their cargo. That is what the verse says: the merchants of the world weep and grieve over the fall of Babylon. Their sorrow is not so much for the city itself, but because no one buys their goods anymore. The word "merchants" refers to those who trade, and "cargo" refers to the goods they carry and sell.

It is part of the vision that John received about the fall of Babylon, which in this book represents a world power full of luxury, pride, and oppression. First the kings weep, and now the merchants, who had grown rich from her. Interpreters understand her in various ways: as Rome, as a future world system, or as a symbol of any culture that lives turned away from God. The list that follows ends by naming the souls of men, which shows that commerce had come to treat people as merchandise.

Today it invites us to examine where our heart is set. We can ask ourselves whether we would grieve more over losing money and comfort than over losing what is eternal. Jesus calls us to trust God and to treat every person with dignity, never as a business.
exp.12:10:
John sees a second beast coming up out of the earth. It has two horns like those of a lamb, meaning it appears gentle and harmless, but it speaks like a dragon, that is, its message is deceptive and comes from the enemy. "Like" here simply means "resembling."

John is recording the vision he received from Jesus Christ. This beast follows the first one, a power that persecutes believers. It supports the first beast and leads people to worship it. Interpreters understand it in several ways: a false religious power, the propaganda of an empire, or a future deception. The text does not fully clarify this. Earlier, the passage calls the saints to patience and faith.

For today: do not be carried away only by pleasing appearances. Test every message against the words of Jesus and the Bible, and stay firm and faithful even when what is false looks attractive.
exp.5:16:
This verse says that the great day of God's wrath and of the Lamb has arrived, and asks who is able to withstand it. "To withstand" means to stand firm against judgment without falling or hiding.

In the sixth seal, John describes people of every social rank, from kings to slaves, fleeing in terror. They recognize that they are before the throne of God and before the Lamb, who is Christ. The final question is often understood as a voice from the scene or from the text itself. Christians interpret it in various ways, but all recognize that it speaks of a real judgment. Chapter 7 gives an answer: the servants of God, sealed and washed in the blood of the Lamb.

Today we can live without fear if we trust in Christ, and at the same time with seriousness, not taking sin lightly. This week, ask him to forgive something you have let slide, and rest in his grace.
exp.15:20:
It says that a huge hail fell from heaven on the people, with stones weighing about a hundred pounds each. Some modern readers wonder what exactly is being described, but the picture is clear: these are enormous stones, far heavier than ordinary hail, and they strike with terrible force. The people are struck by this punishment, and yet they respond by cursing God. To curse here means to speak against God with hatred, and the hailstorm is described as so severe that the people's anger is directed straight at Him.

This is the end of the seven bowls of God's wrath, in a vision that John received and wrote down for the churches. The judgment falls on Babylon and on those who oppose God. There are different ways of interpreting these images: some see them as literal future events, others as symbols of God's judgment. What is clear is that the people do not repent.

For today: a heart can harden when it runs from God instead of drawing near to Him. When difficulties come, ask God for the humility to listen to Him, instead of confronting Him in anger.
exp.10:3:
It says that the two witnesses mentioned in the text are "the two olive trees" and "the two lampstands." These images represent those who serve God and give light in the world. "Standing before the Lord of the earth" means that they are in his presence, under his authority, and at his service.

John writes what Christ showed him in a vision. This image recalls Zechariah 4, where the olive tree and the lampstand speak of God sustaining his work through his Spirit. Christians have interpreted the two witnesses in several ways: as two individuals, or as the faithful Church that bears testimony. The text does not fully clarify this, so it is wise to be humble.

For today: God does not ask us to shine by our own strength. If we live close to him, his Spirit gives us the light and the courage to bear witness, even when the world rejects it.
exp.0:9:
John says that he was "in the Spirit," meaning he was under the influence and guidance of the Holy Spirit in a special way. This happened "on the Lord's day," and suddenly he heard a loud voice behind him, "like a trumpet."

The one speaking is John, who had been exiled to the island of Patmos for preaching the word of God. Many believe that "the Lord's day" is Sunday, the day of the resurrection, though some understand it as the final day of God's judgment. The voice like a trumpet announces that an important message is coming for the seven churches.

Even in difficult circumstances, such as exile or loneliness, God can speak to us. Set aside a quiet moment, especially on Sunday, to pray and to listen for his voice in the Bible, with an attentive heart.
exp.8:9:
The verse says these creatures had tails like scorpions, with stingers in them. Their power to injure people lasted five months. The stingers are the venomous points that wound.

John describes a vision that Jesus gave him. It takes place at the fifth trumpet, a judgment on the earth. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future event, others an image of spiritual forces or of evil in history. All agree that the harm has a time limit, "five months," and that the king over these creatures is the angel of the abyss.

For today: evil may seem strong and painful, but God sets limits on it. If you are going through a trial today, trust that it is not beyond God's control, and seek refuge in Him through sincere prayer.
exp.14:3:
It says that no one should fail to revere God or honor his name, because he alone is holy, that is, completely pure and set apart from everything else. Here "fear" means to respect with awe, not only to be afraid. "Glorify" means to recognize his greatness and praise him. It announces that all the nations will come to worship him, because his righteous acts have been revealed for all to see.

It speaks of the group of victors who, standing on the sea of glass, sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. This recalls the song of deliverance after crossing the Red Sea. They praise God for his justice just before the seven final plagues. Interpreters differ on how all of this will be fulfilled, but the tone is one of confidence in God.

When evil seems to be winning, praise God for who he is, and trust that he is just and will have the final word.
exp.5:9:
What it says: The souls of the martyrs cry out loudly and ask the Lord how long it will be before he judges those who live on the earth and avenges their blood. They call him "holy and true," meaning pure and faithful to his word. "Avenge" here means to bring justice for the blood that was shed.

Context: The speakers are believers who died for their faith in Jesus, seen under the altar, a place of great importance in worship. They do not ask for personal revenge, but for God to show that he is just. He gives them white robes and asks them to wait a little while, until the number of brothers and sisters who will also suffer is complete. Some interpreters see this as a symbolic picture; others read it more literally.

For today: If you suffer injustice, you can bring your pain to God honestly, without taking revenge yourself. He listens, and you can trust that his justice will come in its time.
exp.0:19:
Jesus explains to John the meaning of what he saw. The word "mystery" here means a symbol with a meaning that is now being revealed. The seven stars that Christ holds in his right hand are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven golden lampstands are the seven churches.

It is the risen Jesus who speaks, the one who lives and holds the keys of death. He has just told John to write down what he sees. The word for "angels" can also mean "messengers," and it is not certain whether these are heavenly beings or human leaders of each congregation. Both readings have been held.

For today: Christ walks among his churches and holds those who lead them. Pray for your pastor and your congregation, and remember that your community is a light that he cares for and wants to shine.
exp.9:8:
John goes up to the angel and asks for the small scroll. The angel tells him to take it and eat it. He warns that in the mouth it will be as sweet as honey, but it will make the stomach bitter. "Eat it" means take it in completely, and "stomach" is the part of the body where it turns sour.

John is recounting his vision. A voice from heaven had told him to take the open scroll from the hand of the giant angel. Eating the scroll seems to be a picture of receiving a message from God completely. It resembles what happened to the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 3). Scholars understand the scroll in different ways, but nearly all agree that it represents a message John must proclaim.

For today: the word of God can be sweet to receive, but it can also hurt when it brings hard truths or calls us to speak. Receive it whole, not only the part that pleases you.
exp.8:2:
From the smoke that rose out of the bottomless pit, locusts came down upon the earth. They were given a power like that of the scorpions of the earth, able to sting and cause pain. The phrase "were given" shows that this power came from someone else, and "power" here means authority or ability.

The speaker is John, who reports a vision he received from Jesus Christ. We are in the fifth trumpet, a series of judgments that serve as a warning to humanity. Notice that the locusts' power is "given": it has limits and does not act on its own. Interpreters differ: some see evil spiritual forces, others see a picture of historical or future calamities. The text does not fully settle the question.

For today: even when evil seems enormous and painful, God still places limits on it. You can rest in the knowledge that nothing escapes his control, and seek his protection with confidence.
exp.7:10:
The star that falls from heaven is named "Wormwood," the name of a plant with a very bitter taste. A third of the waters turned bitter like wormwood oil, and many people died from drinking the bitter waters.

John writes what he saw in a vision. The third angel sounds his trumpet, and each trumpet announces a judgment of God upon the earth. These judgments are partial, affecting a third part, and function as a warning before the end. Christians interpret this scene in different ways: some see it as literal future events, others as symbols of judgments in history.

For today: God takes sin and the suffering it causes seriously, but his warnings are also an invitation to turn back to him. Today we can ask him to show us what bitter areas there are in our heart and hand them over to him.
exp.7:7:
This verse says the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a huge mountain on fire was thrown into the sea. As a result, a third of the sea turned to blood. The phrase "turned to blood" describes the change in the water. Notice that the verse says "something like a great mountain," so this is a comparison, an image rather than a literal mountain.

John records what he sees in his vision. The seven trumpets announce judgments from God, and they come in sequence, as a serious call for humanity to recognize its sin. Christians have interpreted this in different ways: some see it as literal future events, others as symbols of judgments throughout history. Notice that the judgment is partial, "a third," not total.

For today: God is serious about evil, but his judgment also contains warning and room to repent. Today you can examine your heart honestly and return to God without delay, trusting in his mercy in Christ.
exp.19:6:
When the thousand years of Christ's reign with his people are complete, Satan will be released from the prison where he was confined. The word "complete" means "has come to an end." Here the devil does not decide: he "will be released," that is, God allows his release.

John, who received this vision from Jesus Christ, speaks here. He had just seen the faithful reigning with Christ and the promise that the second death does not touch them. Now he shows what comes next: a final rebellion, which God defeats with fire from heaven. Christians interpret these "thousand years" in different ways: literally, symbolically, or as the present age.

For today: even when evil seems strong or free, God has the last word and control over the times. We can live with peace and faithfulness, trusting that his victory is certain.
exp.20:5:
He says that God declares, "It is done." That is, his whole plan is now complete. He presents himself as the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, meaning he is the source and the goal of all things. He gives freely from the spring of the water of life to everyone who is thirsty.

The one speaking is the one seated on the throne, in John's final vision. He has just promised that he will wipe away every tear and make all things new. With these words, he confirms that his promise is certain and that the new creation is his work. Then he invites the thirsty and speaks to those who overcome.

For today: if you feel weariness, guilt, or emptiness, you do not have to earn God's favor. Come to him today in sincere prayer, with empty hands, and receive what he offers as a gift.
exp.0:8:
John presents himself as "your brother," meaning he is one more person in the faith alongside his readers. He says he shares with them three things: the tribulation (the suffering), the kingdom (life under the rule of Jesus), and the perseverance (the steadiness to keep going through hard times). He was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and his testimony about Jesus.

The speaker is John, who writes to churches that were under pressure because of their faith. Tradition says he was banished, although the text only states that he was on Patmos because of his faithfulness to Jesus. Before he receives the vision, he joins his readers as a fellow traveler, not as someone standing above them.

Today we can take from this that suffering for following Jesus does not mean God has abandoned us. If you are going through a hard season, keep your patience and seek the support of other believers, because you do not walk alone.
exp.17:8:
This verse says that the kings of the earth, who joined themselves to Babylon and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail when they see the smoke rising from her destruction. "Committed sexual immorality" is used here in a figurative sense: it means joining with her in sin and in power. "Lived in luxury" refers to pleasures and wealth.

The apostle John reports what he sees in his vision. A voice from heaven announces the judgment of Babylon, a city that symbolizes corrupt and proud power. Interpreters connect her with Rome, with a worldwide system, or with both, and not everyone agrees. The kings weep from a distance, not out of love for her, but because they lose what they gained by being at her side.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are tied to something that promises pleasure, success, or security, but opposes God. Everything that does not rest on Him comes to an end. It is wise to set our hearts on what endures.
exp.2:4:
He who overcomes will be dressed in white, like those in Sardis who have kept their clothes clean. Jesus promises that he will never erase that person's name from the Book of Life, and that he will openly declare before his Father and his angels that this person belongs to him. Here "overcomes" means "wins through," and "declare" means "openly say that they are mine."

This is Jesus, risen, speaking in his letter to the church in Sardis. That church had a reputation for being alive, but it was spiritually asleep. He calls them to wake up and turn back to him. Only a few had not soiled their clothes, that is, they had kept a faithful life. White garments often represent purity and victory. Christians interpret differently whether the Book of Life suggests that someone can lose their salvation, but the emphasis is on the security of those who persevere.

For today: don't live by appearances. Ask Jesus to wake you up and keep trusting in him sincerely, one day at a time.
exp.12:3:
They worshiped the dragon because he had given authority to the beast. They also worshiped the beast, and in amazement they said, "Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?"

John writes this vision to Christians in the churches of Asia who were under pressure because of their faith. In the book, the dragon represents God's enemy (Revelation 12:9). The beast is a terrible power that opposes God. Interpreters relate it to the Roman Empire, to political powers of every age, or to a future ruler. Its question mockingly imitates the praise given to God.

For today: do not place your trust or loyalty in any human power that seems invincible. Only God deserves our worship.
exp.19:8:
In this verse, the nations that Satan has deceived march across the broad expanse of the earth and surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Then fire comes down from heaven and consumes them. "Surrounded" means they went all the way around, and "consumed" means completely destroyed.

The one writing is John, who reports a vision he received from Jesus Christ. This takes place after the thousand years, when Satan is released and deceives the nations again. The name "Gog and Magog" is taken from Ezekiel and is understood in various ways; many see it as a symbol of the final rebellion of the nations. The passage is meant to comfort believers: evil does not have the last word.

Today we can live with peace even when there is opposition, because God watches over his people and is the one who gives the final victory. We do not need to defend ourselves with fear or violence; it is enough to trust in him and remain faithful.
exp.21:20:
This verse is the closing blessing of the book of Revelation and of the entire Christian Bible. It is a blessing: a wish that the undeserved favor of the Lord Jesus may be with all the readers. The word "saints" in the verse refers to all who belong to Christ, which includes everyone who reads it.

The one speaking is John, who received this vision while exiled, according to the book itself (1:9). Before ending, he recalled Jesus' promise, "I come quickly," and answered with a prayer: "Come, Lord Jesus." It was a letter for churches that were under pressure and needed encouragement. It ends as other letters of the New Testament do, with a blessing of grace.

Today, you can begin and end your day by asking for that grace. You do not depend only on your own strength or merits; Jesus accompanies you. In this way you can wait with peace, even in difficult times.
exp.8:12:
Here John tells us that the sixth angel sounded his trumpet. Then he heard a voice coming from the four horns of the golden altar before God, the altar of incense that stood in God's presence. The "horns" were the four projecting corners of the altar.

John is the one speaking, recounting what he sees in his vision. The first "woe" has already passed, and now the second begins.
