This voice from the altar gives the command that follows: to release four angels who are bound at the Euphrates. The golden altar is associated with the prayers of the saints (Revelation 8:3). Some see here an answer to those prayers; others interpret it in other ways. Its exact meaning is debated.

For today: even when events seem out of control, God remains on his throne and hears the prayers of his people. You can pray with confidence, knowing that nothing escapes his hand.
exp.17:19:
This verse is a call to celebrate. "Rejoice" is an invitation to be glad. It is addressed to heaven and to the saints, the apostles and prophets, that is, to God's faithful people. The reason is that God "has pronounced for you His judgment against her": he has rendered a verdict in their favor, since they had suffered mistreatment for their faith.

Here a heavenly voice calls God's people to leave Babylon and then announces its fall. The merchants and sailors weep because they lose their riches. The faithful, by contrast, rejoice because the evil that oppressed them has been judged. Interpreters disagree about what Babylon represents: Rome, a corrupt world system, or both.

Today we can trust that God sees every injustice. This lets us wait without bitterness and leave justice in his hands.
exp.20:2:
It says that God himself will live alongside human beings. The phrase "dwelling place of God" refers to the place where God lives among his people; the word "dwell" means "live." God does not stay far away: he is with them, and they are his people.

The one speaking is a loud voice that comes from the throne; the text does not say whose it is. John, the author, is seeing the vision of a new heaven and a new earth. This promise recalls when God dwelt in the midst of Israel. It is given to encourage believers, showing that in the end the relationship between God and his people will be restored. What follows speaks of God wiping away every tear.

For today: even in days of pain or loneliness, we can rest in the fact that God desires to be near us. Today you can speak to him with confidence, knowing that he has not forgotten you and that one day his presence will be complete.
exp.0:6:
He says that Jesus Christ is coming with the clouds, and that every eye will see him, including those who pierced him. All the tribes of the earth will mourn because of him. The closing words confirm that this is certain.

Here John speaks, writing from the island of Patmos to Christians who were suffering for their faith. He has just praised Christ for loving them and washing them clean with his blood. This sentence reminds them that Jesus will return in a visible way. Interpreters differ on whether the mourning comes from repentance or from fear at the judgment.

Today, this promise gives hope if we are tired or suffering. It also invites us to live with sincerity, knowing that Christ will return. Today you can pray: "Lord, help me to live ready for your coming."
exp.14:6:
One of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls. They were full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever.

John describes what he sees in his vision. The four living creatures stand beside God's throne (Revelation 4). Here one of them hands the angels the bowls they will use to pour out the final judgments. This follows the song of those who have overcome. Many understand that it shows God is holy and just against evil, although how these scenes will be fulfilled is debated.

God does not ignore injustice or the suffering of his people. We can rest in knowing that he will judge with justice, and not take revenge ourselves. Today, let us live with reverence, trusting that he lives forever and sees everything.
exp.8:14:
It says that four angels, who were ready and waiting, were released at an exact moment: "this hour and day and month and year." Their task was to kill a third of mankind. The word for "ready" in the verse means prepared or set in place. That is, they do not act on their own, but only when the appointed time arrives.

John is describing a vision. The sixth angel sounds his trumpet, and a voice comes from the golden altar, before God, commanding that these angels, who are bound at the river Euphrates, be released. Then a huge army of horsemen appears. Christians interpret this in several ways: as literal judgments, as symbols of wars, or as general warnings. There is no single position.

For today: although the world sometimes seems chaotic, this passage shows that God controls the times. We can trust Him and live with humility and repentance, without fear.
exp.10:10:
He says that, after three and a half days, God gave life back to his two dead witnesses. The breath of life from God, the same life-giving breath that God gave at creation, is what entered them. The witnesses got up onto their feet, and those who were watching them were overcome with great fear.

John writes what he sees in the vision of Revelation. The two witnesses are prophets who announced God's truth and were killed, and the world celebrated their death. Christians understand them in different ways: as real people, or as a symbol of the Church that bears witness. The message is clear: God has the final word, even when it seems that evil has won.

For today: if you are called to remain faithful to God amid mockery or rejection, do not lose heart. What the world sees as defeat, God can turn into victory. Trust that he keeps his promises.
exp.12:16:
It says that no one could buy or sell unless they had the mark—the name of the beast or the number of its name. Here the verse uses the phrase "the mark," and it describes control over people's everyday economic life.

John wrote Revelation to encourage Christians who were under pressure not to submit to the power of the empire and its worship. The second beast forces everyone to worship the first. Interpreters differ: some see Rome, others a future system. The number 666 is called the "number of a man," and its exact meaning is debated.

Today, the lesson is not to trade our faithfulness to God for economic security. Ask yourself: is there anything in my work or my business that asks me to do something dishonest so I won't lose income? Trust that God cares for you and choose integrity with courage.
exp.1:2:
It says that the church in Ephesus has endured hardships, has persevered, has worked for the sake of Jesus, and has not grown weary. The phrase "without growing weary" here means not losing heart or becoming so tired that one gives up.

The one speaking is Jesus, who walks among the seven lampstands, an image of the churches. Before correcting Ephesus, he warmly acknowledges their effort, their perseverance, and their care for the truth in the face of false apostles. Afterward he will tell them that they have left their first love. Their service was real, but what mattered most was missing: love.

For today: serve with steadiness, but examine your heart. Before you continue working for God, set aside time to be with him, thank him, and renew your love, so that your service comes from closeness to Jesus and not only from duty.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that the believers of Thyatira must keep firm in what they already have. The phrase "than to hold fast to what you have" introduces the contrast, and "hold fast" means keep it or hold on to it. "Until I come" refers to the return of Christ.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, in his letter to the church of Thyatira. Earlier he rebuked those who tolerated a false teaching, represented by a woman called Jezebel. Here he addresses the faithful group who did not follow her. He does not place a new burden on them; he only asks them to persevere. What they "have" probably includes their faith, their love, and their faithfulness to the truth, though the text does not spell this out.

For today: there is no need to invent a more complicated or impressive faith. Stay firm in what you know to be true about Christ, practice it every day, and do not let go of your trust in him, even when the atmosphere around you pushes you to give in.
exp.7:6:
It says that when the first angel sounded his trumpet, hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass.

John writes what he sees in his vision. After the seventh seal is opened, the seven trumpets announce God's judgments on the earth. This first one recalls the plague of hail and fire in Egypt (Exodus 9). Christians interpret it in different ways: some see it as literal future events, others as images of judgment throughout history.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and is not indifferent to evil. This invites us to live with humility, to repent soon, and to trust that God cares for his people, even in difficult times.
exp.7:9:
Then the third angel sounded his trumpet, and a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven. It landed on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.

John writes this vision in Revelation, where seven trumpets announce God's judgments on the earth. As with the plagues of Egypt, these are warnings meant to call people to repentance. Many Christians understand the images symbolically, others more literally, and the Bible does not fully settle the matter. The limit of "a third" shows that the judgment is serious, but it is not yet final.

For today: water is life, and here it becomes bitter. We can be thankful for what God gives us and not take the basics for granted. And if something warns us, let us return to Him with humility.
exp.2:15:
He says that Jesus rejects the one who is "lukewarm," that is, neither hot nor cold, like water that is no longer good to drink. The word "vomit" means he is about to throw it out of his mouth in disgust. It is a serious warning, not a simple scolding.

Jesus Himself speaks, the one who is the Amen, the faithful and true witness, to the church of Laodicea. It was a rich and proud city. Some scholars think the image of lukewarm water refers to its water supply, but this is understood in several ways. What is clear is that the church believed itself self-sufficient, and Jesus shows them their true poverty and offers them His help.

Today, we can ask ourselves whether our faith has become comfortable and routine. Instead of pretending that everything is fine, we can come to Jesus with honesty, ask Him for a sincere heart, and depend on Him again each day.
exp.15:15:
This verse says that demon spirits brought together the kings of the world into a place called Armageddon, a name taken from Hebrew. "Assembled" means brought together or gathered. The text does not name the exact subject of this action, but from the previous verse it is understood that these are the spirits.

John describes a vision of the sixth bowl. The demons deceive the rulers with signs to lead them into the battle of the great day of God. In the middle of this, Jesus gives a warning: "I come like a thief." About "Armageddon" there are several interpretations: a literal place (perhaps connected with Megiddo) or a symbol of the final conflict against God. It is not known with certainty.

For today: Jesus calls us to stay watchful and to guard our faith. We do not need to understand every prophetic detail to live alert, to reject deception, and to trust that God has the final word.
exp.0:12:
In the middle of seven golden lampstands, John saw someone who looked like a human being, a "Son of Man." He wore a long robe reaching down to his feet and a golden sash across his chest. The sash is a belt wrapped around the body, and the golden sash in this verse is that belt.

John is writing as an exile to the seven churches in Asia. The lampstands stand for those churches (Revelation 1:20). The figure is Jesus in his glorified state, the one who once called himself "the first and the last." The long robe and golden sash suggest dignity and authority. Many readers connect them with a priest or a king, though they are interpreted in various ways.

Jesus is not far from his people. He moves among the churches. If you feel small or tired today, remember that he is present and knows you. Seek him in prayer and in fellowship with other believers.
exp.18:3:
The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures bowed down and worshiped God, who sits on the throne. They said, "Amen," meaning "so be it," and "Hallelujah," meaning "praise the Lord."

These elders and living creatures speak here, and in John's vision they surround God's throne. Interpreters explain who they are in different ways, but all agree that they represent heavenly worship. Here they respond to the great multitude that has just celebrated God's judgment on Babylon, the great harlot. They affirm that his judgments are true and just, and that he avenged the blood of his servants.

For today: when you see injustice, do not lose hope. Trust that God is just, and respond with humility and praise, giving to him what you cannot set right yourself.
exp.19:7:
It says that when Satan is released, he will go out to deceive the nations in the corners of the earth, the farthest reaches of the world. It names them Gog and Magog and assembles them for battle. Their number is like the sand of the seashore, a crowd too great to count.

John writes Revelation to encourage believers who were suffering for their faith. Here, after the thousand years, Satan's final deception shows that he still remains an enemy of God. Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel 38 and 39, and here they seem to symbolize the nations that rebel. Christians understand the thousand years in different ways, but all agree that God wins in the end.

Today we can remember that deception is the enemy's chief weapon. For this reason it is good to read the Bible steadily, ask God for wisdom, and trust that Christ has the final victory.
exp.16:12:
These kings have one purpose: to yield their power and authority to the beast. Their agreement is a shared decision and a common plan, and their power and authority are the force they hand over.

An angel explains this vision to John. He shows him how the powers of this world join together to support a system opposed to God. Scholars interpret in several ways who these kings are, and there is no single certain answer. What is clear is that their power lasts only a short time, meaning little time, and that in the end the Lamb overcomes them.

Today we can learn not to be carried along by the crowd's current or by the power of the moment. Before we support a cause or an authority, let us ask whether it agrees with Christ. He is faithful, and his victory is certain.
exp.8:0:
When the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, John saw a star that had fallen from heaven to earth. This star was given the key to the pit of the Abyss. The Abyss is a deep and dark place, associated with forces of evil.

John is describing a vision he received, which Jesus gave him, as recorded in the book of Revelation. The trumpets announce judgments meant to warn humanity. Interpreters do not agree on who the star is: some think it is an angel, others a fallen being. The text only says that it receives a key, which means a limited and granted authority.

For today: even when evil seems to advance, nothing escapes God's control, for all power is given with limits. You can trust Him with your fears and move forward with hope.
exp.1:21:
He says that Jesus will "cast her onto a bed of sickness," that is, he will bring her down into suffering and illness. Those who "commit adultery with her," that is, those who follow her teaching and join in her sin, will "suffer great tribulation," a severe anguish. But there is an open door: if they repent of her deeds, they can avoid it.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, in his letter to the church in Thyatira. He praises their love and their service, but rebukes them for tolerating a false prophetess. "Jezebel" is probably a symbolic name, taken from the queen of the Old Testament who led Israel astray. She had already been given time to repent.

For today: God is patient, but he is not indifferent to sin. If something in your life or in your church is being tolerated even though it displeases God, do not wait any longer; repent today.
exp.18:4:
A voice came from the throne and called all of God's servants to praise him. The verse includes those who fear him, meaning those who honor and respect him, whether they are "small" or "great." The word "Praise" in this verse is the same kind of call to worship that appears in other passages of the book.

In the background is the fall of Babylon, which represents a system of wickedness and oppression. The elders and the living creatures have just worshiped God. Then a voice comes from the throne, and the text does not say with certainty who is speaking; some think it is an angel, and others think it is a voice speaking on God's behalf. The voice invites all of God's people to join in the praise, and immediately a great multitude answers.

For today: praise God without thinking that your life or your service is too small. In the midst of your simple tasks, give thanks to him out loud.
exp.17:3:
It says that a voice from heaven calls those who belong to God to come out of Babylon. The purpose is that they not share in her sins or catch any of the disasters coming upon her. The verse's word "plagues" is what the verse rendered as blows or disasters sent as judgment. The verse's phrase "share in" means taking part in something.

It is a second voice from heaven, separate from the angel who announced Babylon's fall. It is not clearly stated whose voice it is, though it calls the hearers "My people," so it speaks in God's name. Babylon represents a system of power, wealth and idolatry that seduces the nations. Scholars debate whether it points to Rome, to a future city, or to a broader symbol. The call is urgent: judgment is near.

Today, ask yourself whether there are habits, business dealings or environments in your life that draw you into living as if God did not matter. Ask him for wisdom to step away from them with humility and firmness, without ceasing to love the people involved.
exp.1:23:
Jesus speaks to the Christians of Thyatira who did not follow the false teaching of the woman called Jezebel. He tells them he will not place any further burden on them. The "so-called deep things of Satan" refers to the supposed secret teachings of that group, the things they claimed to know. A "burden" is a heavy obligation.

The one speaking is the risen Christ, in his letter to the church of Thyatira. Earlier he praised their love and their service, but he rebuked them for tolerating a false prophetess who led others into immorality and idolatry. Here he addresses the faithful remnant. Some think the "burden" refers to what is said in Acts 15:28, but this is not certain.

For today: if you are firm in the truth, you do not need to look for "special" teachings or additional requirements. Hold fast to Christ and his Word, and remain faithful with humility to the end.
exp.1:13:
Jesus tells the church in Pergamum that, although he commends them, he has a few things against them. Some among them were holding to the teaching of Balaam. According to the Old Testament, Balaam was the one who led Israel into stumbling: into eating food sacrificed to idols and into sexual immorality.

The phrase "a stumbling block" means something that trips a person up and causes them to fall, and "sexual immorality" refers to sexual sin outside the bounds God has set.

It is the risen Christ who speaks, the one with the sharp two-edged sword. He has just acknowledged the church's faithfulness in a hostile city, where Antipas was put to death. But he corrects them because they tolerated those who mixed faith with pagan practices. His correction comes from his love for them.

Today the lesson is that being faithful under pressure is not enough if we let slide what harms the purity of the church. Let us ask God for the courage to live differently, with humility and love.
exp.18:0:
John says that, after this, he heard in heaven a sound like the roar of a great multitude. They all shout "Hallelujah," which means "praise the Lord." They declare that salvation, glory and power belong to our God. The word "power" here means strength.

Those shouting are a great heavenly company, probably the redeemed and the beings of heaven, though the text gives no further detail. They praise God because, according to the verses that follow, his judgments are true and just: he has judged the great prostitute, who represents Babylon, and avenged the blood of his servants.

For today: when you see injustice or evil, do not lose hope. God sees everything and will do justice in his time. In the meantime, you can choose to praise him and trust that he has the last word.
exp.19:4:
This verse says that "the rest of the dead", meaning those who were not part of the resurrection described just before, did not come back to life until the thousand years were complete. It then calls the earlier event "the first resurrection." The phrase "come back to life" is the idea the verse conveys, meaning they did not return to life during that period.

John writes this vision in Revelation to encourage Christians who were being persecuted. He has just described the faithful who reign with Christ for a thousand years. Christians have understood these thousand years in different ways: as literal, as symbolic, or as already happening now. There is also no full agreement on whether the "first resurrection" is physical or spiritual.

For today: even when it seems that losing out for being faithful to Christ is not worth it, this passage invites perseverance, because those who belong to Him have a secure hope beyond death.
exp.5:1:
What it says: John sees a white horse. Its rider holds a bow, is given a crown, and rides out to overcome and conquer. The phrase "was given" means that he is allowed to act. The word "reddish" in the following verse means ruddy or reddish-colored, a word that does not appear in this verse, so it is not explained here.

Context: John describes a vision. Christ, the Lamb, opens the first seal of the scroll, and one of the four living creatures, with a voice like thunder, calls out for someone to come and see. Interpreters differ: some see in the rider Christ, or the gospel advancing; others see a conquering power, or a false conqueror, since the horsemen that follow bring war and famine. There is no certainty.

For today: Although the world has conquests and powers that seem to prevail, nothing escapes the control of the Lamb. Trust in Him, and do not be dazzled by those who appear to be victorious.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that the two witnesses are protected by God while they carry out their mission. If anyone wants to harm them, fire comes out of their mouths and devours their enemies. To "harm" means to injure, and the words "In this way, anyone who wants to harm them must be killed" describe how such an attack will end. Many understand the fire literally, while others see it as a symbol of the power of God's word.

Jesus gives this vision to John. The witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days (about three and a half years) dressed in sackcloth, a sign of mourning and a call to repentance. They are called "olive trees" and "lampstands," images taken from Zechariah 4. Christians disagree about who they are: specific people, the Church, or prophetic testimony in general. The text shows that their protection lasts until they finish their testimony.

God cares for those who serve him until they fulfill their calling. Today we can speak about Christ with courage and confidence, knowing that our lives are in his hands, even though we may not know how or when he will protect us.

sum.16: An angel shows John a woman called Babylon the Great, sitting on a beast. She is dressed in luxury and drunk with the blood of the saints. The angel explains the mystery: the beast and its ten kings fight against the Lamb, but he will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings. God accomplishes his purpose.
sum.1: Jesus sends messages to four churches: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira. He praises their endurance and faithfulness, but he corrects those who have lost their first love or who tolerate false teaching and immorality. He calls them to repent and promises rewards to those who overcome.
sum.11: John sees a woman in heaven about to give birth and a great dragon who wants to devour her child, but the child is taken up to God. Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, which is thrown down to the earth, and he pursues the woman and her offspring. Believers overcome by the blood of the Lamb and their testimony.
sum.15: In Revelation 16, seven angels pour out the bowls of God's wrath, and plagues come upon the earth, the sea, the rivers, the sun, and the kingdom of the beast. Instead of repenting, people curse God, and the battle of Armageddon is prepared. In the end, God says "It is done," and Babylon falls. Jesus calls people to stay awake.
sum.3: John sees a door standing open in heaven, and he is carried away in the Spirit before a throne, where God is seated, surrounded by glory, by twenty-four elders, and by four living creatures covered with eyes. They never stop saying, "Holy, holy, holy," and the elders throw their crowns down before God. It teaches that only God is worthy of worship, because he created all things.
sum.6: John sees angels holding back the winds of destruction while God's servants are marked on their foreheads: 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then he sees a countless crowd from every nation, dressed in white, praising God and the Lamb. They have come out of the great tribulation, and God will care for them and wipe away their tears.
sum.7: When the seventh seal is opened, there is silence in heaven, and the prayers of the saints rise up to God along with the incense. Then four angels blow their trumpets, and judgments come upon the earth, the sea, the waters, and the heavenly bodies. An angel announces three "woes" because of the trumpets that are still to come.
sum.4: John sees a scroll sealed with seven seals, and he weeps because no one in the whole universe is worthy to open it. Then he is shown Jesus, the Lion of Judah, who appears as a Lamb that has been slain, and Jesus takes the scroll. All of heaven and every creature praise and worship him, together with the one seated on the throne.
sum.5: In Revelation 6, the Lamb opens six seals. The first four reveal horses that bring conquest, war, famine, and death. The fifth shows the martyrs who ask for justice and are given white robes and told to wait. The sixth brings signs in the heavens and on the earth, and everyone flees before the wrath of the Lamb.
sum.0: John, exiled on the island of Patmos, receives a revelation from Jesus Christ and sends greetings to the seven churches in Asia. He sees Jesus in glory standing among seven golden lampstands. Jesus tells him not to be afraid, because He is alive, He is the first and the last, and He holds the keys of death. He instructs John to write down what he sees.
sum.14: John sees seven angels holding the last seven plagues, which will complete God's wrath. He also sees those who have conquered the beast standing beside a sea of glass, singing praises to God for his just and true deeds. Then the angels come out of the temple carrying seven golden bowls, and the temple fills with smoke from the glory of God.
sum.2: Jesus writes to three churches. To Sardis he says that it looks alive but is actually dead, and he calls it to wake up and repent. To Philadelphia he gives praise for keeping his word and promises it an open door. To Laodicea, which is lukewarm and proud, he gives a rebuke out of love and tells it that he is standing at the door and knocking.
sum.20: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city, the New Jerusalem, comes down out of heaven. God lives with his people, wipes away every tear, and makes all things new. The city shines with the glory of God and of the Lamb, and only those whose names are written in the book of life may enter.
sum.21: John sees the river of the water of life and the tree of life in the city of God, where his servants will see his face and reign in his light. Jesus promises to come soon and reward each person, and he invites the thirsty to take the water of life freely. The book ends with a warning not to add anything or take anything away, and with the prayer: "Come, Lord Jesus."
sum.17: An angel announces the fall of great Babylon, a city full of corruption, luxury, and deception. A voice from heaven calls God's people to come out of her so that they will not share in her sins. Kings, merchants, and sailors weep over her sudden ruin, but heaven rejoices because God has done justice, and the city disappears forever.
sum.9: John sees a strong and glorious angel coming down from heaven holding a little scroll that is open. Seven thunders speak, and John is told to keep what they say sealed up. The angel swears by God that the divine mystery will be fulfilled when the seventh trumpet sounds. John eats the little scroll, which is sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach, and he is commanded to prophesy again to many peoples.
sum.8: When the fifth trumpet sounds in Revelation 9, smoke rises from the abyss, and out of it come locust-like creatures that look like scorpions. They are allowed to torment for five months those people who do not have God's seal. When the sixth trumpet sounds, a huge army kills a third of mankind. Even so, the rest of the people do not repent of their idolatry or their sins.
sum.18: In heaven a great multitude praises God because he has judged the great prostitute with justice, and the wedding of the Lamb arrives, to which those who belong to him are invited. Then Jesus appears as Faithful and True, King of kings, and defeats the beast, the false prophet, and their armies.
sum.13: In Revelation 14, John sees the Lamb standing with the 144,000 who have been redeemed, following him and singing a new song. Three angels announce the eternal gospel, the fall of Babylon, and punishment for those who worship the beast. The saints are called to endure, and the earth is harvested and gathered in God's judgment.
sum.12: John sees a beast rising out of the sea that receives its power from the dragon. It is worshiped, speaks blasphemies against God, and wages war against the saints. Then he sees another beast, rising out of the earth, which deceives people with signs, requires a mark, and uses a number, 666. The text calls the saints to patience and faith.
sum.10: John receives the command to measure the temple, while two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days with great power. Then the beast kills them, and the world rejoices, but God raises them up and takes them to heaven. When the seventh trumpet sounds, it is proclaimed that the kingdoms of the world now belong to our God and to his Christ, who will reign forever.
sum.19: An angel binds Satan for a thousand years, while the faithful who were martyred reign with Christ. At the end, Satan is released, deceives the nations, and is defeated by fire from heaven, and then he is thrown into the lake of fire. After that, God judges all the dead according to their deeds, and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire.
